items.title: Melanesia as the 'White Man's Grave' for early Australian colonial administrators.
items.abstract: The White Man's Grave was a term summarising the short life expectancy of soldiers and colonial administrators sent into areas of prevalent tropical fevers such as West Africa and Melanesia in the 19th century. Three examples connected to Queensland are described to remind us of the medical risks assumed by early leaders in the development of Melanesia. Captain James Goodenough, Commodore of the Australian Station, died of tetanus in 1875 on his ship HMS Pearl 8 days after being wounded by an arrow from warriors in the Santa Cruz Islands. Sir William MacGregor survived a series of colonial postings, but his first wife died of dysentery in Fiji in 1877, and his second wife nearly died of malaria in Lagos, Nigeria, in 1899 before he became Governor of Queensland in 1909. Major General Peter Scratchley died of malaria within 4 months of becoming the first administrator of Papua in 1885. Disease mortality risks fell over time as tropical medicine improved, but these three high-ranking examples remind us of risks that were perceived to be inherent in tropical assignments in the 19th century.

items.title: "Give and You Will be Given": Provider and Family Views on Donor Human Milk Use in Ethiopia.
items.abstract: Background Donor human milk can improve outcomes for small and/or sick newborns when mother's own milk is unavailable, yet no donor milk program exists in Ethiopia. Evidence regarding perceptions of Ethiopian mothers and newborn care providers on donor milk use in routine newborn care settings is limited. Aim To explore how mothers and newborn care providers in Addis Ababa perceive the acceptability, feasibility, and educational needs related to donor human milk. Methods A qualitative descriptive study using nine focus group discussions was conducted at a tertiary hospital in Addis Ababa. Participants included mothers of infants admitted to the newborn intensive care unit, community mothers, and newborn care providers. Audio recordings were transcribed, translated, and analyzed using directed content analysis. Results We conducted nine focus group discussions with 47 participants amongst them. Four themes emerged. Participants described breastfeeding as valued and closely tied to infant health, maternal identity, and bonding. Concerns about donor human milk centered on infection risk, uncertainty about milk from outside the maternal-infant pair, and possible effects on attachment. Both mothers and providers also expressed openness to donating and using donor human milk, especially when framed as supporting newborn survival. Education, trusted screening, and pasteurization processes were viewed as essential for implementation. Conclusion Donor human milk appears acceptable for newborn care in an Ethiopian context, but successful implementation will depend on culturally responsive communication and education, clear safety systems, and approaches that respect the central importance of a mother's own milk while building trust in donor milk use.

items.title: THOR: A GPU-accelerated and MPI-parallel radiative transfer code
items.abstract: Emission and absorption line features are important diagnostics for the physics underlying extragalactic astronomy. The interpretation of observed signatures involves making comparisons against forward-modeled spectra from galaxy formation simulations as well as more simplified geometries, while including the complex scattering radiative transfer (RT) of resonant emission lines. Here, we present þor, a modern C++ RT code focused initially on resonant emission lines. þor is a high-performance, distributed-memory, multi-target code that uses the message passing interface (MPI) for parallel execution. It runs on CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators, yielding large ∼ 10-50 speed-ups compared to previous CPU-only codes. Our code supports multiple grid-based and grid-less data structures, enabling comparisons across different hydrodynamical codes as well as toy model geometries. We demonstrate its science capabilities with a number of example use cases across scales: (i) Lyman-alpha RT on simple shell-like gas distributions; (ii) Lyman-alpha RT applied to a high-resolution, high-redshift (z ∼ 6) cosmological hydrodynamical galaxy formation simulation; (iii) magnesium-II halos, namely, scattering and emission from the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of a z ≃ 1 galaxy drawn from a cosmological magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulation; (iv) the large-scale cosmic web in gas emission, a 6144^3 volume element RT scaling calculation; and (v) synthetic absorption spectra of the Lyman-alpha forest. We employed extensive verification and benchmarking to validate our approach and its computational efficiency. x

items.title: Loop quantum gravity black holes surrounded by quintessence
items.abstract: Quantum gravity corrections act on the near-horizon geometry of a black hole (BH), while dark energy acts on its asymptotic region, and how the two imprints combine is still poorly understood. We study a static, spherically symmetric BH of Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) surrounded by a quintessence field. The metric function carries the LQG parameters [Formula: see text] and the quintessence parameters [Formula: see text], and for suitable values it has three horizons, a structure found neither in pure LQG BHs nor in classical quintessence BHs. We analyze null and timelike geodesics, photon spheres and the shadow seen by a static observer placed between the event and the cosmological horizons. Sixth-order WKB quasinormal modes (QNMs) of scalar and electromagnetic fields confirm stability over the ranges examined. The quantum term behaves as a short-range repulsive correction: it shrinks the photon sphere and the shadow, raises the QNM oscillation frequency and lowers the light deflection. Quintessence works the other way on the photon sphere, the ringing frequency and the bending. With the Gauss–Bonnet method, we obtain a weak deflection angle valid for [Formula: see text], which we check against direct numerical integration, and in which quintessence dominates at large impact parameters and the LQG terms at small ones.

items.title: Photometric classification of supernovae detected by the Zwicky Transient Facility using noise augmentation
items.abstract: Modern time-domain surveys, such as the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), detect far more extragalactic transients than can be spectroscopically classified. Photometric classification offers a scalable alternative, enabling the identification of larger, fainter, and higher-redshift supernova (SN) samples suitable for applications such as Type Ia SN (SN Ia) cosmology. We present a feature-based photometric classifier for SNe detected by ZTF, with the primary goal of constructing a photometric SN Ia sample for cosmological analyses. Our approach utilises the autoencoder architecture from the model to capture the intrinsic diversity of SN light curves. We trained the model on a spectroscopically classified ZTF SN sample, incorporating a realistic redshift and augmentation procedure that simulates the flux uncertainties of fainter sources. This enables the model to generalise to noisier, higher-redshift populations. Light curve features were used to train a gradient-boosted decision tree classifier, implemented in both binary (SN Ia vs non-Ia) and multi-class configurations. We validated our classifier on independent, fainter ZTF data with and without augmentation. To evaluate real-time performance, we also applied our classifier to live ZTF alerts and conducted a spectroscopic classification survey within the ePESSTO+ collaboration. ParSNIP We found that redshift and noise augmentation significantly improves classification performance, particularly for fainter sources. Our binary classifier achieves an SN Ia recall of $(98.1 ± 0.4)%$, averaged across five train–test splits. SN Ia recall exceeds 98% for events with more than 10 detections and a peak apparent magnitude of up to 20, remaining above 96% up to a magnitude of 20.5. Overall, 95% of the sources were correctly classified in both binary and multi-class modes. In our live classification survey, we correctly identified the class for 78% of the targets, including rare events such as superluminous SNe, despite a median of only nine detections per object. Our classifier performs efficiently on real ZTF data, including faint and noisy light curves. Applied to the full ZTF transient sample, it will enable the construction of a large photometric SN Ia dataset for cosmology. It also provides a practical tool for real-time spectroscopic target prioritisation, which will be essential for large-scale surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time.

items.title: Cross-simulator transfer with foundation-model summaries: Toward robust SKA-era reionization inference
items.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) for parameter estimation is vulnerable to model misspecification: neural summaries and density estimators trained on a specific forward model typically fail when applied to data drawn from another model or from real observations, and no training simulator can capture the full observational pipeline of a real measurement exactly. We show that a self-supervised vision transformer (ViT), pretrained label-free on a fast approximate simulator, produces transferable data summaries that generalize across simulators. Without retraining, it can be reused as a frozen encoder to infer astrophysical parameters from a completely different simulator that explicitly resolves radiative transfer and on which it was never trained. As a concrete use case in 21cm cosmology, SKATR, a ViT pretrained with a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), serves as a foundation model for reionization inference from upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA) measurements: SKATR was pretrained once on 67k low-cost, noiseless semi-numerical 21cmFAST light cones, frozen, and applied to hydrodynamical Loreli II light cones, where a lightweight conditional flow matching (CFM) head infers five astrophysical parameters. The encoder is never shown Loreli data, its parameters, or any noise. In our comparison, SKATR yields the most precise and best-calibrated posteriors across all five parameters, matching the accuracy of the fully supervised in-domain baseline while requiring 2.6 fewer radiative-transfer simulations. Under realistic SKA AA* noise, only SKATR remains simultaneously accurate, informative, and calibrated, outperforming even a supervised baseline retrained from scratch on noisy data. Self-supervised pretraining on computationally efficient semi-numerical simulations is therefore a viable route to calibrated, simulator-, and noise-agnostic reionization inference for the SKA-era.

items.title: Low-Cost Visual Art in Stroke Neurorehabilitation: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Objective Each stroke survivor's path to recovery is highly individualized, often needing support and collaboration from an interdisciplinary team of experts. This scoping review aims to explore how low-cost visual art is used as an intervention in stroke neurorehabilitation beyond traditional therapy alone. Design Medline, CINAHL, Embase, Scopus, PubMed, and DOAJ databases were searched using keywords: art, art communication, art therapy, stroke, and neuroplasticity. Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer; full texts by two reviewers, with conflicts resolved by a third. 42 papers were included and mapped across three themes: communication, stroke therapy, and neuroplasticity. Results Visual art supported self-expression and patient-clinician communication, particularly for patients with language or visuospatial deficits, while art-based assessments were used to identify cognitive-perceptual impairments. Low-cost therapeutic interventions, including drawing, painting, and other group art programs, were associated with improvements in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy, social connectedness, and fine motor or speech outcomes. However, visual arts-based research directly linking to neuroplastic changes remains limited. Conclusion Visual art can be applied as low-cost and accessible interventions, although further research on the relationship between visual art, neuroplasticity, and clinical implementation is needed.

items.title: Cerebellar-Extracerebellar Relations: Editorial Overview of Current Knowledge, Open Questions, Technical Limitations, and the Where-What-How Method.
items.abstract: The cerebellum contributes to neurological function by influencing activity in other parts of the nervous system. This statement, apparently simple, underscores the inherent complexity of cerebellar neuroscience, because complex cerebellar-extracerebellar relations are central in the study of the cerebellum. To study the cerebellum means to study how the cerebellum relates to the brain, as much as studying the visual system means studying how the visual system relates to light. As far as we know, there is no direct behavioral output stemming from isolated cerebellar activity, unlike in primary motor cortex, and no cognitively accessible content stemming from isolated cerebellar activity, unlike in cerebral associative cortex. Extracerebellar relations are not extra credit for cerebellar neuroscience; they are a central element of what cerebellar neuroscience is. We discuss (i) open questions in cerebellar-extracerebellar relations; (ii) technical challenges related to these questions, with an emphasis on human research, including issues highlighted in the present special issue; and (iii) the Where-What-How method as a framework to organize the analysis of cerebellar-extracerebellar relations. An example of this framework is that right arm dysmetria can be decomposed into where function is affected (right arm, rather than left arm or right leg); what function is affected (motor function, rather than language or emotion regulation); and how function is affected (deficits in precision and coordination, rather than in speed or initiation). Open questions in the study of cerebellar-extracerebellar relations, and methodological limitations that apply to these questions, can be organized following the Where-What-How method.

items.title: Clozapine beyond schizophrenia: an umbrella systematic review of the off-label uses of clozapine in managing psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions.
items.abstract: To systematically appraise the literature for systematic reviews on the off-label uses of clozapine for psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions beyond psychotic disorders. Systematic searches of Medline, PsychInfo, CINAHL, and Cochrane Database were performed on February 8th, 2025, using the search terms "clozapine" AND "systematic review". Systematic reviews investigating clozapine as an intervention for conditions aside from schizophrenia (or related psychotic disorders) were included in this review. Risk of bias was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 assessment tool. The search yielded 571 studies after removal of duplicates, with 20 studies being suitable for systematic review. Six meta-analyses were found to meet the inclusion criteria demonstrating clozapine's efficacy in managing Parkinson's psychosis (SMD = -4.23; 95% CI = -6.53, -1.93), tardive dyskinesia (SMD = - 2.56, p = 0.02), insomnia (OR = 0.45, p < 0.01), substance use disorder (OR = 0.10, p < 0.00001), and in reducing suicidality (OR = 0.229, p < 0.0001) and mortality (RR = 0.43, 95% CI = 0.34-0.55). Additionally, systematic reviews were found meeting the inclusion criteria demonstrating that clozapine was efficacious in managing treatment-resistant bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, catatonia, psychogenic polydipsia, essential tremor, behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), neurodevelopmental disorders, violence and aggression, and aggression in children. Confidence in the quality of evidence was assessed to be high in 7, moderate in 3, low in 3, and critically low in 7 reviews. Clozapine is potentially efficacious in the off-label management of a wide range of psychiatric and neurological conditions beyond treatment-resistant schizophrenia. There is evidence justifying re-evaluation of clinical guidelines for Parkinson's psychosis.

items.title: Reducing the burden of cervical cancer in Zambia in the next 40 years: impact of enhanced screening efforts.
items.abstract: Zambia bears one of the world's highest cervical cancer burdens, driven by high human papillomavirus (HPV) prevalence, gaps in vaccination and screening, and the intersecting human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic. In this study we assess the potential impact of scaling up HPV screening alongside vaccination efforts, based on a community outreach plan designed by ICAP Columbia and Zambia's Ministry of Health. The plan targets Zambia's rural communities and promotes self-collection of samples, on-site HPV testing, and same-day treatment when eligible, with referral to hub sites for severe cases. To estimate the expanded screening's impact, we developed an individual-based model capturing HPV transmission through age-structured sexual partnership, and subsequent progression from infection to cervical lesions and cervical cancer. The model was calibrated to Zambia's demographic profile, 2022 HPV prevalence, 2020 cervical cancer incidence. We compared five 40-year scenarios: no intervention, vaccination only (girls 9-14 years); vaccination plus visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA)-based screening targeted towards women living with HIV, and scenarios extending screening to all women ( ~ 200,000 vs ~400,000 tests/year with 5% annual increase). Outcomes were cervical cancer incidence, percent reduction across intervention scenarios, and cumulative cases averted. Uncertainty was quantified via repeated stochastic simulations with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Sensitivity analyses examined alternative HIV incidence trajectories and reduced screening accessibility. By 2060, HPV vaccination alone reduces cervical cancer incidence by 47% (95% CI: 39%-55%) compared to current rates but has limited effect in the first 20 years. Adding population screening accelerates impact: under ~400,000 tests/year, incidence falls 64% (95% CI: 56%-70%) by year 20 and 97% (95% CI: 96%-98%) by year 40, averting ~35,000 cases by 2040 and ~183,000 by 2060 and reaching the World Health Organization elimination threshold by 2060. Exploratory analyses suggest additional long-term benefit from vaccinating boys, especially when vaccination coverage is suboptimal. In Zambia, vaccination alone will not meaningfully reduce cervical cancer burden in the near term, and pairing vaccination with a community-based HPV-screening/treatment could prevent tens of thousands of cancer cases within two decades and place elimination within reach.

items.title: Proceedings from the 2025 precision public health transdisciplinary conference: capacity building.
items.abstract: The 2025 Precision Public Health Transdisciplinary Conference brought together over 150 attendees from five continents to discuss innovative research and advances in precision health and promote sharing of insights, with an emphasis on capacity-building in different contexts of precision public health, including non-Western settings and settings with constrained resources. The conference was hosted by the Precision Public Health Network and held virtually on 19-20 November 2025, featuring 11 invited speakers with expertise across key areas of precision public health and genomic medicine, and 20 oral and poster presentations selected from submitted abstracts. This report summarises the conference proceedings and key emerging themes, including the need to strengthen capacity through robust, inclusive data systems that reflect population diversity; meaningful community involvement in genomic medicine; integration of clinical, genomic and national health datasets; and evidence-based incorporation of innovative tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) to support analysis and decision‑making.

items.title: Surveillance of selected infectious agents in captive felids from Polish zoological gardens - preliminary study.
items.abstract: Infectious diseases threaten the health and welfare of captive nondomestic felids, yet data on the occurrence of infectious agents in zoological collections remain limited. The aim of this study was to investigate the exposure to selected feline viral pathogens together with Toxoplasma gondii in captive white lion, Amur (Siberian) tiger, white Bengal tiger, Eurasian lynx, cheetah, and sand cat maintained in two Polish zoological gardens using molecular and serological methods. Serum samples and nasal swabs were collected for analysis. Serological testing was performed for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), feline leukemia virus (FeLV), and T. gondii, while real-time PCR assays were used to detect feline calicivirus (FCV), feline herpesvirus type 1 (FHV-1), feline leukemia virus (FeLV), and feline coronavirus (FCoV). Nasal swabs were also used for conventional bacteriological examinations. Feline calicivirus RNA was detected in nasal swabs from one white lion and white Bengal tiger, whereas all tested animals were negative for FHV-1, FCoV, and FeLV by real-time PCR. Serological analysis revealed: (i) no evidence of FIV infection; (ii) antibodies against T. gondii in two animals; and (iii) FeLV seropositivity in one white lion despite a negative PCR result. Staphylococcus aureus and Acinetobacter beijerinckii were detected in the sample of white Bengal tiger, as well as Staphylococcus haemolyticus and Psychrobacter maritimus cultured in the sample of white lion. These isolates were distinguished by their low resistance to antimicrobials: : ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, cephalothin, tetracycline and oxytetracycline (A. beijerinckii), clindamycin (S. aureus), as well as streptomycin (P. maritimus). These findings contribute to knowledge of infectious diseases in zoo-housed felids in Central Europe and highlight integrated molecular and serological surveillance for health monitoring and disease management in zoological collections.

items.title: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies in Latin America: clinical diversity, diagnostic challenges, and unmet needs.
items.abstract: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are a heterogeneous group of rare, systemic autoimmune diseases that remain understudied in Latin America despite the region's ethnic admixture, socioeconomic heterogeneity, and unequal access to rheumatologic care. This narrative review synthesizes the literature on IIM from Latin American centers, integrating single- and multicenter cohorts, national registries, and collaborative networks. Dermatomyositis is the most frequently reported subtype in most national series, although this may partly reflect differences in patient selection and classification, and regional autoantibody profiles show distinctive features, including a high frequency of anti-Mi-2 in Mexican cohorts and among Colombian patients in a multinational survey and emerging data on anti-MDA5-associated dermatomyositis in Latin American cohorts that diverge phenotypically from Asian cohorts. Anti-synthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis, and juvenile dermatomyositis are characterized mainly through Brazilian series, complemented by Argentine data and multinational collaborations, alongside multicenter data on myositis-associated interstitial lung disease from Argentina, Chile, and Mexico. The COVID-19 pandemic further complicated regional care, prompting pharmacovigilance and vaccine-safety collaborations, including a Brazilian interventional trial of an inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. We highlight neglected dimensions of regional IIM care, including reproductive health. Persistent obstacles include diagnostic delay, restricted access to myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibody panels, heterogeneous availability of muscle MRI and biopsy, and inequitable access to immunosuppressive and biologic therapies across public and private health systems. We highlight priority actions, including expansion of multinational registries, harmonization of diagnostic algorithms, and investment in translational research reflecting the admixed ancestry of Latin American populations, which may help reduce diagnostic delay and improve long-term outcomes.

items.title: Profiling antibiotic resistance genes, virulence factors, and carbohydrate-active enzymes using metagenomics: implications for Plateau Wetland ecological health.
items.abstract: This study employs metagenomic analysis to systematically characterize the diversity and abundance of CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs in water and soil samples collected from the Napahai Plateau Wetland. Significant differences in α-diversity were observed across the sample types, with VFs exhibiting the most pronounced variation. PCoA revealed distinct clustering of water and soil samples based on the abundance profiles of ARGs and VFs, whereas CAZymes displayed relatively uniform distribution across both environments. Among CAZymes, GH and GT were the most prevalent, with PL and AA enriched in water, and CBM and GH more abundant in soil. ARGs associated with aminoglycoside and sulfonamide resistance were more prevalent in water, whereas soil samples exhibited a higher abundance of genes such as acrR and vanI. Additionally, VFs related to exotoxins and motility were significantly more abundant in aquatic environments, indicating a potentially heightened pathogenic potential in these settings. Environmental variables, including pH, TN, TP, and metal ions (Zn, Mg), were significantly correlated with CAZymes and VFs abundance. For ARGs, these correlations are likely indirect and mediated by shifts in microbial community composition and abundance. Notably, a positive correlation among CAZymes, ARGs, and VFs suggested their co-enrichment, likely driven by microbial adaptation to ecological stressors such as antibiotic pollution. These findings highlight the critical role of plateau wetlands as reservoirs and potential dissemination hubs for antibiotic resistance and microbial virulence, with important implications for ecosystem health and public health surveillance amidst global environmental change.

items.title: A hypothesis-generating integration of single-cell and bulk transcriptomics nominates SPP1-CD44 innate-adaptive crosstalk in ocular hypertension.
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation accompanies retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss in glaucoma, but the immune states elicited by intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation and the crosstalk among them remain incompletely characterized. We performed a hypothesis-generating re-analysis integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomes from four public cohorts. Among 30,063 CD45 + immune cells from the microbead ocular hypertension (OHT) model (GSE293358), the retinal homeostatic-microglia compartment was relatively depleted under OHT. In contrast, MHCII+ macrophage/APC and lymphocyte compartments, including γδ T, NK, and T cells, were relatively expanded, whereas DAM-like microglia showed a non-significant upward trend. These changes reflect composition within the CD45 + fraction and should not be interpreted as absolute changes in cell number. Diffusion pseudotime organized microglia along an inferred homeostatic→DAM→interferon/MHCII transcriptional continuum, with module scores showing directional concordance in an independent bulk time-course cohort (retina DAM Δ=+1.00, nominal p = 0.044; two pooled libraries per group, exploratory). In sorted Müller glia, expression of the microglia-restraining ligand Cx3cl1 was markedly reduced (log2FC = - 5.30; nominal p = 0.010, with no gene passing FDR correction in this n = 3-per-group cohort). Cell-cell communication inference further predicted an OHT-associated SPP1→CD44 ligand-receptor interaction from activated myeloid cells to lymphocytes. Together, these findings nominate candidate hypotheses involving immune-state reorganization and ligand-receptor signaling in OHT; we present them as parallel, compartmentalized responses and do not claim a validated causal cascade. Exploratory Mendelian randomization and compound-reversal analyses (Figs. S1 and S2 in Online Resource 1) did not provide definitive causal or therapeutic evidence. All proposed mechanisms are inferred from transcriptomic data and require protein-level, spatial, and functional validation.

items.title: FAP-targeted 211 At radiotherapy remodels the tumor microenvironment and is associated with enhanced anti-PD-L1 efficacy.
items.abstract: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP)‑positive cancer‑associated fibroblasts contribute to immune exclusion and resistance to checkpoint blockade in the tumor microenvironment (TME). This study evaluated whether 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, a FAP‑targeted alpha‑emitting radiopharmaceutical, could remodel the TME and enhance responsiveness to PD-L1 blockade. Given the complex and immune-excluded microenvironment of lung cancer, we analyzed public datasets to define the clinical and immune context of FAP in this malignancy. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr was synthesized and characterized for radiochemical purity, stability, FAP‑specific uptake, DNA damage, and PD‑L1 induction. Biodistribution, PET/CT imaging, therapeutic efficacy, histology, immune remodeling, and systemic cytokine profiles (MSD platform) were assessed in LLC/3T3‑FAP tumor‑bearing mice treated with saline, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr, TPP-1 (a PD-L1-blocking peptide), or combination. FAP was enriched in stromal regions and correlated with advanced stage, reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and immunosuppressive signatures. 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr showed > 95% radiochemical purity, FAP‑dependent uptake, induced γ‑H2AX foci, and upregulated PD‑L1 in vitro. Tumor uptake peaked at 5.63 ± 0.72%ID/g (1 h) and remained 4.53 ± 2.13%ID/g at 24 h. Combination therapy exhibited the most potent tumor growth inhibition, reduced 18F‑FDG uptake, increased PD-L1-specific 68​Ga-TPP-1 uptake, decreased proliferation and angiogenesis, and enhanced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. At the immunological level, MSD‑based cytokine analysis revealed that combination therapy induced more extensive alterations in systemic immune modulation than either monotherapy, whereas 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr alone shifted the profile toward pro‑inflammation. No overt organ histopathology or sustained body-weight loss was observed during the assessment period (8 days), while treatment-associated haematological changes (reduced WBC and RBC counts) were detected. In the engineered LLC/3T3-FAP model, 211At-FAP-2286-Tyr selectively targets FAP-rich tumor stroma, induces DNA damage and adaptive PD-L1 upregulation, and is associated with a shift of the immune-excluded TME toward a state that is more responsive to PD-L1 blockade. These findings suggest that FAP-targeted alpha radiotherapy may be a promising strategy for TME remodeling and immunotherapy sensitization in preclinical NSCLC models, and support further investigation toward clinical translation in more physiologically relevant systems.

items.title: Clinical characteristics, genetics, and long-term outcomes in children with very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease: a Turkish cohort.
items.abstract: Very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease (VEO-IBD) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity, a higher prevalence of monogenic disease, and an increased risk of an aggressive disease course. We evaluated clinical, genetic, and nutritional profiles and long-term outcomes in VEO-IBD and identified predictors of disease severity. This retrospective longitudinal cohort study included 49 children with VEO-IBD followed at a tertiary center between 2015 and 2025. Patients were stratified into infantile-onset (< 2 years) and non-infantile-onset (2-5 years) groups to compare clinical characteristics, nutritional status, biologic-free survival, and predictors of aggressive disease. Median age at diagnosis was 3.25 years (median follow-up: 56.6 months); 57.1% had ulcerative colitis, 32.7% Crohn disease, and 10.2% IBD-unclassified. Genetic testing was performed in 57.1% of patients and identified monogenic disease in 21.4% of those tested. Infantile-onset patients had higher rates of identifiable genetic variants (88.9% vs. 47.4%, p = 0.049) and baseline stunting (33.3% vs. 5.6%, p = 0.047). Biologic-free survival did not differ by onset age (p = 0.719). Crohn disease (OR 11.82, 95% CI 1.32-106.22) and moderate-to-severe baseline disease activity (OR 21.55, 95% CI 2.29-202.70) independently predicted an aggressive course, whereas age at onset and monogenic disease were not independent predictors of an aggressive disease course. Infantile-onset VEO-IBD was associated with more genetic abnormalities and baseline stunting. These findings support early molecular genetic evaluation in infants. Long-term disease severity was primarily determined by disease phenotype and baseline disease activity rather than age at onset or monogenic disease. • Very early-onset inflammatory bowel disease is characterized by marked clinical and genetic heterogeneity. • Monogenic disease is more frequently identified in children with very early disease onset. • Infantile-onset VEO-IBD was associated with a higher frequency of stunting at diagnosis. • Disease phenotype and baseline disease activity, rather than age at onset or monogenic disease, independently predicted an aggressive disease course.

items.title: Consumers' perceptions of environmental sustainability labelling and dual front-of-pack labelling on packaged foods: an exploratory qualitative study.
items.abstract: Little is known about how consumers understand the concept of food sustainability and how they process combinations of nutrition and sustainability information provided on food products. This study aimed to explore consumers' awareness and perceptions of sustainability information on food packaging, the importance they place on sustainability in food choices and their suggestions for implementing dual labelling systems that provide both nutrition and sustainability information. Qualitative study using focus group discussions analysed through thematic analysis. Twelve online focus groups were conducted with participants from three Australian states: New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland. (n 112) discussed their perceptions of sustainability labelling and appropriate methods of displaying dual labelling on food packages. Three key themes emerged: (i) low salience of sustainability during food purchase decisions; (ii) barriers to sustainability label use were scepticism, misinterpretation, and lack of trust due to label proliferation and lack of standardisation; and (iii) suggested approaches to labelling included the introduction of evidence-based sustainability labels endorsed by trusted organisations presented in simplified formats, with nutrition and sustainability information displayed separately. Participants reported limited engagement with sustainability labelling, often prioritising cost and healthiness. Trust and comprehension issues were commonly cited as barriers to label effectiveness. Participants viewed clear, credible and standardised labelling, presented separately from nutrition information, as potentially useful for improving consumer understanding and use of sustainability information on packaged foods.

items.title: Association Between Social Isolation and Stroke Risk among Survivors Following the Great East Japan Earthquake: A Prospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Evidence linking social isolation (SI) with incident stroke remains limited, especially regarding post-disaster populations and potential sex-based differences. We examined sex-based differences in the association between SI and incident stroke among Great East Japan Earthquake (GEJE) survivors. This prospective cohort study included 27,379 GEJE survivors. SI was assessed at baseline using the Lubben Social Network Scale. Incident stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic) was identified using the population-based Iwate Stroke Registry. Three sequential, sex-stratified Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for age, BMI, systolic blood pressure, HbA1c, LDL, HDL, estimated glomerular filtration rate, drinking and smoking status, exercise habit, marital status, living arrangement, educational attainment, employment status, psychological distress (K6), and housing damage. 208 men and 156 women developed stroke during follow-up (mean follow-up: 5.99 years). SI was significantly associated with an increased risk of stroke in men (HR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.06-1.92), but not in women (HR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.62-1.40; p for interaction = 0.005). The association was observed mainly for ischemic stroke in men (HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.07-2.12). Subgroup analyses by housing damage showed a stronger association among men without direct housing damage than among men with housing damage (adjusted HR, 1.48; 95% CI, 1.02-1.90 vs. 1.19; 95% CI, 0.68-1.91). In post-disaster populations, SI is significantly associated with incident stroke in men but not women. Socially isolated men in disaster-affected areas represent a priority group for public health interventions to reduce stroke risk.

items.title: Towards a Physiologically Rigorous Heartbeat Dynamics Foundation Model
items.abstract: Capturing long-range heartbeat dynamics accurately from wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings is a key challenge in personalized healthcare and autonomic neuroscience. Although classical methods are physiologically grounded and statistically rigorous, they cannot learn across population data and therefore cannot scale. Time series foundation models, on the other hand, can scale, but fail to capture physiologically meaningful beat-to-beat dynamics. We present, to our knowledge, the first probabilistic foundation model of heartbeat dynamics: a density-based neural temporal point process (NTPP) pretrained on RR-interval sequences from 11,226 subjects across five public datasets spanning normal sinus rhythm, arrhythmia, atrial fibrillation, and ischemia. We establish a physiological scaling law in this domain, showing that held-out metrics improve predictably with cohort size. We additionally show that scaling behavior in stochastic output domains like physiology should be evaluated by distributional calibration metrics (KS distance, goodness-of-fit) rather than point-error (MAE, RMSE), because point errors approach their irreducible floor while distributional properties continue to improve. Our pretrained model transfers zero-shot to a held-out ambulatory dataset, reaching 94.7% goodness-of-fit with no subject-specific data. In 5-minute autoregressive simulation, the model remains calibrated (87-88% goodness-of-fit) and generates trajectories with real physiological variability. Finally, we show that the learned representations are physiologically interpretable. The recurrent history embeddings separate normal and arrhythmia windows in held-out test subjects with a balanced accuracy of 95.7%. The lognormal mixture distributions show that arrhythmia subjects differ mainly in predictive spread (3.5x larger standard deviation than normal cohort), with only a small shift toward shorter mean RR than the normal group (0.79 vs. 0.86s). These results establish population-scale pretraining as a foundation for physiologically grounded modeling and simulation of heartbeat dynamics.

items.title: EEG morphology and peri-ictal MRI abnormalities in status epilepticus and ictal-interictal continuum.
items.abstract: Objective Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency that may have long-term consequences. Peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (PMAs) may serve as marker of potential acute ictal brain injury and can be used for estimating the risk of SE-defining electroencephalography (EEG) patterns. We hypothesized that excitatory-predominant EEG morphologies reflect higher metabolic demand and a greater likelihood of PMAs than inhibitory-predominant morphologies. Methods In this single-center prospective cohort (February 2019-April 2025), we included patients who had either SE or ictal-interictal continuum (IIC) reported on EEG and underwent acute magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (≤48 h). Excitatory-predominant morphology was defined by a sharp-wave amplitude greater than those of the positive and slow wave, a broad sharp wave (>200 ms), or superimposed fast activity. Inhibitory-predominant morphology was defined by the positive or slow-wave amplitude greater than that of a sharp wave. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between EEG morphology and PMAs on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho assessed correlations between the number of excitatory features (0-2) and MRI sequences showing PMAs (none, arterial spin labeling [ASL] hyperperfusion only, or DWI/FLAIR). Results Among 205 included patients (134 IIC, 71 SE), excitatory-predominant patterns and lateralized periodic discharges were associated with increased risk of DWI/FLAIR PMAs (p = .001 and p = .02, respectively). In IIC patients, excitatory-predominant morphology was the only predictor of PMAs (p = .002). In the subset with ASL, DWI, and FLAIR sequences (n = 145), the number of excitatory features correlated strongly with types of sequences affected by PMAs (Kendall's tau p Significance Excitatory-predominant morphology, as opposed to inhibitory-predominant patterns, was associated with a more frequent occurrence of PMAs. These findings support an EEG morphology framework based on excitatory-inhibitory balance across IIC and SE.

items.title: Hippocampal representations differentiate reactive and anticipatory responses during foraging under threat.
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior under threat requires balancing reward pursuit against the risk of harm. During approach-avoidance conflict, animals often pause at decision points, but whether these pauses reflect a unified process or distinct decision states remains unclear. Here, we replicate and extend findings from Calvin et al., 2025, by analyzing hippocampal activity in rats performing a pseudo-predator foraging task across two cohorts. We compared mid-track aborts (MTAs), mid-track continues (MTCs), and retreats. Behaviorally, MTAs and MTCs emerged from a shared pause state but diverged in outcome, whereas retreats reflected rapid escape following attack. Despite similar endpoints, retreats and MTAs differed in movement dynamics and neural activity. During retreats, hippocampal representations remained biased toward the attack location. In contrast, representations during MTAs shifted toward safe locations. During pauses, representations differed according to subsequent behavior: pauses preceding MTAs showed greater decoded probability near the attack region, whereas pauses preceding MTCs showed greater decoded probability to goal locations. These differences were present during the outbound approach, suggesting decision-related processes emerged early on in the journey. Together, these findings dissociate hippocampal representations associated with reactive escape from those underlying anticipatory, anxiety-like decision-making, suggesting that the hippocampus dynamically tracks behaviorally relevant features to guide decisions under threat.

items.title: Estrogen alleviates noise-induced hearing loss by regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamic balance in pericytes of the cochlear stria via GPER/PGC-1α pathway.
items.abstract: Objective Estrogen protects against noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) by ameliorating hair cell loss in noise-exposed (NE) rodents. However, whether the cochlear stria vascularis (SV) is involved in this function and the mechanism remains unclear. Methods The hearing thresholds of mice were determined by ABR. HE and EB staining were respectively used to observe the morphology of SV and the permeability of the blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB). Immunofluorescence staining and WB were performed to detect protein expression. TEM was utilized to assess mitochondrial integrity. DCFH-DA, MitoSOX™-Red and JC-1 probes were used to detect ROS content, superoxide levels and mitochondrial membrane potential. Results Estrogen reduced oxidative stress levels in SV of NE mice, alleviated BLB leakage and SV atrophy. Activation of the G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPER) by G1 increased TOM20 and mtDNA copy number, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis-related proteins (PGC-1α, NRF1, and TFAM) and the mitochondrial fusion protein MFN1, and downregulated the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1, which improved mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics and further protected the mitochondria in the SV pericytes by NE . Pharmacological inhibition or gene knockdown of PGC-1α eliminated the effect of G1 in the pericytes. Conclusion Estrogen alleviates NIHL by regulating mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamic balance in the SV pericytes via the GPER/PGC-1α pathway.

items.title: Postpartum Mice Exposed to (Pre)eclampsia-like Conditions During Pregnancy Have Altered Electron Transport Chain Activity Linked to Mild Spatial Navigation and Prefrontal Cortex Hypoperfusion.
items.abstract: Women with a history of preeclampsia (PE) and eclampsia are at increased risk for long-term neurological complications, including vascular dementia. Although placental mitochondrial dysfunction is well documented in PE, the lasting impact of PE and pregnancy-associated seizures on maternal brain bioenergetics remains unclear. This study investigated whether exposure to placental hypoperfusion and seizures during pregnancy alters spatial learning, cerebral perfusion, and mitochondrial respiratory function in the postpartum brain. Timed-pregnant C57BL/6 mice underwent sham or reduced uteroplacental perfusion pressure (RUPP) surgery on gestational day 13.5 and received either pentylenetetrazol (PTZ, 40 mg/kg) or no injection on gestational day 18.5. At two months postpartum, spatial navigation was assessed using the Barnes maze. Cerebral perfusion was measured using laser speckle imaging. Mitochondrial electron transport chain complex activities, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, aconitase activity, and mitochondrial quality-control markers were evaluated in anterior brain tissue. Mice exposed to RUPP, PTZ, or both demonstrated greater reliance on indirect search strategies during Barnes maze acquisition, suggesting subtle impairments in spatial learning. PTZ increased complex I activity, whereas combined RUPP+PTZ exposure attenuated this response and was associated with elevated complex III and IV activities. No differences were observed in complex II activity, ROS production, aconitase activity, or PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)-mediated mitochondrial quality-control signaling. Additionally, mice exposed to RUPP+PTZ exhibited reduced prefrontal cortical perfusion and alterations in nitric oxide bioavailability. Thus, exposure to RUPP and pregnancy-associated seizures induces cerebral hypoperfusion, abnormal mitochondrial respiration, and less efficient navigation strategies, potentially contributing to later-life neurovascular dysfunction following PE/E.

items.title: Limbic circuit alterations in bipolar disorder.
items.abstract: Introduction This study investigated the spatial and temporal pattern of brain white matter (WM) alterations and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in bipolar disorder (BD). Methods Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 67 BD patients (during manic, depressive, or euthymic phases) and 125 healthy controls (HC) at baseline, and from a subsample of 33 BD patients (in a different illness phase) and 23 HC after follow-up. Analyses of diffusion MRI and resting-state functional MRI were performed to characterise fixel-based metrics in WM and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in BD and HC, as well as across timepoints. Results BD exhibited a spatial pattern of WM alterations characterised by reductions in fibre density and/or bundle cross-section involving fornix and cingulum (major limbic pathways), alongside portions of other tracts, compared with HC. Reduced fibre density in the fornix was associated with intrinsic activity changes involving midbrain, thalamus, and connected fronto-temporal cortical areas within the default-mode network in BD. These alterations showed no significant changes over time or across illness phases. Conclusions These findings converge on limbic circuit alterations and suggest a relationship between structural abnormalities of the fornix and functional changes in intrinsic brain architecture in BD.

items.title: Beyond the hype: Exploring online health information on coconut oil consumption in a global perspective.
items.abstract: Objective Online nutrition information substantially influences dietary behaviors. Despite evidence of coconut oil's unfavorable health effects, the accuracy of online content remain uncertain, particularly concerning cardiometabolic outcomes. We aim to analyze the quality and accuracy of online information regarding coconut oil's effect on cardiometabolic health. Design Structured Google searches for "coconut oil and health" assessed web pages' position toward coconut oil consumption (encouraging, discouraging, neutral) and claimed cardiometabolic benefits. Websites were independently reviewed to evaluate cardiometabolic outcomes (e.g., lipid profile, weight change, glycemic control) in two separate search rounds. Setting Websites from six countries (Australia, Brazil, India, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Participants A total of 976 webpages discussing coconut oil consumption as food or supplement. Results Among assessed pages, 59.5% encouraged coconut oil intake, 25.3% discouraged it and 15.2% were neutral. Among pages expressing a clear position, lipid profile improvement (60.7% in first search and 34.9% in the total) and weight loss (60.2% and 45.5%) were the most frequently cited benefits. Citing official health entities' positions was associated with a lower likelihood of promoting consumption (PR=0.245, 95% CI 0.183-0.329, p Conclusions This study highlights the inaccuracy of online information about coconut oil and reveals structural vulnerabilities in digital nutrition communication, underscoring the need to improve information quality and strengthen infodemiological surveillance.

items.title: Developmental axon diameter growth in the absence of central nervous system myelination.
items.abstract: Appropriate axon diameters are crucial for establishing conduction speeds that support neural circuit function, yet regulation of axon diameter remains poorly understood despite over 100-fold variation across neurons. In the CNS, large-calibre axons are myelinated, and axon diameter changes following demyelination or disruption of myelin-associated proteins suggest a role for myelin in regulating axon diameter; however, whether these changes reflect a developmental requirement for myelin in establishing axon diameter or a secondary pathology remains unclear. Here, we examined developmental axon diameter growth in the absence of myelination across zebrafish CNS neurons with axons that grow to distinct diameters. We find no difference in the initial establishment of diameters for Mauthner (∼4.0 μm), MiM1 (∼1.3 μm) and CoPA (∼0.8 μm) axons with and without myelin; however, CoPA axons exhibited subtle differences during later diameter refinement. In mice, optic nerve axons in unmyelinated postnatal day 14 Myrffl/fl;Olig2cre mutants and postnatal day 75 Mbpshi/shi mice lacking compact myelin also achieved normal and diverse (∼9-fold range) diameters. Together, these findings show that developmental diameter growth of many CNS axons occurs largely independently of myelination.

items.title: Modulating cognitive reappraisal and hedonic capacity to alleviate depressive symptoms: A randomized controlled fNIRS-based neurofeedback intervention study.
items.abstract: Background Depression imposes a significant global health burden, with traditional interventions often limited by accessibility and sustained efficacy. This study investigated the efficacy and mechanisms of functional near-infrared spectroscopy neurofeedback training (fNIRS-NFT) in alleviating depressive symptoms. Methods A total of 88 participants were involved in the study (data collected November 2022-June 2024), with 59 completing a one-week fNIRS-NFT protocol targeting right lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) activity across 11 sessions, while the remaining 29 served as a no-intervention control group. Based on their neural trajectories across training sessions, participants receiving fNIRS-NFT were further stratified into high-improvement (HI, n = 37) and low-improvement (LI, n = 22) groups. Clinical and behavioral outcomes were assessed at baseline, with depressive symptoms (i.e. BDI score) reassessed at a three-month follow-up. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we employed mediation analyses, change-based Spearman's correlation analysis (CSCA), and representational similarity analysis (RSA). Results fNIRS-NFT significantly reduced depressive symptoms only in the HI group with effects sustained for three months. Mediation analyses within the HI group revealed that fNIRS-NFT enhanced cognitive reappraisal, which in turn increased hedonic capacity, sequentially reducing depressive symptoms. CSCA and RSA confirmed that fNIRS-NFT-induced LPFC activity changes correlated with improvements in hedonic capacity and cognitive reappraisal. Conclusions The study identifies hedonic drive and cognitive reappraisal as key mechanisms underlying the sustained antidepressant effects of fNIRS-NFT, underscoring its potential as a scalable, noninvasive intervention for depression.

items.title: Hybridization chain reaction variants with enhanced sensitivity for detecting challenging mRNA targets.
items.abstract: Compared to traditional enzyme-based in situ amplification methods, Hybridization Chain Reaction v3.0 (HCR v3.0) offers high specificity for spatial RNA visualization but lacks the sensitivity required to robustly detect short or low-abundance targets, particularly in thick tissue with high autofluorescence. Here, we describe three HCR variants that combine the specificity of HCR v3.0 with additional signal amplification through catalytic reporter deposition (HCR-Cat), immunostaining (HCR-Immuno), or iterative HCR and immunodetection (HCR-Multi). These methods substantially enhance detection sensitivity, enabling robust spatial visualization of low-abundance transcripts, improved performance in challenging tissue environments, and compatibility with fluorescence- and alkaline phosphatase-based chromogenic detection. These methods enable transcript-resolution imaging, even when using a limited number of probes, thereby expanding the range of biological applications accessible to HCR.

items.title: Longitudinal trajectories of plasma biomarkers, amyloid-β burden and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.
items.abstract: Plasma p-tau217 biomarkers support Alzheimer's diagnosis but most evidence remains cross-sectional. Understanding how these biomarkers change over time, whether assays perform similarly, and how such changes relate to Aβ plaque accumulation and cognitive decline is needed to guide patient care. We analyzed 393 cognitively unimpaired and impaired participants from the ADNI-FNIH consortium (mean age 72.7 years; 49% female; 37% Aβ-PET positive) with longitudinal plasma biomarkers across 14 assays, Aβ-PET and cognitive assessments over a mean follow-up of 5.4 years. Plasma p-tau217 was measured across five assays, and Aβ42/40, p-tau181, GFAP and NfL were examined in secondary analyses. Linear mixed-effects models estimated individual rates of change for plasma biomarkers, Aβ-PET Centiloids, and cognitive performance. Linear regressions related concurrent rates of change in plasma biomarkers, Centiloids and cognition in the whole group, by Aβ-PET status, and by Aβ and tau (AT) PET status in a subsample of 272 participants. For comparison, analogous cross-sectional analyses examined associations between plasma biomarker levels and baseline Centiloids or cognitive performance. Finally, semipartial R² values were calculated across all models to quantify the relative variance explained by plasma biomarker and other covariates. Plasma p-tau217 levels increased across all five assays (standardized β = 0.06-0.08, P < 0.001), whereas Aβ42/40 was largely stable. Among Aβ-PET negative individuals, greater p-tau217 increases were consistently associated with concurrent Aβ accumulation (standardized β = 0.40-0.52, P < 0.001), but not in Aβ-PET positive individuals. Conversely, greater p-tau217 increases were most strongly associated with cognitive decline in Aβ-PET positive individuals (standardized β = 0.41-0.56, P < 0.001). In the tau-PET subsample, p-tau217 change was associated with Aβ accumulation in A-T- and, to a lesser extent, A+T- individuals, but not in A+T+ individuals. P-tau217 was the largest contributor to Aβ-PET variance in longitudinal (20.9-28.8%) and cross-sectional (31.8-47.9%) models. For cognition, however, p-tau217 change was the largest contributor in longitudinal models (22.2-30.6%), whereas cognitive status contributed more than p-tau217 cross-sectionally. Although of lower magnitude than for p-tau217, rates of change in p-tau181 and GFAP showed similar stage-dependent associations. In earlier stages, longitudinal changes in p-tau217 paralleled ongoing Aβ accumulation, whereas once Aβ pathology was established, p-tau217 change was more closely associated with cognitive decline than with further Aβ accumulation. These findings indicate that p-tau217 reflects an early Aβ-associated tau response before aggregated tau pathology, supporting the value of longitudinal p-tau217 for stage-dependent disease monitoring.

items.title: Genotype and Phenotype Correlations in PDCD10 (CCM3) Related Cerebral Cavernous Malformations: A Systematic Review of Clinical, Radiological, and Molecular Evidence.
items.abstract: Introduction Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are angiographically occult vascular anomalies. Familial CCM is caused by loss-of-function variants in KRIT1, CCM2, or PDCD10 (CCM3), with PDCD10 deficiency associated with an early and aggressive multisystem phenotype. We synthesized evidence comparing CCM3 with CCM1 and CCM2 and assessed its implications for genotype-informed management. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 and a PROSPERO-registered protocol (CRD420261475958), we searched MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science through January 2026 for clinical and experimental studies of PDCD10/CCM3. Study quality was appraised using JBI checklists, NIH tools, and SYRCLE RoB. Results Forty-six studies were included. Compared with CCM1 and CCM2, CCM3 was associated with earlier symptom onset, greater lesion burden, seizures, and intracerebral hemorrhage. Reported extra-CNS manifestations included multiple meningiomas and hematologic cytopenias. Mechanistic studies linked PDCD10 deficiency to disrupted STRIPAK signaling, impaired endothelial-barrier integrity, and altered gut-brain signaling. Conclusions PDCD10-related disease has a severe multisystem phenotype distinct from other familial CCM genotypes. Recognition of its genotype-specific features may inform surveillance, genetic counseling, and therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Gut feelings: host identity shapes microbiomes in cartilaginous fishes
items.abstract: This study provides the first characterization of the gut microbiome for several cartilaginous fishes and assesses the influence of host systematics and ecology on microbial diversity and composition. Cloacal swabs from 100 individuals representing 14 species of sharks, rays, and a chimaera were collected along the Portuguese coast across coastal, shelf and deep-water habitats (90-760 m depth). Gut bacterial communities were analysed using 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding targeting the V4 region. The results showed that microbiome diversity and structure varied significantly among host species, and that host identity is the main driver of gut microbiome composition. In contrast, habitat had no significant effect, although coastal species showed a tendency towards higher microbial diversity than deep-water taxa. Two phyla, Bacillota and Pseudomonadota were the dominant bacterial phyla across nearly all species, although their relative abundances differed between sharks vs. rays. In particular, three deep-water sharks displayed distinct and less diverse microbiomes dominated by a single bacterial genus, suggesting a stronger host-microbiome specialization. Functional predictions revealed differences in metabolic pathways associated with habitat and host systematics, particularly in nutrient processing and carbohydrate metabolism. Overall, these findings provide new insights into host-microbiome associations in this ancient vertebrate group, and highlight the importance of host-specific factors in shaping gut microbial communities.

items.title: Internal states and animal movement
items.abstract: Animal movement emerges from an interplay between external factors, including both environmental conditions and interactions between individuals, and an individual's internal physiological and psychological state. However, movement ecology has traditionally focused on how external factors drive patterns of movement and habitat selection. This imbalance limits our understanding of the drivers underlying animal movement decisions and variation among individuals. Advances in biologging technologies, mechanistic modelling, and analytical approaches are creating new opportunities to quantify internal states and link them to movement behavior and fitness consequences. Recent studies demonstrate how integrating data on energy balance, disease, experience and learning, fear, body condition and fitness can offer new perspectives on habitat selection and responses to environmental change. Despite these advances, approaches that explicitly represent the dynamics of internal states and their impact on animal movement remain relatively uncommon. Here, we review recent advances in movement ecology that incorporate internal states into movement models and habitat selection analyses. In this perspective, we consider physiological states, including energetic and disease states, as well as psychological states, such as cognition and emotion. We then examine how these components interact with external conditions to influence movement decisions. We advocate that movement ecologists integrate movement data with physiological, behavioral, and ecological information to develop more biologically realistic models of animal movement.

items.title: Functional analysis of the cocoa (Theobroma cacao L.) value chain in the Tshopo province in Democratic Republic of the Congo, A review
items.abstract: Abstract Cocoa ( Theobroma cacao L.) was introduced in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 1885, and in Tshopo province, it was first introduced in Barumbu (1914) and Ngazi (1920). However, since the 20 th century, the cocoa value chain (CVC) has remained underdeveloped, despite original breeding research. Therefore, a functional analysis of this value chain and mapping of actors to identify bottlenecks impeding its revitalisation is essential. This research is based on documentary and analytical methods, as well as interviews with key actors involved in this value chain. The governance of the CVC remains ineffective, despite the involvement of a wide range of actors. Indeed, cocoa is produced and exported without a clear vision or regulatory framework; nevertheless, the ratification of the Abidjan agreement, which recommends operational planning for cocoa-producing countries. The lack of horizontal coordination among various cocoa initiatives has exacerbated the overlap of the actors' roles in the CVC. The availability of arable land and suitable ecology for cocoa (strengths) and mobilization of numerous actors as well as abundance of cocoa materials selected in Yangambi (opportunities) constitute comparative advantages for the CVC in Tshopo. The lack of expertise in cocoa post-harvesting and the less involvement of autochthons (weaknesses), as well as the risk of land conflict (threat), could impact the CVC if strategies are not undertaken. The limited adoption rate of improved cocoa cultivars developed by the INERA research centre in Yangambi could accelerate the dissemination of cocoa diseases across the Tshopo landscape and further jeopardize the sustainability of the CVC. This study recommends an interprofessional re-organisation to align all cocoa initiatives, strengthen governance and boost cocoa production to diversify the Congolese economy. Therefore, the functional analysis can serve as a baseline for strategic development and decision-making by international agencies, public authorities, scientists and private investors.

items.title: Indole Coordinates Ecological Defence and Quality-Related Metabolism in Tea Plants.
items.abstract: Herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs) play pivotal roles in mediating plant defence, yet their ecological efficacy and metabolic consequences under realistic field conditions remain poorly resolved. Here, we conducted field experiments in a tea plantation to assess whether the HIPV indole can coordinate ecological defence and quality-related metabolism in tea plants (Camellia sinensis). Using slow-release exposure and foliar spraying approaches, we surveyed pest populations and natural enemy assemblages in 2022 and 2023, and characterised key taste-related metabolites and transcriptomic responses using leaf samples collected in 2023. Indole application consistently suppressed major piercing-sucking pests, including the tea green leafhopper, whitefly, and citrus spiny whitefly, while enhancing the abundance of predatory spiders and parasitoid wasps. Importantly, indole exerted selective effects across herbivore taxa, indicating ecologically precise modulation rather than indiscriminate suppression. Beyond its effects on arthropod communities, indole markedly reprogrammed tea metabolic profiles by reducing bitterness-associated catechins and caffeine while increasing umami- and sweetness-related amino acids, particularly theanine. Transcriptomic analyses further showed that indole redirected phenylpropanoid and flavonoid metabolism, supporting a coordinated shift toward defence-associated branches while suppressing catechin biosynthesis. Foliar spraying produced stronger ecological, metabolic and transcriptional responses than slow-release exposure under the tested field conditions. Together, these results provide the first comprehensive field-based evidence that a single HIPV can simultaneously contribute to pest suppression and reshape quality-related metabolite profiles, with metabolic changes potentially associated with reduced bitterness/astringency and increased umami/sweetness. Our findings position indole as a multitiered regulator linking ecological defence with metabolic optimisation, highlighting the broader potential of volatile-based strategies for sustainable pest management and functional crop improvement.

items.title: "Ecology-based approaches for prevention of biofilm formation on the surface of restorative materials in the oral cavity".
items.abstract: Dental caries and periodontal disease continue to be a public health issue, especially among underserved and aging populations throughout the globe. With the increasing evidence that the oral microbiome affects systemic health, such as coronary valve disease, cancer, and others, combating pathogenic species in the oral cavity has gained a much broader imperative. Rather than focusing on broad spectrum antibiotics, a more responsible and efficacious approach lies in preventing biofilm formation instead of bacterial growth inhibition strategies. Several examples have emerged in the past few years, ranging from antifouling surfaces to small molecules designed to bolster commensal species colonization/growth. One example is the prevention of biofilm coalescence by using selective inhibitors of enzymes responsible for Streptococcus mutans glucan production in oral biofilms, which impair the formation of the main extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) in its biofilm matrix. To further improve antibiotic stewardship, the sequestration of such inhibitors on the surface of biomaterials has been recently proposed. This review will focus on these ecology-based approaches to prevent biofilm formation specifically on the surface of materials, which has implications for the biomedical field in any application where biomaterials interface with the body.

items.title: Dietary tyrosine alters cuticular properties and predator susceptibility in oribatid mites.
items.abstract: The cuticle of arthropods is central for body stability and mechanical protection. While it is primarily composed of chitin as structural polysaccharide, cuticular mechanical properties are modulated by sclerotization, crosslinking of matrix proteins, and/or the incorporation of metals. Tyrosine is a key component in the first steps of the sclerotization process, and being a semi-essential amino acid, dietary tyrosine concentration should affect the sclerotization process and resulting cuticular properties. This study explores the effects of increasing dietary tyrosine availability on cuticular properties (darkness, thickness, mechanical resistance) in the oribatid mites Archegozetes longisetosus and Scheloribates laevigatus, and the resulting ecological consequences for predator defence in predator-prey experiments. Higher dietary tyrosine levels led to darker, but not thicker, cuticle in A. longisetosus. The effect in S. laevigatus was less pronounced. Mechanical resistance showed a non-linear response in both species but was only affected significantly with high nutritional tyrosine concentrations in S. laevigatus. Predator-prey experiments revealed complex results with different responses in respect to predation type: predator identity / type of predation significantly affected prey consumption. These non-linear findings contribute to understanding the complex interplay between dietary factors, cuticular properties, and predator-prey dynamics.

items.title: Life in the shadows: how mycoheterotrophy reorganizes plant-animal interactions across the life cycle.
items.abstract: Background Mycoheterotrophic plants obtain organic carbon from fungi, so their ecology has been studied chiefly through plant-fungus interactions. However, their persistence and reproduction also depend on animals that transfer pollen, consume exposed tissues, and destroy or disperse seeds, as well as on the natural enemies of these animals. Early syntheses predicted autonomous selfing because of carbon limitation and brief flowering, and minute seeds were widely assumed to be wind-dispersed. Later work has revealed a broader range of strategies, including specialized pollination, brood-site interactions, and animal-mediated seed dispersal. Scope This review integrates plant-animal interactions across the life cycle of fully mycoheterotrophic angiosperms, using holoparasites and photosynthetic forest-floor plants as comparison groups. I propose the forest-floor interaction filter, in which correlated shifts in habitat, architecture, phenology, stoichiometry, and propagule traits alter animal encounter rates, signal transmission, and vector performance without generating a single syndrome. Three concepts refine its predictions. The forest-floor pollinator paradox distinguishes reliable visitation by abundant, short-ranging insects from effective outcrossing, a mismatch that can favor autonomous selfing. Compatible-fungus encounter incorporates fungal compatibility into the seed-dispersal effectiveness framework. Reproduction-linked emergence connects subterranean persistence with brief aboveground exposure during reproduction. The review also considers antagonism and defense, and how environmental change can affect several life-cycle transitions at once. Conclusions Mycoheterotrophy reorganizes plant dependence on animals rather than uniformly reducing it. Autonomous selfing, crypsis, and limited aboveground emergence can buffer vulnerable life-cycle transitions, whereas specialized pollination and seed dispersal by forest-floor animals create new dependencies. These pathways can partly compensate for each other, but partner richness confers resilience mainly when effective partners respond differently to environmental change. Progress requires tracing the effects of visitation, consumption, and gut passage on mating, viable seed production, mycorrhizal colonization, recruitment, and population growth. Conservation should protect the complete sets of interactions that sustain these transitions.

items.title: Abiotic and biotic factors jointly shape the ecological niche of a widespread poisonous weed.
items.abstract: Background and aims The expansion of poisonous weeds threatens grassland biodiversity, livestock production and ecosystem functioning. Controlling poisonous weeds effectively requires an understanding of their ecological niche. Here, we test the hypothesis that while abiotic constraints determine large-scale habitat suitability, local occupancy is affected by biotic factors. Methods We developed an ecological niche model (ENM) to determine the realized niche of Stellera chamaejasme, a widely distributed poisonous weed to cattle and sheep across degraded grasslands in East Asia, by assembling a dataset comprising 4,183 occurrence records. We modelled the ecological niche, incorporating both abiotic (climatic and soil) and biotic factors (plant diversity and livestock density). We also used an independent field survey in the core of the species' distribution, to validate the ecological niche based on model predictions. Key results Climatic predictors made the largest contribution to habitat suitability, led by isothermality, precipitation of warmest quarter and mean temperature of wettest quarter. High suitability occurred at isothermality of 36-40% and warm-quarter precipitation of 210-290 mm. Biotic predictors contributed 31.2%, led by sheep density, and suitability responses differed among livestock species. Soil factors contributed comparatively little (4.7%). Field validation broadly confirmed the modelled realized niche. Conclusions Our findings show that abiotic and biotic factors jointly characterize the realized niche of S. chamaejasme. Climatic conditions are fundamental components of the abiotic niche. Biotically, we suggest that controlling grazing intensity can be an effective management strategy to restrain this poisonous species. Our work can inform grassland management to control the expansion of poisonous weeds in a changing global environment.

items.title: Workplace Spirituality and Employee Well-Being: A Systematic Review and Preliminary Quantitative Synthesis of Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: Abstract Workplace spirituality has gained increasing attention in organisational psychology due to its potential relationship with employee well-being, work engagement and occupational burnout. It refers to employees' experiences of meaningful work, belongingness, shared values and connection with a purpose beyond financial or professional goals. Although several empirical studies have explored these relationships, differences in conceptual definitions, measurement instruments and research designs make it difficult to establish the consistency and strength of the available evidence. The present paper examines empirical evidence on the relationship between workplace spirituality and three employee outcomes: burnout, work engagement and psychological well-being. A preliminary literature search was conducted to identify relevant empirical studies and systematic reviews. The selected studies were examined based on their sample sizes, research designs, conceptualisation of workplace spirituality and reported statistical associations. Pearson's correlation coefficients were considered suitable for a correlation-based meta-analysis, while other statistical findings were examined separately where direct conversion was not possible. Listopad et al. (2021), in a study involving 439 working adults, reported a negative correlation between perceived meaningfulness of work and burnout (*r* = −.64) and a positive correlation with work engagement (*r* = .65). Similarly, Khatri and Gupta (2017), using a sample of 298 employees from Delhi NCR, found that workplace spirituality significantly predicted employee well-being. Additionally, a systematic review by Syahir et al. (2025), which examined 38 studies, reported generally positive relationships between workplace spirituality and employee well-being. However, the available primary studies do not provide sufficient comparable effect-size information to calculate reliable pooled estimates across all three outcomes. The findings suggest that workplace spirituality, particularly the experience of meaningful work, is associated with favourable employee outcomes. Nevertheless, differences in conceptualisation, measurement and incomplete statistical reporting limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Further extraction and verification of primary study data are necessary to conduct a comprehensive and reproducible meta-analysis.

items.title: Atypical Visually Guided Organization of Reach-To-Grasp Actions in Cerebral Visual Impairment (CVI) with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).
items.abstract: No standardized behavioral assessment exists for dorsal stream dysfunction related to cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Because the dorsal stream uses vision to integrate reach-to-grasp actions, we hypothesized that altered reach-to-grasp integration would distinguish a CVI cohort with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from sighted controls, and from both groups' blindfolded performance. Consistent with this, sighted CVI participants displayed atypical performance on three individual measures of reach-to-grasp integration, and a novel composite Reach-to-Grasp Integration (RGI) score, which distinguished them from all other groups. The findings provide preliminary evidence that the RGI score could potentially serve as a behavioral marker of CVI-related dorsal stream dysfunction in a clinical cohort with CVI and ASD.
