items.title: The Transition of Feeding and Swallowing Difficulties From Birth to Adult Age in 23 Cri du Chat Syndrome Patients.
items.abstract: Cri du chat syndrome (CdCs) is a rare genetic disorder caused by deletions of various sizes in the short arm of chromosome 5. The clinical course of CdCs involves neurodevelopmental and communication features, including feeding and swallowing difficulties. Dysphagia is common in CdCs, with reported deficits meeting criteria for pediatric feeding and swallowing disorder, yet characteristics and symptom progression from birth to adulthood have not been studied in depth. The aim of this article is to describe the prevalence and evolution of feeding and swallowing difficulties from birth to adult age. Adult patients with a confirmed cytogenetic and/or molecular diagnosis of CdCs were recruited from the Italian Cri du chat Association (ABC Associazione Bambini Cri du chat Onlus, Italy) over a 1-year period. Pathogenic variants, along with key information regarding oral-motor features, were collected. Twenty-three patients were included in this study (10 M; mean age 34.3 years; SD 8.3 years; median age 34 years; age range 18-50 years). None of them were siblings to other participants. All patients were of Italian origin. While the whole cohort underwent typical karyotyping, Array CGH was performed in 13 patients. In individuals with CdCs, feeding and swallowing difficulties begin in the neonatal period (96%) and persist throughout life. Adulthood is characterized by a marked dependence on carers and has a significant impact on the family's care burden. In the present study, we reported their prevalence and evolution from birth to adulthood. Our study may improve the patients' management and support the introduction of preventive supporting habits in this rare disease.

items.title: Reduced spike adaptation in RHEB/mTORC1-hyperactive excitatory neurons influences network hyperactivity.
items.abstract: The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway plays a crucial role in structural brain development by regulating cell growth, metabolism and other cellular processes. Hyperactivation of this pathway causes refractory epilepsy and enhanced network activity through increased synaptic connectivity. However, patch-clamp recordings of neurons in which the mTOR pathway is hyperactive revealed reduced intrinsic excitability. To unravel the mechanism underlying this paradoxical finding, we combine whole-cell recordings from dissociated murine hippocampal neurons overexpressing the gain-of-function Ras-homolog enriched in brain (RHEB)-p.P37L mutation, with an in silico model to connect cellular changes to network dynamics. We found an increased rheobase, decreased depolarization-induced excitability and increased afterhyperpolarization current in mTORC1-hyperactive neurons, confirming hypo-excitability. Further characterization of spike-trains revealed a lack of adaptation in these neurons, enabling neurons to reach shorter interspike intervals in response to higher current injections. We built a computational model of the neurons that reproduces the electrophysiological parameters we measured. This model revealed the interaction between the afterhyperpolarization current and voltage-dependent refractory mechanisms as a potential cause for the reduction in spike adaptation. Network simulation revealed how passive properties, afterhyperpolarization current, and synaptic connectivity contribute to aberrant network activity, suggesting the altered passive properties in RHEB-p.P37L neurons as a cause of reduced burst rhythmicity on network level. Our findings indicate that, in mTORC1-hyperactive neurons, excitability is regulated in a state-dependent manner, where baseline hypo-excitability coexists with poor adaptation, promoting high-frequency firing in high-input states. Based on our results, we propose that, in addition to altered synaptic connectivity, differences in state-dependent neuronal excitability underlie mTOR-hyperactivity-induced disruptions of network activity. KEY POINTS: The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway is essential for brain development, and hyperactivation of the pathway causes refractory epilepsy and increased neuronal network activity. Neurons with induced mTORC1-hyperactivity display intrinsic hypo-excitability at the single-cell level but exhibit stronger synaptic connectivity in networks than controls. Single-cell recordings from murine primary hippocampal neurons expressing the gain-of-function Ras-homolog enriched in brain (RHEB)-p.P37L mutation reveal increased afterhyperpolarization currents and a marked reduction in spike-frequency adaptation, allowing neurons to fire at shorter interspike intervals during strong current injection. A biophysically constrained computational neuron model recapitulating the biological single-cell intrinsic properties reproduced faster firing in response to strong current injection, and revealed how passive properties, afterhyperpolarization and synaptic connectivity contribute to aberrant network activity. The findings demonstrate state-dependent regulation of excitability in mTORC1-hyperactive neurons, where baseline hypo-excitability coexists with impaired adaptation and high-frequency firing, suggesting that altered intrinsic excitability, in addition to increased synaptic connectivity, contributes to mTOR-driven network dysfunction.

items.title: Pain Interference and Buprenorphine Dosing in Patients With Opioid Use Disorder and Chronic Pain: A Secondary Analysis From the Prescription Opioid Addiction Treatment Study.
items.abstract: Background Chronic pain is a significant comorbid condition among patients with opioid use disorder (OUD), yet little is known about the relationship between pain intensity and interference, and prescribed buprenorphine (BUP) dose. The current study examined the association between pain intensity, interference, and concurrent pain medication use with BUP doses, and differences in pain outcomes between baseline and 12 weeks of BUP treatment. Methods This study of individuals with OUD and chronic pain (n = 111) is a secondary analysis of data collected in a National Institute on Drug Abuse Clinical Trials Network study. Logistic regression models were used to investigate the association between pain intensity and interference and BUP doses. Results Participants reported significant improvement in pain intensity and interference from baseline to 12 weeks of BUP treatment. In the adjusted analysis, greater pain interference with mood (adjusted odds ratio [﻿aOR] = 1.55, 95% confidence interval [CI 1.03-2.32], P = .036) and enjoyment of life (aOR = 1.54, 95% CI [1.03-2.29], P = .033) were significantly associated with higher odds of receiving higher BUP doses. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (34.5%, n = 204), acetaminophen and/or aspirin (31.3%, n = 185), and opioid analgesics (25.7%, n = 152) were most frequently used by participants to treat pain. Concurrent pain medication use was not significantly associated with odds of receiving higher BUP doses (aOR = 0.79, 95% CI [0.38-1.66], P = .533). Conclusion Among individuals with OUD and chronic pain, greater pain interference with mood and enjoyment of life were associated with receiving higher BUP doses.

items.title: Cilostazol for Secondary Prevention of Stroke and Cognitive Decline: An Updated Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Background Cilostazol may benefit secondary stroke prevention and cerebral small vessel disease (SVD). Evidence for its role in preventing recurrent stroke and cognitive decline, particularly after lacunar stroke, remains limited although evolving. Aim We updated a previous systematic review to evaluate cilostazol effects on long-term outcomes after stroke or cognitive decline. Summary of review The protocol was registered on PROSPERO and conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. We searched MEDLINE and EMBASE from January 2019 to August 2026 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of cilostazol, alone or with other antiplatelets, in adults with stroke, SVD, or cognitive impairment. We cross-checked prior searches (1990 - 2019) and manually checked additional relevant sources. Meta-analyses and sensitivity analyses were performed where possible with data from the previous review. Twenty-one publications were identified since 2019, including 14 new RCTs, which synthesised with 20 previous trials, gave 34 RCTs overall (n=16,740). Cilostazol reduced recurrent ischemic stroke (OR 0.75 [95% CI 0.65-0.87]), hemorrhagic stroke (OR 0.46 [0.33-0.66]), all stroke (OR 0.68 [0.59-0.77]), major cardiovascular event (OR 0.71 [0.61-0.82]), dependency (OR 0.86 [0.73-0.99]) and depression (OR 0.33 [0.20-0.53]), with a non-significant trend towards improved mood scores. The reduction in ischemic stroke was most consistently observed in chronic-phase long-term trials and those with ≥40% lacunar stroke, although the associations in meta-regression were weak and further attenuated after adjustment for comparator antiplatelet regimens. Trials reporting cognitive function were sparse and methodologically inconsistent, without clear effects on cognitive scores. Cilostazol increased headache, palpitations, diarrhoea, dizziness, and tachycardia or arrhythmia. Conclusions Cilostazol appears effective and safe for long-term secondary stroke prevention, including after lacunar stroke, while its effects on cognition and mood require confirmation in further randomised trials.

items.title: Gaps and Recommendations for Universal Eating Disorder Screening in Youth: Proposal of a Novel Screening Tool.
items.abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) are common in youth, yet often under-detected in pediatric healthcare settings due to lack of universal screening. This is a significant gap in the ED field. Current ED screening tools are not well-validated in youth, were not designed to detect symptoms across sociodemographic groups, anthropometric classes, and symptom presentations, and do not include parent/caregiver input. Our group has worked with key stakeholders to develop a novel ED screening tool for youth that was designed for use in the primary care and specialty settings, the Screening Kids And Teens for Eating disorders (SKATE), child (C-SKATE) and parent/caregiver (P-SKATE) versions. One hundred forty six 8-18-year-olds and their parent/caregiver at two sites completed the C-SKATE and P-SKATE, respectively. Children completed the diagnostic section of the Eating Disorder Examination (EDE) or the full EDE. A subset of youth repeated the C-SKATE 2 weeks later. Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) for the C-SKATE and P-SKATE were 0.75 (95% CI: 0.68, 0.81) and 0.76 (0.69, 0.81), respectively. Test-retest reliability was strong, with an intraclass correlation for total C-SKATE score of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.74-0.95, p < 0.001). Overall agreement and specificity were high for behaviors when comparing SKATE items to diagnostic items on the EDE. Among those completing the full EDE, the SKATE showed moderately strong positive correlations with the EDE Shape- and Weight-Concern subscales. Next research steps include validation in larger, more representative clinical and community samples, consideration of potential harms of screening, studying implementation factors, and examining the SKATE in high-risk and under-represented groups.

items.title: Not the chosen one: Aftereffects of nonselected responses.
items.abstract: In choice reaction tasks, correctly chosen responses have aftereffects on subsequent responding (e.g., response repetition benefits), and so have incorrectly chosen responses (e.g., posterror slowing). Here we studied whether correct but not chosen responses exert similar aftereffects. Doing so allows us to assess whether codes of possible but eventually not executed action alternatives become inhibited, because they lost response competition, or remain in a heightened activation state. In three experiments, we had participants in a prime trial freely choose among two response alternatives, while a third response alternative was labeled as invalid. In a subsequent probe trial, we measured the performance of these three responses in a forced-choice reaction task. In the probe trial, we observed benefits for the feasible but not chosen prime response compared with the execution of a previously invalid response. The results suggest a sustained activation of unexecuted action alternatives. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Aftereffects of response selection have primarily been investigated in forced-choice scenarios, in which nonselected correct responses can be examined only following errors. In this article, we show that aftereffects also occur for nonselected, yet feasible, responses in free-choice scenarios. These effects became smaller as free choices grew more biased, suggesting that they depend on the extent to which the nonselected response functioned as a genuine competitor. Our results suggest that nonselected responses continue to influence later behavior when they function as genuine alternatives during action selection. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The trial-level data and analysis code for all experiments are publicly available on OSF ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/V524H ). Experiment 1 b was preregistered ( https://aspredicted.org/9bq4zg.pdf ).

items.title: Performance of intracortical microelectrode arrays in people with implanted brain-computer interfaces over a 20-year period.
items.abstract: The silicon microelectrode 'Utah' array has enabled people with paralysis to control computer cursors, operate prosthetic limbs and communicate using high-performance brain-computer interfaces. However, reports so far have typically been limited to one or two individuals, with no systematic assessment of array longevity, decoding accuracy and day-to-day stability. Here we present a comprehensive 20-year evaluation of neural data from the BrainGate clinical trials, spanning 2,289 recording sessions, 20 arrays and 14 participants. On average, arrays successfully recorded neural spiking waveforms on 35.6% of electrodes, with a modest 7 percentage point decline over the recording period (up to 7.3 years). Using a 'decoding signal-to-noise ratio' (dSNR) metric, we found that 11 of 14 arrays provided meaningful movement decoding throughout participation (median dSNR >1), with three achieving >70% accuracy compared with able-bodied mouse control. We also found that dSNR increased approximately logarithmically with the number of electrodes, providing a pathway for scaling performance. While longevity exceeded previous nonhuman primate studies, achieving peak performance consistently may require further improvements.

items.title: The identity gene Fezf2 is repurposed postnatally to specify inhibitory input in an activity-dependent manner.
items.abstract: The development and function of cortical circuits require an appropriate balance of excitation and inhibition. Pyramidal cells, the principal excitatory cells in the cerebral cortex, recruit inhibitory synapses in proportion to their activity. How each pyramidal cell subtype achieves the cell-type-specific levels of inhibition it requires is unknown. Here we show in mice that a neuronal identity gene is repurposed postnatally to regulate inhibitory connectivity. Fezf2, which encodes a transcription factor that establishes the identity of extratelencephalic pyramidal cells in layer 5 during embryonic development, is regulated by activity after birth only in those neurons. Activity-dependent FEZF2 controls the number of inhibitory synapses formed by parvalbumin-expressing interneurons through regulation of the cell-surface protein Cadherin-22. Our findings reveal that a gene specifying neuronal subtype identity is redeployed to control how activity refines wiring, giving activity-dependent circuit development its cell-type specificity.

items.title: Stage-dependent loss of AXL kinase activity shapes microglial immunometabolic dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
items.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), microglia acquire a distinct disease-associated transcriptional signature termed disease-associated microglia (DAM). AXL, a receptor tyrosine kinase, is prominently induced in DAM and has been linked to phagocytosis of pathologic substrates such as amyloid-β. However, although AXL expression rises as AD progresses, microglial phagocytic capacity declines, highlighting a discrepancy between AXL expression and function. Here we define this divergence using human postmortem data and mechanistically interrogate its basis in complementary in vitro and in vivo models. Postmortem microglial transcriptomes indicate that inferred AXL activity peaks early but declines with advancing amyloid pathology despite continued increases in AXL expression. Across in vitro and in vivo models, acute exposure to amyloid-β increases relative AXL phosphorylation, engages AKT-mTOR and STAT1 signaling, leading to glycolytic remodeling and enhanced phagocytosis. By contrast, repeated amyloid-β exposure or advanced pathology is associated with reduced relative AXL phosphorylation and blunted downstream responses even as AXL expression increases. Together, these findings reconcile a divergence between DAM-associated AXL expression and signaling output, and raise the possibility that restoring AXL kinase activity could enhance microglial function in AD.

items.title: Tissue stiffening induces histone serotonylation and primes migratory cell states in vivo.
items.abstract: Collective cell migration (CCM) is pivotal in several biological contexts, and post-translational modifications of histones have been implicated in the onset of this process. Here we provide evidence for the involvement of a recently discovered chromatin marker, termed histone serotonylation, in the CCM of cranial neural crest (NC) cells-an embryonic multipotent stem cell population. Our in vivo data revealed that histone serotonylation occurs in NC cells just before they start migrating and that its occurrence supports their CCM. Notably, we found that stiffening of the NC cells' migratory substrate, the mesoderm, induces histone serotonylation by promoting the nuclear translocation of transglutaminase 2 (Tgm2), an enzyme that catalyses the addition of serotonin to histones. Moreover, mechanical and molecular perturbations establish that shuttling of Tgm2 into the nucleus and concomitant increases in histone serotonylation are essential to trigger CCM in vivo. Furthermore, a combination of sequencing analyses is consistent with the idea that histone serotonylation is associated with a chromatin landscape that supports the switch from non-migratory to migratory cell states.

items.title: Transnasal minimally invasive deep brain sensing and stimulation for mental disorders.
items.abstract: A holy grail of mental health diagnoses and treatments is sensing and stimulating the deep brain at high resolution without performing complex and expensive neurological surgeries. Here, we summarize a minimally invasive approach involving transnasal placement of sensing and stimulation elements. Specific nasal cavities, including the olfactory cleft, the sphenoid sinus, and the nasopharynx, make contact with the skull base, and are located just below several deep brain structures engaged in the reward circuit, limbic system, circuit of Papez, and hypothalamic-pituitary axis. These cavities are routinely accessed transnasally, e.g. for endonasal procedures. We discuss how transnasal sensing and stimulation through acutely placed wired devices and wireless implants offer a minimally invasive gateway to the deep brain for diagnosing and treating mental health conditions and motivate the need for further advances including in vivo validation, engineering and instrumentation, and clinical human studies.

items.title: Cognitive and autistic traits in individuals with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome.
items.abstract: The sex steroid theory of autism proposes that exposure to elevated prenatal androgens and oestrogens interacts with genetic predisposition to contribute to the development of autism. In line with this theory, several studies report increased rates of autism and autistic traits in people assigned female at birth with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), a common endocrine condition characterised by hyperandrogenism, as well as increased rates of autism in their children. Using data from existing online databases, two case-control studies were conducted to explore autistic and associated cognitive traits in individuals with and without PMOS. In Study 1, N = 734 participants from the general population (n = 367 with PMOS; n = 367 controls) completed the 50-item Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ), the 40-item Empathy Quotient (EQ), and the 75-item Systemising Quotient (SQ). In Study 2, N = 2,184 participants (n = 1,092 with PMOS; n = 1,092 controls) completed 10-item versions of these measures. Across both studies, individuals with PMOS were shifted towards the psychological profile associated with autism, with elevated levels of autistic traits, increased systemising scores, and reduced empathising scores in comparison to controls without PMOS. Further, in Study 1, the PMOS group demonstrated elevated autistic traits across all AQ subscales, especially in communication. These findings are consistent with the sex steroid theory of autism, suggesting that elevated prenatal androgen exposure may influence developmental and cognitive outcomes related to autism.

items.title: Genetic risk effects on psychiatric disorders act in sets.
items.abstract: Investigations of psychiatric genetic architecture have centered around methodology that assume all genetic effects contribute additively to disease liability. However, it is likely that psychiatric disorders have unrecognized subtypes each driven primarily by different sets of risk variants, which cannot be detected by current approaches. These unrecognized subtypes induce statistical interactions between polygenic effects of these sets, termed coordinated epistasis (CE), which can also be detected using family-based genetic risk scores. We test for CE in five psychiatric disorders and their comorbidities using both GWAS and family-based genetic risk scores, and find evidence for unrecognized subtypes within disorders, as well as genetic support for current diagnostic distinctions despite high comorbidities between disorders. Finally, we identify shared genetic effects consistent with indexing common confounders across disorders, such as help-seeking and dysphoria, rather than disorder-specific etiology.

items.title: Primate area FST: a nexus for synthesizing a world in motion.
items.abstract: Encoding the content of the dynamic, three-dimensional (3D) world is an overarching function of the visual system. Research on the middle temporal area (MT) has been instrumental in establishing the neural basis of two-dimensional velocity and depth computations in primates. In this review, we explore how the fundus of the superior temporal sulcus (FST), an area downstream of MT, may contribute to the construction of behaviorally relevant representations of where objects are headed, what shape they have, and why they move. We survey structural and functional evidence from macaques and humans that implicates FST in this complex synthesis. Based on the collective evidence, we propose that FST supports the perception of a cohesive 3D world by bridging the dorsal 'where', ventral 'what', and more recently posited lateral 'social' visual pathways.

items.title: Neonatal Intensive Care Unit Therapy Delivery for Infants with Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy: Factors Associated with Receipt, Timing, and Frequency.
items.abstract: The objectives of this study are to characterize neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) therapy delivery among infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE); identify infant characteristics associated with feeding and developmental therapy receipt, timing, and frequency; and evaluate differences in therapy delivery between sites. Retrospective cohort study of infants with HIE treated with therapeutic hypothermia and admitted to two Level IV NICUs between 2017 and 2024. Multivariable regression models evaluated factors associated with therapy receipt, timing, and frequency after adjustment for infant clinical characteristics, sociodemographic factors, and site. Among 379 infants, 367 (97%) received at least one NICU therapy session during hospitalization, including 348 (92%) who received feeding therapy and 320 (84%) who received developmental therapy. Developmental therapy receipt differed substantially between sites (98 vs. 70%). In multivariable analyses, site was associated with receipt (adjusted odds ratio: 0.06, p < 0.01), initiation (adjusted time ratio [aTR]: 1.22, p < 0.01), and frequency (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR]: 0.62, p < 0.01) of developmental therapy, even after adjustment for infant clinical and sociodemographic factors. Longer duration of ventilator support was associated with later initiation of both feeding (aTR: 1.03, p < 0.01) and developmental therapy (aTR: 1.02, p < 0.01). Higher birth gestational age was associated with greater developmental therapy frequency (aIRR: 1.08, p < 0.01), whereas longer duration of ventilator support was associated with lower feeding (aIRR: 0.99, p = 0.01) and developmental therapy frequency (aIRR: 0.99, p < 0.01). NICU therapy was common among infants with HIE, but developmental therapy delivery varied substantially between sites independent of measured infant characteristics. These findings highlight opportunities to standardize therapy referral and delivery across NICUs. · Most infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy received NICU therapy.. · Nearly all infants received feeding therapy.. · Developmental therapy varied between sites.. · Standardization of therapy referrals may improve care delivery..

items.title: Timing-Specific Deviations in Trajectories of Frontoparietal Network Connectivity in Adolescence Precede the Onset of Depression and Anxiety.
items.abstract: Background Adolescence is marked by heightened vulnerability to depression and anxiety, and by continued maturation of cognitive control, which is disrupted in both disorders. It is not yet clear, however, how and when developmental trajectories of the coordination of the frontoparietal network (FPN) with large-scale networks, that together support cognitive control, diverge before the first onset of disorder in youth. Methods We conducted resting-state fMRI scans and clinical interviews with 121 individuals (73 females) up to five times between ages 9 and 21 years. Sixty-three participants remained free of psychiatric diagnosis (diagnosis-free group), whereas 58 developed a first onset of depression or anxiety (diagnosed group) during the study. Using Generalized Additive Mixed Models, we compared trajectories of functional connectivity (FC) of the frontoparietal network (FPN) with the default mode (DMN), dorsal attention (DAN), salience (SN), and reward (RN) networks between groups, while all participants were asymptomatic. We then identified significant windows of divergence using 95% confidence intervals of difference smooths. Results The diagnosed group had a stronger FPN-DMN FC beginning at age 12.1 (p FDR = .022); both a stronger mean level and a different trajectory of FPN-RN FC (both p FDR ≤ .001), with hyperconnectivity emerging at age 15.3; and a significantly different trajectory of FPN-SN FC (p FDR = .008), with hyperconnectivity emerging at age 16.8. Conclusions While youth were asymptomatic, network- and timing-specific differences in FPN coupling with the DMN, SN, and RN preceded the onset of depression or anxiety, potentially reflecting aberrant regulation of their self-referential and affective processing.

items.title: Loss of P2Y<sub>6</sub> receptor signaling reduces hyperexcitable feature manifestation in a model of temporal lobe epilepsy.
items.abstract: Multiple forms of brain injury can increase the risk for epilepsy development. Neuroinflammation may contribute to post-injury epilepsy development risk and disease severity. The purinergic damage receptor, P2Y 6 R, is almost exclusively expressed by microglia in the brain and can contribute to neuroinflammatory processes when activated. In prior work inducing excitotoxic brain injury, P2Y 6 R activation enhances microglial pro-inflammatory cytokine production, microglial lysosome biogenesis, and CA3 hippocampal neuron phagocytosis. However, P2Y 6 R signaling has not been explored in the context of chronic epilepsy. We adopted the intrahippocampal kainate (IHKA) model to explore how the presence or absence of P2Y 6 R function impacts the severity of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy using 24/7 video EEG monitoring (single-channel hippocampal depth EEG). We first determined that P2Y 6 deficiency (general knockout: P2ry6 -/- ) reduces acute inflammation (astrogliosis, microgliosis, and CD68 phagolysosome immunoreactivity) in the IHKA model. We then developed an integrated EEG analysis platform to automatically detect excitable network features in chronic epilepsy. Through our automated analysis platform, we discovered that P2Y 6 R deficiency reduces the rate of network spiking and hippocampal discharges in the IHKA model. On the other hand, generalized seizures are similar in rate and severity between genotypes. Our findings suggest that P2Y 6 R deficiency can reduce acute inflammation in the IHKA model and certain forms of network hyperactivity in epilepsy.

items.title: Downregulation of glycolysis-related transcripts is a shared feature between advanced age and early synucleinopathy.
items.abstract: Aging, the primary risk factor for developing Parkinson's disease (PD), is associated with global decreases in glucose utilization. Nigrostriatal dopamine neurons have a high energy requirement; therefore, metabolic impairments are predicted to play a role in their susceptibility to degeneration. To understand the impact of advanced age on synucleinopathy, we examined glycolysis-related transcripts in young (2 mo) and aged (18 mo) male Fischer 344 rats. Evaluations were conducted during the peak of inclusion formation in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), two months following bilateral intrastriatal injections of either alpha-synuclein preformed fibrils (α-syn PFFs) or monomer. Advanced age did not impact the number of pSyn (α-syn phosphorylated at serine 129) inclusion-containing nigral neurons or loss of tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactive (THir) neurons. However, aged rats displayed significantly more compact pSyn inclusions in the SNc, indicative of advanced maturity. In both rats of advanced age and rats with pSyn inclusions, multiple glycolysis-related transcripts were decreased, including Gpi, Pfkm, Aldoa, Tpi1, Pgk1, Pgam1, Eno2 and Pkm. Only Hk2 displayed a trend toward increased expression in both the aged and pSyn-bearing SNc and was observed to be significantly increased in aged rats with pSyn inclusions. Hexokinase 2 (HK2) protein was primarily expressed in microglia but also expressed in pSyn-bearing SNc neurons. These findings suggest that co-occurrent glycolytic deficits associated with aging and pSyn inclusion formation result in metabolically compromised SNc neurons that may attempt to regulate glycolysis via increased HK2 expression.

items.title: Dissecting Age-Related Macular Degeneration: From Human Histology to Clinical Imaging and Therapeutic Translation.
items.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) remains classified largely by visible lesions, yet human histology shows that clinical appearance only partially reflects the underlying biology. This review integrates historical pathology, donor-eye morphometry, lipid biochemistry, and modern multimodal imaging to reframe AMD as progressive failure of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), Bruch's membrane (BrM), and choriocapillaris (CC) exchange unit. A deposit-centric, compartment-resolved approach is proposed, emphasizing that drusen, basal linear deposit (BLinD), basal laminar deposit (BLamD), subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDD), acquired vitelliform lesions, calcified drusen, geographic atrophy (GA), and macular neovascularization (MNV) represent distinct but interacting expressions of interface dysfunction. Human histology demonstrates that clinically visible drusen often underestimate disease burden because diffuse, lipid-rich BLinD may extend widely within BrM while remaining largely occult on routine optical coherence tomography (OCT). Conversely, OCT-conspicuous elevations may contain heterogeneous mixtures of lipid, matrix elements such as collagen, mineralization, cellular debris, and remodeling tissue, limiting the specificity of size-based grading. Fixation, staining, postmortem interval, eccentricity, and ex vivo imaging registration determine what lesions can be recognized and how histologic findings can be translated into clinical imaging biomarkers. Lipoprotein-like particle retention, esterified cholesterol accumulation, complement dysregulation, RPE stress responses, CC attenuation, and vascular remodeling are discussed as inter-related mechanisms rather than independent pathways. AMD heterogeneity is best explained by parallel deposit systems, especially basal sub-RPE/BrM deposits and apical subretinal deposits, whose topography, composition, and vascular context influence progression toward atrophy or neovascular disease. Existing Wisconsin, AREDS, AREDS2, and Beckman classifications remain valuable for clinical assessment, reproducibility and population risk prediction, but they should be complemented by a biological overlay based on compartment, configuration, RPE state, vascular context, and topography. This framework has direct implications for prognosis, imaging interpretation, and trial design, because therapies targeting complement, lipid trafficking, inflammation, or vascular pathways are likely to show clearer effects when enrollment and endpoints are aligned with active lesion biology. By linking lesion identity to mechanism, it may also improve patient stratification and clarify why structurally similar eyes follow divergent clinical trajectories. A deposit-centric classification may therefore bridge human histology, clinical imaging, and therapeutic translation in AMD. Emerging high-resolution OCT may further narrow the histology-imaging gap by revealing previously unresolved microstructural deposit phenotypes, including presumed basal laminar deposit (BLamD) and associated RPE abnormalities.

items.title: Reorganization of whole-brain functional networks in cervical spinal cord injury: distinct supraspinal connectomic alterations associated with neuropathic pain.
items.abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) is associated with supraspinal network reorganization and often with chronic neuropathic pain (NP). We examined whole-brain functional connectivity with 3.0-T resting-state fMRI in 37 patients with chronic cervical SCI (25 with NP, 12 without NP) and 23 matched healthy controls (HC), using 116 cortical, subcortical, and cerebellar regions of the AAL atlas. We applied the network-based statistic (NBS; component-level p_FWE < 0.05) and graph metrics (local, global, and nodal efficiency; AUC across 0.02 <= sparsity <= 0.40). Compared with HC, patients with SCI showed a hyperconnected subnetwork (94 edges, 68 nodes; p = 0.006) spanning sensorimotor, prefrontal, and cerebellar regions. Local efficiency was higher in SCI (p = 0.0010, eta_p^2 = 0.216), whereas global efficiency did not differ (p = 0.2760, eta_p^2 = 0.044). Pain-free patients showed higher connectivity than patients with NP in a subnetwork linking sensorimotor, visual, and cerebellar cortices (23 edges, p = 0.038). Nodal efficiency differed among groups in eight regions; right putamen efficiency was lower in patients with NP than in pain-free patients (p = 0.018) and HC (p = 0.031). These findings suggest that chronic cervical SCI is associated with increased local network efficiency, whereas NP is associated with weaker sensorimotor-cerebellar coupling and reduced right putamen efficiency.

items.title: Superior frontal and precentral atlas label contact and naturalistic saccade amplitude across geometric estimators.
items.abstract: We explored whether MRI-derived geometry near the superior frontal-precentral sulcal junction differs between hemispheres and relates to naturalistic saccade amplitude. Structural MRI was available for 38 adults, and 37 had usable eye tracking during movie viewing. We compared two measurements of contact between atlas-defined sulcal regions: the length of their reconstructed shared border and the summed lengths of mesh edges that cross between them. The primary reconstructed-border measure did not provide statistically significant evidence of hemispheric asymmetry or an association with saccade amplitude after correction for the two principal tests. The amplitude estimate was negative (Spearman ρ = -.336; unadjusted bootstrap 95% confidence interval -.566 to -.045; Holm-adjusted P = .084). The crossing-edge measure showed a stronger association, but represents a different geometric quantity. Additional analyses examined mesh resolution, normalization, eye-tracking processing, movie segment, recording quality, anatomical comparison regions, and other saccade characteristics. The additional kinematic associations were nonsignificant after correction. Estimates depended on measurement choices, and regional specificity was not established. The primary analysis therefore did not establish an association between the reconstructed anatomical measure and naturalistic saccade amplitude. This exploratory study illustrates how the definition of an MRI-derived measure can affect brain-behavior results. A nonsignificant result does not demonstrate the absence of an association. Independent anatomical validation and replication with participant-specific functional localization are needed.

items.title: Regional brain T2 relaxation time changes during neuropathic pain chronification: a longitudinal study in a rat model of orofacial pain.
items.abstract: Trigeminal neuropathic pain (TNP) is an insidious form of chronic pain and current treatments are often ineffective reflecting an incomplete understanding of the biological processes. Whilst cross-sectional human studies have demonstrated structural and functional changes in multiple components of the pain-processing network, they cannot determine when these changes emerge during progression from injury to chronic pain. The primary aim of this study was to track T2 relaxation time changes as indicators of microstructural changes during TNP development following infra-orbital nerve chronic constriction injury (ION-CCI) in rats. Multi-echo T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging scans were acquired 7-days prior to injury and then at +2, +7, +14, and +28 days, in male ION-CCI (n=11), sham-injured (n=6), and naïve (n=8) groups. T2-relaxation time maps were used to identify early- and late-onset changes in T2 relaxation times over the entire brain and within the ascending pain pathway. Early after injury, transient, T2 relaxation time increases within the periaqueductal gray matter, ventroposterior thalamus and primary somatosensory cortex. In contrast, late-stage changes occurred in multiple components of the trigeminal pain pathway, including the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract as well as in sensory, affective and cognitive processing regions such as the hypothalamus, entorhinal cortex, retrosplenial cortex, insula and secondary somatosensory cortex. Many of these late T2 alterations occurred in regions previously shown to undergo volumetric changes and astrogliosis in the same animals. These findings reveal early dynamic T2 relaxation time changes of ascending trigeminal pain pathways followed by sustained alterations across trigeminal brainstem nuclei, limbic-hypothalamic systems, and higher-order cortical networks.

items.title: Associations between dogs' sociability towards humans and three facets of social motivation: social orienting, reward and maintaining.
items.abstract: Dog sociability towards humans can be operationalized as an individual's tendency to approach and interact positively with unfamiliar humans. Dogs' behaviours during encounters with strangers may be associated with their social motivation in other contexts involving humans. We aimed to examine the relationship between dogs' sociability and three potential aspects of social motivation: 1) attentional bias towards social stimuli (social orienting), 2) the value of social interactions (social reward), and 3) the expression of behaviours that may foster and maintain social bonds (social maintaining). We tested 104 dogs in a battery to assess their sociability and behaviours indicative of their social orienting, reward and maintaining, which we hypothesized would be positively correlated with sociability. We found limited support for this hypothesis, as only two out of six social motivation tests had significant correlations with sociability variables. Dogs that established physical contact with the experimenter earlier during the sociability test had a longer gaze duration during the eye contact test. Moreover, dogs that spent more time in proximity and in contact with the experimenter during the active phase of the sociability test were more likely to interact first with the "social" toy during the play test. Our results provide evidence (albeit weak) of an association between dogs' sociability and behaviours taken as indicators of their social orienting and social reward, which could imply that more sociable dogs preferentially attend to social stimuli and find social interactions more rewarding. Building on this multifaceted analysis of social motivation, future studies could provide further insights into the relationship between sociability and specific aspects of social motivation in dogs.

items.title: Diverse biophysical defects converge on a gain-of-function mechanism in five SCN8A missense variants, including two de novo variants in early-onset epilepsy.
items.abstract: Background Pathogenic variants in the sodium voltage-gated channel alpha subunit 8 gene (SCN8A) are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, ranging from benign familial infantile epilepsy (BFIE) to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Several pathogenic mechanisms have been proposed, including those involving the isoleucine-phenylalanine-methionine (IFM) motif. Nevertheless, the precise effects of variants within the conserved IFM-containing III-IV linker on channel kinetics has yet to be fully elucidated. Methods Genetic analysis was performed in two unrelated families with early-onset epilepsy. The two identified causative variants, along with three previously reported variants, located in the III-IV linker, were systematically characterized at both the electrophysiological and protein levels. Results Two de novo heterozygous SCN8A variants, c.4397A > G (p.N1466S) and c.4435A > G (p.I1479V), were identified in two unrelated probands. Electrophysiological recordings revealed gain-of-function effects in all five investigated missense variants, yet with diverse biophysical changes. Three variants, p.N1466S, p.G1475R and p.I1479F, induced a depolarizing shift in inactivation, and the first two additionally increased persistent current and accelerated recovery from fast inactivation. Two other variants, p.I1479V and p.K1498M, induced a hyperpolarizing shift in activation and increased persistent current. Conclusion Two de novo SCN8A missense variants, c.4397A > G (p.N1466S) and c.4435A > G (p.I1479V), were identified as the genetic causes of early-onset epilepsy in two families, diagnosed as BFIE5 and DEE13, respectively. All five investigated variants converge on a gain-of-function mechanism through highly diverse biophysical changes. This phenotypic and biophysical heterogeneity underscores the importance of developing precision therapies tailored to specific gating defects.

items.title: Mecobalamin ameliorates neonatal postnatal immune activation-induced depressive-like behavior in adult mice.
items.abstract: Postnatal immune activation (PIA) could induce neuroinflammation and disrupts neural functions, ultimately causing depressive-like behaviors, and astrocytes activation is one of the key causes. So it is particularly important to develop effective neuroprotectants to inhibit inflammatory mediated by astrocytes for depression. Now, the protective effect of Mecobalamin (MeCbl) on nervous system diseases has attracted much attention. However, whether MeCbl can suppress inflammatory mediated by astrocytes and improve depressive-like behaviors triggered by PIA remains unclear. For this study, we found that Mecbl treatment effectively suppresses the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and LPS-induced astrocyte activation in both in vivo and in vitro models, and ameliorates PIA-induced depressive-like behaviors. Importantly, our mechanistic observations show that MeCbl treatment is associated with elevated TIGAR expression alongside suppressed NF‑κB signaling activation, accompanied by the mitigation of astrocyte‑mediated neuroinflammation. Our work identifies a potential MeCbl‑related TIGAR/NF‑κB signaling correlation in the PIA model, which offers new clues and theoretical hints for exploring clinical interventions for PIA‑induced depressive‑like behaviors.

items.title: Frequency-dependent effects of transcranial alternating current stimulation on working memory and medial prefrontal cortex integrity in an ICV-STZ rat model of AD-like cognitive impairment.
items.abstract: Working memory impairment is a central cognitive deficit in Alzheimer's disease (AD). In recent years, non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, particularly transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), have attracted considerable attention as potential tools for cognitive enhancement. While transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been widely investigated, transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may offer additional advantages through frequency-specific modulation of neural oscillations. However, its effects in AD remain insufficiently understood. In the present study, we evaluated the behavioral and structural effects of low- and high-frequency tACS in comparison with anodal tDCS on working memory in both healthy rats and in an ICV-STZ rat model of AD-like cognitive impairment. Male Sprague Dawley rats received intracerebroventricular injections of STZ (3 mg/kg) on days 1 and 3, followed by seven consecutive days of tES. Cognitive performance was assessed using the eight-arm radial maze and novel object recognition tests. Structural alterations in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) were examined using stereological techniques. Both tACS and tDCS significantly improved working memory performance in STZ-treated rats. High-frequency tACS enhanced recognition memory, whereas low-frequency stimulation reduced both working and reference memory errors. These behavioral improvements were accompanied by preservation of mPFC structure. Overall, the findings suggest that frequency-specific tACS particularly at lower frequencies may have potential for further investigation as a neuromodulatory approach for STZ-associated cognitive impairment.

items.title: Pharmacotherapy for Alzheimer's disease: A Bayesian network meta-regression and FAERS disproportionality analysis.
items.abstract: Background Despite the widespread use of pharmacotherapies for Alzheimer's disease (AD), comprehensive head-to-head comparisons of amyloid-beta (Aβ) antibodies, cholinesterase inhibitors (ChEIs), and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists remain limited. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of AD therapies and to develop sequential treatment algorithms stratified by covariate-adjusted therapeutic windows. Methods Endpoints comprised covariate-adjusted comparisons of the Alzheimer's disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog) and MMSE scales, their therapeutic windows, and selected safety outcomes. For efficacy, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to 26 March 2026 to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Bayesian network meta-regression (NMR) was performed in R 4.4.2. For safety, pharmacovigilance (PV) signals were assessed using Bayesian disproportionality analysis of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database in STATA 18.0 MP. Results For the ADAS-Cog, donepezil 10 mg (SMD = -0.53, 95% CI: -0.68 to -0.39) showed significantly superior efficacy compared with placebo and ranked in the first echelon. Its longest therapeutic window extended from the 1st to 56th week (after adjustment for follow-up duration), across the full range of MMSE scores (after adjusting for the MMSE score), and across all ages (after adjusting for age). With respect to psychiatric disorders, a safety signal was detected for memantine (IC 025 = -0.008; ROR = 1.105; 95% CI: 1.023 to 1.194). Conclusion We propose three series of sequential therapies for AD stratified by age, disease severity, and follow-up duration. Additionally, we recommend that Aβ-targeting drugs be initiated early but not excessively early.

items.title: L-DOPA receptor GPR143 enhances dopamine D2 receptor signaling in striatal indirect pathway neurons and contributes to the regulation of anxiety-like behavior in male mice.
items.abstract: Dopaminergic transmission regulates neuropsychiatric functions via dopamine receptors. Here, we demonstrated that GPR143, a G protein-coupled receptor for L-DOPA, in the striatal indirect pathway regulates dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) function and anxiety-like behavior. Quinpirole-induced hypolocomotion was attenuated in striatal indirect pathway-specific Gpr143-deficient mice. Anxiety-like behavior assessed using the elevated zero-maze was enhanced in whole-body and striatal indirect pathway-specific Gpr143-deficient mice. Intracerebroventricular administration of a peptide that disrupts the interaction between GPR143 and D2R induced anxiety-like behavior. These findings suggest that GPR143 in the striatal indirect pathway modulates D2R function and contributes to the regulation of anxiety-like behavior.

items.title: Ascending somatosensory systems processing affiliative social touch.
items.abstract: Affiliative social touch is a fundamental channel of mammalian communication that influences attachment, parenting, social buffering, play, and reproduction. Traditionally, somatosensory research focused on discriminative properties of touch, while later studies emphasized affective touch mediated by C-tactile afferents and related pathways. Here, we propose a broader framework in which affiliative social touch is understood not as a specialized affective modality but as a multidimensional social signal whose meaning depends on context, internal state, social relationship, and behavioral goals. Drawing primarily on rodent models, we review the ascending somatosensory systems that convey affiliative tactile information from the periphery to the brain. We discuss the contributions of low-threshold mechanoreceptors, the vibrissal system, and also spinal circuits that begin transforming tactile signals into affectively relevant representations. We further examine parallel ascending pathways through the brainstem, thalamus, and cortex, highlighting the roles of the parabrachial nucleus, posterior intralaminar thalamic nucleus, hypothalamic and limbic networks, and cortical systems involved in sensory processing, salience detection, and social cognition. Neuromodulatory systems, including oxytocin, endogenous opioids, dopamine, and serotonin, which shape the behavioral interpretation of affiliative social touch are also discussed. Finally, we consider the conservation of these mechanisms in human. The paper argues that affiliative social touch is not encoded by dedicated pathways for specific social behaviors; rather, common somatosensory signals gain social meaning through interactions with distributed neural circuits and state-dependent modulatory mechanisms. Understanding how ascending somatosensory pathways transform affiliative social contact into socially meaningful representations provides a unifying framework for investigating the neural basis of social behavior.

items.title: Context-dependent social learning in the social transmission of food preference paradigm: Behavioral and neurobiological mechanisms.
items.abstract: Social behavior is context-dependent, yet most neurobiological studies examine it under narrowly defined experimental conditions. The social transmission of food preference (STFP) paradigm in rodents, in which an observer uses social information from a demonstrator to learn about food safety, provides a tractable model for investigating how animals integrate social and contextual information. In this review, we synthesize evidence that STFP is shaped by contextual factors operating at the individual, dyad, and experimental-context levels, and propose that these factors modulate the threshold at which acquisition occurs. This threshold modulation is implemented across distributed olfactory, cortical, hippocampal, and amygdalar circuits, and regulated by neuromodulators including oxytocin, arginine-vasopressin, dopamine, glucocorticoids, and gonadal steroid hormones. The amygdala, ventral hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex emerge as candidate sites where contextual and socially acquired information may be integrated. We conclude that context should be treated as an experimentally controlled variable rather than a source of unwanted variance when investigating the neural mechanisms of STFP, and potentially of social behavior more broadly, and discuss the translational relevance of this perspective.

items.title: Scutellarin suppresses glioma cell proliferation and metastasis in vitro through microRNA-133b regulate pyroptosis pathway.
items.abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor with a poor prognosis. Current treatments are often ineffective, necessitating the exploration of novel therapeutic strategies. Scutellarin, a bioactive flavonoid, has shown potential in inhibiting cancer cell proliferation and metastasis. This study investigates whether Scutellarin can inhibit glioblastoma cell proliferation and metastasis by regulating the pyroptosis pathway through miRNA-133b. To provide in silico corroboration for our in vitro mechanistic findings and to address the limitation of missing in vivo data, we supplemented our cellular results with TCGA-based transcriptomic profiling and molecular docking analyses as complementary computational evidence. Methods U87 glioblastoma cells were treated with five gradient concentrations of scutellarin (25, 50, 100, 200, 400 μg/ml). U87 glioblastoma cells were treated with various concentrations of Scutellarin. Cell viability, proliferation, migration, and invasion were assessed using CCK-8, EdU, scratch, and Transwell assays. The induction of pyroptosis was evaluated by measuring the expression of inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β) and pyroptosis-associated proteins (GSDMD), N-terminal GSDMD antibody using ELISA and Western blot. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assay kit was used to measure cell necrosis. The expression of miRNA-133b was analyzed by RT-qPCR.To complement the in vitro experimental evidence, we performed in silico analyses including TCGA/GBM transcriptomic data mining and molecular docking simulations, which provided computational corroboration for the mechanistic regulation. Results Scutellarin significantly reduced cell viability and proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, with 200 μg/ml being the optimal concentration. It also decreased cell migration and invasion, induced apoptosis, and upregulated key inflammatory mediators and pyroptosis-associated proteins. Furthermore, Scutellarin treatment increased miRNA-133b expression, which enhanced the inhibitory effects on cell proliferation and pyroptosis when overexpressed. TCGA data revealed miRNA-133b downregulation in glioma and its inverse correlation with GSDMD. Molecular docking suggested a potential interaction between miRNA-133b and scutellarin, providing additional computational support for the role of miRNA-133b and GSDMD in scutellarin-induced pyroptosis. Conclusion Scutellarin inhibits glioblastoma cell proliferation and metastasis by inducing pyroptosis through the upregulation of miRNA-133b. TCGA transcriptomic data and molecular docking results further support the potential involvement of the miRNA-133b and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis pathway in scutellarin's anti-glioma effects. This study highlights the potential therapeutic role of Scutellarin in glioblastoma treatment and provides a foundation for further exploration of its anti-tumor mechanisms.

items.title: A longitudinal data-driven approach to cluster tnreatment-resistant depressed patients treated with ketamine using immunomethylomics with 12 estimated immunological cell types.
items.abstract: Background As the understanding of the involvement of immunological processes in the cause and treatment of depression increases, immunological markers become more relevant for response stratification. Based on cell type-specific DNA methylation, cell type compositions can be estimated for immunological cells. We used the DNA-methylation-based cell type estimates of 12 immunological cell types and tested whether these immune-based parameters can be useful for patient profiling. We then tested these profiles and their validity in the context of treatment response for a sample with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) treated with ketamine as part of a randomized controlled trial. Methods From a sample of 181 participants with depression, 113 participants had blood available for biomarker research. Participants were treated with midazolam or ketamine as part of a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Blood and phenotype data were collected at multiple time points. We estimated multivariate functional principal components (PC) over 12 DNA-methylation-based cell type proportion estimates over the course of 4 time points (Baseline, Day 1, End of RCT, and 4 weeks Follow-up) based on the individuals with at least two measuring time points available (N = 91: 40 individuals received ketamine, 51 received midazolam; 32% female; M age : 48.0 years; MADRS Baseline : 29.6 points (SD = 6.0)). Based on the PCs, we built participant clusters and tested those for a cluster-by-treatment group interaction associated with treatment response using ANCOVA. Results Our multivariate functional principal components analysis returned seven PCs. These seven PCs were mapped back onto three distinct clusters. There was a significant cluster-by-treatment interaction: individuals of cluster 1 benefited significantly more from treatment with ketamine (F Interaction (2,79) = 4.34; p = 0.016) than individuals in other clusters or individuals in cluster 1 receiving midazolam. Individuals from cluster 1 receiving ketamine showed an estimated marginal mean reduction in MADRS over the course of 4 weeks of 11.2 points (95%CI: [-16.0; -6.4]). In addition, individuals could be classified with baseline data only with an accuracy of 82%. Conclusion Immunomethylomics based on 12 DNA-methylation-based cell type proportion estimates provides a useful tool to investigate immunological involvement in major depressive disorder and treatment response. By summarizing the longitudinal course of each of the cell types into PCs, we could build patient clusters, which were related to treatment response, particularly for individuals receiving ketamine. Our data contribute to the growing evidence that immune-related markers, including immunomethylomics, can contribute to patient stratification for treatment optimization.

items.title: The gut microbiota-immune-brain axis in psychiatric disorders: towards psychobiotics.
items.abstract: Psychiatric disorders arise from complex interactions across biological systems, extending beyond brain-centered models. The microbiota-gut-brain axis provides a framework linking gastrointestinal, immune, endocrine, and neural pathways, with the gut microbiome emerging as a key modulator of mental health. This review outlines the foundations of gut microbiome science, details the immunological mechanisms underlying microbiota-brain communication, and synthesizes current evidence linking microbial alterations and immune dysregulation to major psychiatric disorders. The review also examines emerging interventions targeting this axis, including psychobiotics, microbiome-targeted diets, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), alongside their clinical limitations. Clinical findings remain heterogeneous and largely associative. However, preclinical models demonstrate that microbial signals shape mucosal immunity, blood-brain barrier integrity, and microglial function. Advances in longitudinal designs, multi-omics, and systems-level analytics are beginning to clarify causal pathways. Integrating microbiome science into psychiatry as an adjunctive strategy may support more personalized, lifestyle-oriented mental health care. Further research should determine which interventions benefit which patient subgroups and identify the mechanisms underlying these effects.

items.title: Frontal ripples cooperate with mixed-selectivity neurons for compositional sequence control.
items.abstract: In mammals, bursts of high-frequency local field potential oscillations, or "ripples," often accompany sequential spatiotemporal associations. However, whether and how ripples support the control of sequences remains largely unexplored. We trained two macaque monkeys to perform a visuospatial sequence working memory task that required flexible assembly and manipulation of sequence constituents. We found that frontal ripples preferentially cooccurred with mixed-selectivity neurons that encoded multiple sequence items and that ripple rates predicted the neurons' contributions to sequence representations. Crucially, co-ripples and phasic synchronization with local spiking activity delineated a potential time window for coordinating or binding sequence constituent information. Furthermore, this binding process could be generalized to longer sequences and even sequence reconstruction. Thus, coupling of frontal cortical ripples with mixed-selectivity neurons underlies sequence formation and reorganization in working memory.

items.title: Metabolomic signatures of augmented renal clearance in traumatic brain injury and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: A Neuro-Metabolome study.
items.abstract: Augmented renal clearance (ARC), defined as a creatinine clearance (CrCl) ≥ 130 mL/min/1.73 m2, occurs commonly in critically ill patients and accelerates elimination of renally cleared drugs, potentially leading to worse outcomes. The underlying mechanisms driving ARC however remain poorly characterized. We aimed to characterize the serum metabolomic signature of ARC in patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) to elucidate the underlying pathophysiology and identify candidate biomarkers. In this single-center, cross-sectional analysis of prospectively collected samples, serum samples from the first 50 consecutive eligible patients with TBI or SAH were classified by measured CrCl and analyzed by untargeted chemical isotope labeling LC-MS. Primary findings were defined by fold change and Storey q < 0.25 across 10,503 peak pairs, and associations were re-estimated with age as a continuous covariate. Thirty-two patients (64%) had ARC and were younger than non-ARC patients (median 47 vs. 66 years). In the overall comparison, of 1481 identifiable features, 10 met q < 0.25, including hypoxanthine (higher in ARC). No feature met q < 0.25 in SAH, whereas 52 peak pairs did in TBI, including noradrenaline, metanephrine, and β-hydroxybutyrate. After adjusting for age, twenty annotated metabolites remained significant with less than 20% change in effect size, including, dipeptides, N-acetyl-serine, and homocitrulline. This is the first metabolomic investigation of ARC in neurocritical care. ARC was characterized by reduced circulating levels of nitrogenous solutes, amino acid derivatives and purine metabolites, reflecting enhanced renal clearance within a systemic response to brain injury. These preliminary, diagnosis-stratified findings require validation in larger cohorts to advance biomarker development and targeted therapy.

items.title: Tandem repeat expansions in autism spectrum disorder: From discovery to therapeutic opportunities.
items.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition for which currently identified genetic variants explain only a subset of cases. Tandem repeat expansions have recently emerged as an underappreciated source of genetic risk for ASD and other complex disorders. Advances in genome sequencing technologies, from short-read to long-read platforms, have substantially expanded the discovery of tandem repeat expansions and their contribution to ASD-risk, implicating their involvement in ASD etiology. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the genetics of ASD and discuss how the molecular mechanisms of established tandem repeat expansions provide mechanistic insights into ASD biology. We highlight the FMR1 CGG and DMPK CTG repeat expansions, which, through distinct pathogenic mechanisms, contribute to the high prevalence of ASD in fragile X syndrome and congenital myotonic dystrophy type 1, respectively. Emerging evidence suggests that disruption of post-transcriptional gene regulation, particularly developmental RNA splicing, may represent a convergent pathway across syndromic and idiopathic ASD. Finally, we discuss the emerging therapeutic strategies and consider how advances in tandem repeat expansion disease biology may facilitate further development of potential therapies for ASD.

items.title: Somatic mosaicism in mTORopathies: recent advances.
items.abstract: Somatic mosaicism is a major driver of epileptogenic cortical malformations, arising from post-zygotic mutations present in only a subset of brain cells. Many malformations of cortical development are caused by mutations in genes regulating the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, leading to hyperactivation of mTOR complex 1. These disorders, such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), focal cortical dysplasia type II (FCDII), and hemimegalencephaly (HME), are collectively referred to as mTORopathies. Somatic mutations arising in proliferating cortical progenitors can be transmitted to descendant cells. The numbers and spatial distribution of cells carrying the mutation are influenced by the developmental timing of mutation acquisition, the progenitor type in which it occurred, and the biological consequences of the variant. Advances in single-cell, spatial, and multi-omic profiling have linked transcriptional states in dysplastic human tissue to cellular phenotypes, revealing that mTOR-activated cells influence neighboring neuronal, glial, and vascular cells through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Beyond these local cell-to-cell interactions, we propose that mosaic mTORopathies may also involve 'community effects,' defined here as emergent tissue-level properties arising from reciprocal interactions among multiple somatic variant-containing and non-variant-containing cell types within FCDII lesions and TSC cortical tubers. These interactions may help explain how rare somatic mutations contribute to broader cortical disorganization and epileptogenic network activation. Still, detection of somatic mutations remains challenging owning to spatial heterogeneity and low variant allele frequency, leading to diagnostic gaps while the potentially widespread effects of rare mutation-bearing cells highlight the need to examine both cell-autonomous and community effects.

items.title: Implementing Digital Mental Health Interventions for Children and Young People in Emergency Care Settings: Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Emergency departments play a central role in crisis management for children and young people's (CYP) mental health. These settings face significant challenges in delivering effective support, such as shortages of mental health specialists, long waiting times, and overcrowding. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may have the potential to expand access to care, bridge service gaps, and alleviate pressure on emergency settings for CYP experiencing mental health crises. This review systematically reviews the current evidence for the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs for CYP in emergency care settings. We conducted database searches using APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, and Web of Science from January 2015 to September 2025. We included quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods studies that related to the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs in acute settings. Acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility were added as post hoc outcomes for this secondary review after implementation-related evidence was identified in the original search. DMHIs included telepsychiatry, phone calls, SMS text messaging, and computerized interventions. In addition to studies reporting data from CYP under the age of 25 years, we included those evaluating data from caregivers and care providers. All selected studies were assessed for quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Overall, 6778 articles were retrieved from the database searches, of which 13 articles met the inclusion criteria. In total, data from 1495 patients, of whom 1048 received a DMHI, 413 caregivers, and 250 care providers were included across studies, excluding 1 study that did not report the sample size for care providers. Mental health presentations included depressive symptoms, violent behaviors, suicidal ideation and attempts, intoxication, and multiple mental health conditions. DMHIs were broadly acceptable, particularly for interventions such as telepsychiatry and structured follow-up phone calls. Feasibility, appropriateness, and cost-effectiveness outcomes were more varied. These were affected by the specific intervention design, emergency care context, and user characteristics. CYP valued computerized interventions that incorporated age-appropriate design and language; telepsychiatry, phone calls, and automated SMS text messaging interventions that enabled continued support and connectedness with health care professionals; and interventions delivered at appropriate intervals. Conversely, health care providers raised concerns about increasing workloads for interventions that required specialist facilitation. Electronic cognitive behavioral therapy was viewed as more appropriate for CYP with prior therapy experience, and SMS text messaging intervention outcomes were limited in CYP with histories of behavioral violence. DMHIs show promise in supporting the mental health care needs of CYP in emergency care settings. CYP, caregivers, and care providers demonstrated a willingness to use these tools, but careful consideration is needed to improve the appropriateness and feasibility of these interventions. More diverse studies are needed to explore these findings in different contexts and to address existing shortcomings to support the implementation of DMHIs.

items.title: Hydrostatic Pressure Overrides Matrix Stiffness in Regulating Cancer Cell Morphology and Proliferation in 3D Gelatin Microtissues.
items.abstract: Developing reliable in vitro cancer models is essential for advancing personalized medicine. A key challenge is recreating the complex tumor microenvironment (TME), including the biochemical and mechanical cues provided by the extracellular matrix. Here, we examined how interstitial fluid pressure (IFP) influences breast cancer cell behavior in a three-dimensional (3D) culture system. Using a modular, valve-locked fluidic platform, we applied hydrostatic pressures (0-6 kPa) to MDA-MB-231 cells encapsulated in soft (5%) and stiff (7%) gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogels. Hydrostatic pressure suppressed proliferation across both matrices and reduced metabolic activity at high pressure, in a time-progressive manner. At 6 kPa (high pressure), metabolic activity fell ∼22 to 24% below control in soft gels and up to ∼64% in stiff gels by Day 14. Pressure drove a pronounced morphological transition, reducing the mean cell spread area by approximately 72%, from ∼1150 µm2 at low pressure to ∼320 µm2 at high pressure in soft gels, and increasing roundness from ∼0.42 to 0.65. Thus, pressure can override the morphological phenotype otherwise dictated by matrix stiffness. N-Cadherin expression showed a biphasic pressure response, peaking at 0.5 kPa (low pressure) before declining at 6 kPa. These findings establish IFP as a dominant, quantifiable regulator of cancer-cell morphology and proliferation, with matrix stiffness governing metabolic activity, and provide a tunable platform for studying IFP-driven tumor mechanobiology.

items.title: Identification of early disease biomarkers in a mouse model of IMPG2-associated retinal degeneration.
items.abstract: The interphotoreceptor matrix (IPM) is a proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix in the retina that supports photoreceptor structure and function. Mutations in the gene encoding interphotoreceptor matrix proteoglycan 2 (IMPG2), a key IPM component, can cause rod-cone dystrophy with early macular involvement or an adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy, each leading to vision loss that is presently untreatable. Impg2Q244Ter/Q244Ter knockout (Impg2-KO) mice were previously developed as a testbed for therapeutic development for both forms of IMPG2-associated retinal degeneration, but the model's utility is limited by its slow degenerative phenotype. To accelerate interventional preclinical experiments, we identified early biomarkers of retinal pathology in Impg2-KO mice. While Impg2-KO mice did not begin to exhibit retinal thinning and functional deficits until postnatal day 90 (P90) or later, they presented with highly penetrant vitelliform-like subretinal lesions, mislocalized IMPG1, truncated cone matrix sheaths, and reactive gliosis by P60 or earlier. Each early disease biomarker was quantifiable, persisted for months to years, was potentially therapeutically resolvable, and differed sufficiently between WT and Impg2-KO mice to serve as a sensitive outcome measure. This work identified multiple early disease biomarkers in Impg2-KO mice, establishing a robust, clinically relevant model for evaluating vision-preserving therapeutics for patients with IMPG2 mutations.

items.title: Serum β-glucuronidase activity in patients with acromegaly before and after pituitary surgery.
items.abstract: Acromegaly is caused by excessive growth hormone (GH) secretion mainly due to a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Surgical removal of the GH-secreting adenoma decreases both GH and soluble α-Klotho serum levels. α-Klotho is structurally related to β-glucuronidase. We tested whether serum β-glucuronidase activity, like α-Klotho, decreases along with GH levels after removal of the GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. We assessed GH, α-Klotho and β-glucuronidase activity in 66 patients with confirmed, newly diagnosed and treatment-naive acromegaly before and 1-8 months after transsphenoidal adenomectomy. Surgery decreased levels of GH and α-Klotho in all and β-glucuronidase activity in 57 of the 66 patients. Based on the postoperative GH levels, 44 patients achieved remission, while 22 patients remained with persisting non-suppressible GH. Reduction in β-glucuronidase activity was much less pronounced than reduction in GH and in α-Klotho, and comparable between patients achieving remission and those with residual disease activity after surgery. There was a positive correlation between logGH and α-Klotho, stronger in the preoperative and weaker in the postoperative state. No such correlation was found for β-glucuronidase. β-glucuronidase activity, compared to α-Klotho, appears to be a less promising diagnostic serum biomarker reflecting disease activity in patients with acromegaly. Nevertheless, β-glucuronidase activity was clearly reduced by pituitary adenomectomy, suggesting that serum activity of this enzyme is also regulated by GH. Increased β-glucuronidase activity may reflect enhanced extracellular matrix remodeling in patients with acromegaly.

items.title: Practical Clinical Examination Framework for Parkinsonism: Integrating Bedside Phenomenology and Biomarkers.
items.abstract: This review presents a practical framework for the work-up of patients with parkinsonism, including an overview of the appropriate use and interpretation of imaging and biomarkers in this patient population. In recent years, new biomarkers have been developed to detect alpha-synuclein in cerebrospinal fluid, skin, and other tissues, and alpha-synuclein biomarkers are now available in clinical practice for the work-up of Parkinson's disease and related disorders. In addition, research is ongoing into neuroimaging techniques to distinguish Parkinson's disease from atypical neurodegenerative parkinsonisms. Important questions remain for the practicing clinician regarding when to pursue advanced neuroimaging or biomarker analysis. In this review we present an overview of the diagnostic work-up of patients with parkinsonism, including a discussion of neurologic exam findings and phenomenology, and an update on available imaging, fluid, and tissue biomarkers. We further provide an assessment of the appropriate clinical contexts in which to consider pursuing imaging and biomarker assessments and how to appropriately interpret the results of such tests.
