items.title: Shadow of Contagion: How the Plague, Spanish Flu and SARS-Cov-2 Reshaped History
items.abstract: This paper provides an expanded comparative historical and scientific analysis of three of the most devastating pandemic events in human history: the Black Death (1347–1353), the Spanish Flu (1918–1920), and the COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2023). Through an interdisciplinary lens combining microbiology, computational epidemiology, economic history, sociology, and urban planning, this study examines how distinct pathogens exploited the transport networks and mobility vectors of their respective eras to spread globally. The investigation highlights the historical constants and structural asymmetries in how human societies react to invisible threats: from the evolution of public health countermeasures to the profound restructuring of labor markets, as well as the impact on collective psychology, mourning rituals, and artistic-literary expression. In conclusion, the paper demonstrates that pandemic management is not a purely biological challenge, but a complex systemic process, where the efficacy of biomedical innovation remains inextricably linked to institutional strength, social trust, and global cooperation.

items.title: Interpretation and Translation-Mediated Telemental Health Services for Adults With Limited Language Proficiency: Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Background Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) or limited host-language proficiency (LLP) represent a growing, medically underserved population at disproportionate risk for poor mental health outcomes. Most mental and behavioral health services provided to individuals with LEP or LLP are delivered by providers who do not speak the patient's preferred language, due to a shortage of bilingual mental health professionals. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of telehealth-delivered outpatient mental health (telemental) visits has increased, yet little is understood about the provision of interpretation and/or translation-facilitated telemental health care in populations with LEP and LLP. Objective This study is a scoping review that aimed to characterize the existing evidence on interpretation- and translation-mediated telemental health services for adults with LEP or LLP. We examined study characteristics, populations, and settings represented, telemental health modalities used, reported barriers and facilitators, and the methodological quality and gaps within the current evidence base. Methods Included studies focused on adults receiving interpreter and/or translation-mediated telemental health services. All studies were published in the English language, which may limit generalizability. Studies with bilingual providers, nonbehavioral health care, mobile health (mHealth) applications, or deaf or hard-of-hearing populations were excluded. Online databases were used to identify papers published through May 2026, from which we selected 15 publications from 137 full-text articles retrieved for full-text screening. Results A total of 60% (9/15) of publications reported qualitative or mixed method designs, while 40% (6/15) were quantitative. Most were conducted with Spanish-speaking populations. Of the 15 studies, 12 achieved >4 out of 5 using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Thematic analysis yielded the following four themes across the articles reviewed: (1) facilitators of access, (2) barriers to access, (3) therapeutic process considerations, and (4) recommendations to improve quality of and access to interpreter- or translation-mediated telemental health care in LEP and LLP populations. Conclusions As previous reviews focused primarily on in-person mental health care, this scoping review is among the first to synthesize evidence specifically on interpreter and translation-mediated telemental health for individuals with LEP or LLP. In addition, its inclusion of literature published after COVID-19 allowed for an examination of how the literature has evolved from the prepandemic period to the post-2020 telemental health expansion. Findings underscored the following needs: (1) address access barriers to telemental health care in populations with LEP and LLP, which persist following the postpandemic increase in telemental health adoption; (2) standardize training for clinicians and interpreters; and (3) update clinical guidelines in the context of rapid telehealth uptake in behavioral health care. It also highlighted the potential impact of emerging AI technologies for real-time translation in mental health care, calling for further research on their ethical and clinical implications.

items.title: Assessment of Engagement and Satisfaction Within a Community Advisory Board to Advance Cancer Prevention and Early Detection Research Among Latinos.
items.abstract: Unlabelled Community advisory boards (CABs) are a key component of community-based participatory research, ensuring that community perspectives and priorities are meaningfully integrated into research studies. Despite their recognized importance, assessments of engagement within CABs remain limited. In 2018, we convened a CAB to advance cancer prevention and early detection research among Latinos. The CAB has supported multiple studies across the research continuum, including qualitative, feasibility, efficacy, and dissemination studies. These studies have promoted tobacco cessation and prevention, physical activity, and lung cancer screening. The purpose of this study was to assess engagement and satisfaction within the CAB. Engagement was assessed using the Partnering for Health Improvement and Research Equity scale, and satisfaction was assessed with 2 items evaluating members' experiences with the research team and their willingness to continue working with the CAB. CAB members reported high levels of engagement and satisfaction. Moreover, based on assessment results, CAB members and the research team identified new engagement initiatives, including co-developing infographics summarizing study findings. These findings highlight the value of assessing engagement to understand the dynamics of community-academic partnerships and identify strengths and areas for improvement.

items.title: Exploratory observations of sleep during contest preparation in a natural bodybuilder: a case study.
items.abstract: Natural bodybuilders undergo prolonged caloric restriction combined with high training volumes in the lead-up to competitions to achieve extremely low body fat levels while preserving lean mass. Although sleep plays a critical role in recovery and metabolic regulation, its response to contest preparation remains under-explored. This case study followed a 24-year-old male natural bodybuilder across four months: off-season (AS-1) and a three-month contest preparation phase (AS-2 to AS-5). Body composition, energy status and sleep were assessed. The athlete lost 5.7 kg (6.6%) of initial body mass, including approximately 4.0 kg of estimated fat mass, reaching an estimated body fat percentage of 5.4% two weeks before competition. Energy intake dropped from 4345 to 2080 kcal per day, shifting energy balance from a 1159 kcal surplus at AS-1 to a 1052 kcal deficit at AS-5. Estimated energy availability progressively declined, reaching 23.9 kcal·kg FFM -1 ·day -1 at AS-5, below a proposed male-specific threshold for potentially low energy availability. Sleep quality deteriorated markedly: sleep efficiency declined from 93% to 83%, wake after sleep onset nearly tripled, and rapid eye movement sleep dropped from 30.8% to 4.4% at AS-4 and 12% at AS-5. Hypnograms showed sleep fragmentation and impaired REM transition. These findings suggest that sleep characteristics may vary during periods of severe energy deficit in bodybuilding contest preparation.

items.title: Paternal and Maternal Psychological Control and Adolescents' Smartphone Addiction: A Two-Wave Study of Chinese Adolescents.
items.abstract: Parental psychological control is relatively common in Chinese parenting, and some strategies are culturally specific. As an important form of negative parenting, it has been identified as a significant family risk factor for adolescents' smartphone addiction. However, previous research on parental psychological control and adolescents' smartphone addiction has rarely distinguished paternal from maternal psychological control or examined their associations at the dimension level. We conducted a two-wave longitudinal survey of 893 Chinese adolescents ( M age = 11.63 years, SD age = 1.61, 47.1% girls) and constructed contemporaneous networks and a cross-lagged panel network including paternal and maternal psychological control and adolescents' smartphone addiction. The results showed that, in the contemporaneous networks, loss of control had the highest bridge expected influence, and maternal love withdrawal was positively associated with loss of control at both time points. In the cross-lagged network, associations emerged in both directions between parental psychological control and smartphone addiction. Among the higher-weight cross-lagged pathways, paternal shame induction positively predicted higher subsequent levels of adolescents' loss of control and inefficiency, whereas maternal anxiety induction showed a reciprocal positive association with adolescents' loss of control. In addition, paternal shame induction and maternal love withdrawal had relatively high point estimates of bridge expected influence. These findings highlight the importance of examining paternal and maternal psychological control at the dimension level in understanding adolescents' smartphone addiction.

items.title: Observer presence and observer condition in relation to attention and response control in children with ADHD.
items.abstract: This study examines the impact of observer presence and observer condition on attention and response inhibition in children diagnosed with ADHD, compared to their typically developing peers. Utilizing a sample of 162 male children, participants were assigned to one of three observational conditions: familiar observer (i.e., mother), unfamiliar observer (i.e., therapist), and no observer (i.e., absence of observer). A controlled observational methodology involving computerized attention and response control tasks revealed that both groups showed improved performance under observation compared to the absence of observer conditions. Performance was consistently highest in the unfamiliar observer condition and lowest in the no observer condition. Observer condition was associated with differences in performance; however, the specific contribution of familiarity could not be isolated because the unfamiliar observer differed from the familiar observer in relationship, professional role, and potentially perceived authority. These findings are discussed in terms of social facilitation and evaluation-related motivation. No measures of anxiety, self-efficacy, or perceived support were collected; mechanistic interpretations are therefore presented as hypotheses. Clinical implications for assessment protocols are discussed, with explicit caution regarding the risk of diagnostic masking bias.

items.title: Evaluating cognitive bias modification in smoking cessation: a systematic review and Bayesian individual participant data meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Cognitive Bias Modification (CBM) targets automatically activated cognitive processes implicated in smoking maintenance. This pre-registered two-stage Bayesian individual participant data meta-analysis evaluated CBM efficacy across 20 randomised controlled trials (N = 3,078), following PRISMA-IPD guidelines. Outcomes included smoking-related cognitive biases, cigarette consumption, and abstinence among smokers motivated to reduce or quit. Within- and between-study moderators were examined. Bayesian analyses provided moderate evidence against an overall effect of CBM on cigarette consumption (Cohen's d = -0.005, 95% CrI [-0.08, 0.00], BF₁₀ = 0.11). Evidence for cognitive bias was inconclusive in the unadjusted model (Cohen's d = -0.05, 95% CrI [-0.16, 0.00], BF₁₀ = 1.22), but favoured the null after adjustment, and abstinence remained inconclusive (log OR = -0.17, 95% CrI [-0.56, 0.00], BF₁₀ = 1.10). Frequentist sensitivity analyses showed significant effects favouring CBM on cognitive bias and abstinence only in unadjusted models. Robust Bayesian analyses indicated moderate evidence for publication bias in abstinence outcomes. Moderator analyses indicated specification-dependent patterns: within-study adjusted analyses favoured minimal therapy and face-to-face delivery for consumption reduction. Overall, CBM did not demonstrate reliable standalone benefits for smoking cessation. Future research should test integration with structured psychological treatment and clarify when CBM may provide incremental benefit.

items.title: High-risk diabetes: Psychiatric diagnoses in a cohort with recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.abstract: Aims Diabetic ketoacidosis is linked to poorer mental health, chronic hyperglycaemia and early complications including mortality. We describe the complex psychiatric presentations of people with recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis undergoing specialist assessment. Methods This cohort study examined diabetic ketoacidosis admissions in adults with type 1 diabetes between January 2020 and June 2025. Recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis was defined as at least two recorded admissions during this period. Psychiatric diagnoses were recorded following comprehensive specialist assessment. Results Among 750 adults experiencing 1501 diabetic ketoacidosis episodes, 263 had recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis, accounting for 1015 episodes (67.6%). Of these, 90 (34.2%) underwent psychiatric assessment. Their median age was 28 years (IQR: 22-40), 54 (60.0%) were female and mean HbA1c was 102 mmol/mol (11.5%). Psychiatric diagnoses were identified in 84 (93.3%), including personality disorder in 57 (63.3%) and depressive disorders in 49 (54.4%). Of those with personality disorder, 48 (84.2%) had no such diagnosis documented at referral. Housing insecurity affected 20 (22.2%), and 64 (71.1%) were not in employment or education. Conclusion Psychiatric diagnoses, particularly personality disorder and depression, were common in this assessed population. Psychiatric treatment embedded within diabetes services (diabetes psychiatry) warrants prospective evaluation to establish its effectiveness in improving clinical outcomes and reducing admissions.

items.title: Self-calibrated SERS nanoprobe with an α-ketoamide caged switch for tracking peroxynitrite dynamics in living cells.
items.abstract: Peroxynitrite (ONOO - ) is a biologically active nitrogen species that plays a critical role in cellular redox regulation and the pathogenesis of various diseases. In this work, we developed a novel self-calibrated surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) nanoprobe with an α-ketoamide caged switch and successfully applied it to track ONOO - dynamics in living cells. The SERS nanoprobe employed 60 nm gold spheres as the SERS substrate, on which the Raman reporter DPNO and the internal standard 4-MBN were separately conjugated to the gold surface via Au-S bonds. When ONOO - was present, the Raman peak at 1150 cm -1 , assigned to the C-N stretching (amide III) of the α-ketoamide moiety, decreased in a concentration-dependent manner due to cleavage of the α-ketoamide bridge, whereas the signal from the cyano stretching vibration at 2224 cm -1 remained constant. Quantitative detection of ONOO - was achieved by measuring the Raman intensity ratio I 1150 /I 2224 , with a detection limit as low as 89.2 nM. Using the ratio SERS nanoprobe, visualization of ONOO - behavior at single cell resolution was achieved during both its generation and suppression. Notably, the nanoprobe was successfully employed to visualize acetaminophen-induced hepatocellular injury via tracking ONOO - dynamics. We anticipate that this SERS sensing method could be applied to study ONOO - -related physiological functions in the future.

items.title: Effects of Milk or Yogurt Supplementation on Bone Health, Body Composition, and Gut Microbiota in Canadian Young Adults: Protocol for a Three-Arm Parallel-Group Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: Background Osteoporosis is a major global public health concern. Optimizing peak bone mass during young adulthood is the main preventive strategy for reducing fracture risk later in life. Dairy foods, such as milk, provide nutrients, including calcium and protein, that support bone health, while fermented dairy foods, including yogurt, may confer additional benefits through potential modulation of the gut microbiome. However, the long-term comparative effects of milk and/or yogurt supplementation compared with no dairy supplementation on bone health, body composition, and the gut microbiome in Canadian young adults remain unknown. Objective This study aims to evaluate the effects of 2-year supplementation with fermented (yogurt) and nonfermented (milk) dairy products, compared to a habitual diet, on femoral neck bone mineral density (BMD) in Canadian adults aged 19 to 30 years, and to directly compare the effects of milk versus yogurt supplementation. The secondary objectives include assessing changes in BMD at skeletal sites, including the total hip, lumbar spine, and whole body, as well as body composition, hormonal factors, bone turnover markers, and gut microbiota composition and diversity following the intervention. Methods The Fermented-Non-Fermented-Dairy trial is a 2-year, prospective, randomized, 3-arm, parallel-group controlled trial. Eligible healthy adults (N=120) aged 19 to 30 years living in Saskatoon, Canada, with calcium intake of Results Recruitment was conducted between July 2024 and July 2025, with an allocation ratio of 1:1:1 for the 3 study arms. Currently, month 12 follow-ups are ongoing. Month 24 assessments will take place from November 2026 to July 2027, followed by data analysis and dissemination of findings. Conclusions This study uses a robust methodology and multidimensional outcome assessment to evaluate the effects of dairy supplementation on skeletal and metabolic health in young adults. The findings will contribute to evidence on dairy-based nutritional strategies to optimize long-term bone health in Canadian young adults.

items.title: Exploring the gaps and opportunities for development of an antimicrobial resistance educational package for higher education.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a complex and rapidly evolving global health challenge that requires well-trained professionals within a One Health framework. However, AMR education remains fragmented, with limited interdisciplinary integration and inconsistencies across disciplines. Although AMR is included in undergraduate and postgraduate curricula in human medicine, veterinary medicine, biological sciences, microbiology and pharmacology, the educational focus differs substantially between fields. Moreover, teaching focuses on biomedical and pharmacological aspects, while social, behavioural and policy dimensions are often underrepresented, limiting the ability to address AMR as a multifaceted societal challenge. To identify gaps in AMR teaching, associated challenges and unmet educational resource needs, we conducted a 3-month international survey among professionals from diverse scientific fields involved in AMR teaching. A total of 85 professionals participated in the survey, of whom 94% were actively involved in AMR teaching. AMR was most often taught within microbiology (35%) or health-related (33%) courses and was typically presented as a few lectures within a module (33%). Although the general perception was that engaging teaching approaches, such as case-based learning, better support effective learning, many participants (31%) reported relying primarily on traditional lecture-based materials. Furthermore, the survey identified limited curriculum time, behavioural barriers and funding constraints as the principal challenges to effective education. Overall, these findings indicate a strong demand for additional teaching resources, particularly interactive and application-oriented materials that support active learning and interdisciplinary education. These findings will support the development of an open educational resource-based interactive online educational platform, designed to enhance AMR education within a One Health context and support the training of future health professionals.

items.title: Genomics of Water Lilies: Floral Evolution, Polyploidy, Aquatic Adaptation.
items.abstract: Water lilies (Nymphaeales), together with Amborellales and Austrobaileyales, constitute the ANA grade, the earliest-diverging lineages of extant flowering plants, and are therefore pivotal for reconstructing the evolution of angiosperms. Over the past 6 years, advances in sequencing technology have propelled water lily genomic research from a single reference genome to nearly 20 genome assemblies spanning the order, five of them telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genomes, and complementary single-cell-scale investigations have substantially advanced water lily genomics. Herein, we review progress in water lily genomics, focusing on the evolutionary assembly of the flower (including its organ-identity toolkit, color and scent pathways), recurrent polyploidization events, and the developmental genetics of the diploid endosperm. We also discuss genome-wide mechanisms for aquatic adaptation and the development of giant leaves and flowers in Victoria, along with putative molecular mechanisms and conceptual models underlying pollination in Victoria. We further highlight how single-cell transcriptomics is being deployed to resolve long-standing questions of petal evolution. Nymphaeales have emerged as the fourth reference lineage of comparative angiosperm biology, alongside eudicots, monocots, and magnoliids, and their genomes supply trait genes for both fundamental plant biology and translational applications.

items.title: Interaction-Rich Odorant Receptor Neighborhoods and Olfaction-Dependent Subsocial Behavior in a Parasitoid Wasp.
items.abstract: Insect social behaviors are closely linked to olfaction; yet the genomic mechanisms shaping chemoreceptor expansion and behavior remain poorly understood. The subsocial ectoparasitoid wasp Sclerodermus guani relies on olfaction to coordinate host-seeking, reproduction, and maternal care, providing a tractable system to investigate these relationships. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly for S. guani and integrate chromatin conformation, transcriptomics, electrophysiology, and functional genetics to examine the organization and behavioral significance of odorant receptors (ORs). We identify 148 ORs marked by tandem expansion and sex-biased antennal expression. These ORs preferentially occupy interaction-rich topologically associating domains characterized by elevated interaction frequency, identifying a distinctive higher-order genomic context for this expanded sensory receptor family. To functionally characterize this structurally organized receptor family, we generated a heritable null mutation in the OR co-receptor (Orco). Orco mutants displayed severe impairments in host-seeking, mating, oviposition, and maternal care. Strikingly, mutants frequently laid eggs on conspecific larvae, indicating a loss of kin recognition and raising the possibility that OR-mediated olfaction contributes to parasitism and maternal care in this lineage. Together, these findings suggest that genome architecture may bias chemosensory gene diversification and that OR signaling is necessary for coordinated subsocial behavior in S. guani.

items.title: Casting the networks wide: three facets of technological organization from the late Middle Paleolithic of Kalavan-2, Armenia.
items.abstract: Context Reconstructing when, where, and how past hunter-gatherers moved to obtain resources, and how that mobility related to the surrounding environment, is central to understanding how they organized their activities across the landscape. Objectives: We ask wether raw-material provisiong at Kalavan-2 tracked simple procurement distance or the ecological structure of the surrounding landscape. Objectives We ask wether raw-material provisiong at Kalavan-2 tracked simple procurement distance or the ecological structure of the surrounding landscape. Methods We integrate techno-typological analysis with Module Flake Analysis, a recently developed approach that classifies the debitage byproducts of tool maintenance into diagnostic categories (Modules M0-M4), at three independent assemblages from the Late Middle Paleolithic open-air site of Kalavan-2, situated within the ecologically and elevationally diverse Armenian Highlands. Building on this classification, we introduce a new quantitative Maintenance-Intensity (MI) index and combine it with obsidian sourcing data. Results Three distinct provisioning strategies. One draws on a wide catchment spanning multiple ecological zones, from the site's own forest belt to distant subalpine and high-alpine sources. Another relies on locally available volcanic rock within the site's immediate ecological zone, with limited obsidian input. A third is dominated by heavily maintained obsidian, including material from high-elevation sources subject to reduced seasonal access. Together, these patterns show that procurement distance alone does not account for how raw materials were treated at Kalavan-2: the elevational and ecological mosaic of the Armenian Highlands shaped provisioning as much as distance did. Conclusions The three assemblages from Kalavan-2 thus provide complementary insight into how Late Middle Paleolithic groups structured mobility and provisioning within a landscape defined by sharp ecological and elevational contrasts.

items.title: Intraoperative Blood Pressure Targeting in Noncardiac Surgery: A Bayesian Random-effects Meta-analysis of Randomized Trials.
items.abstract: Background Whether protocolized intraoperative arterial pressure-targeting strategies provide incremental benefit beyond contemporary usual care remains uncertain. The authors performed a Bayesian meta-analysis of randomized trials in major noncardiac surgery. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to January 5, 2026, with additional literature surveillance through June 29, 2026. Randomized trials comparing protocolized intraoperative arterial pressure-targeting strategies with usual care or lower-pressure approaches were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were acute kidney injury (AKI) and myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS). Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis was prespecified as the primary analytical framework, with confirmatory frequentist analyses. Results Fifteen randomized trials met the inclusion criteria. Mortality (13 trials) remained centered around an odds ratio (OR) of 1.00 (frequentist OR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.83 to 1.21; Bayesian median OR, 1.00; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.73 to 1.38), with wide Bayesian prediction intervals (OR, 0.56 to1.78). AKI (14 trials) showed the most favorable estimates (frequentist OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.73 to 1.03; Bayesian median OR, 0.88; 95% CrI, 0.70 to 1.05), but estimates remained compatible with no clinically important benefit, heterogeneity was moderate, and leave-one-out analyses, excluding each trial in turn, showed sensitivity to individual trial exclusion. MINS (eight trials) likewise remained compatible with no treatment effect (frequentist OR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.93 to 1.15; Bayesian median OR, 1.05; 95% CrI, 0.90 to 1.26). Exploratory analyses suggested that any potential renal benefit may depend on the broader hemodynamic context in which arterial pressure targets are implemented. Conclusions Protocolized intraoperative arterial pressure-targeting strategies did not demonstrate a consistent incremental benefit over contemporary usual care in major noncardiac surgery. Mortality and MINS remained compatible with no treatment effect. Although AKI showed the most favorable estimates, the evidence remained uncertain, was sensitive to individual trial exclusion, and should be interpreted cautiously.

items.title: Beneath the glass ceiling: an examination of gender disparities in Canadian medical education leadership.
items.abstract: This study aims to assess gender representation in leadership and academic ranks within Canadian universities and affiliated medical schools during 2020-2021, and describe scholarly productivity by inferred gender. This cross-sectional study identified 1,163 faculty leaders across 17 medical schools and parent universities. Public records, NamSor-inferred gender and Scopus bibliometrics were analysed using contingency tables, Cramér's V and exploratory unadjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Productivity comparisons were descriptive. Gender was associated with leadership category among 1,110 tabulated leaders (χ2(3) = 24.49, p < 0.001; V = 0.149) and academic rank among 823 leaders (χ2(2) = 16.39, p < 0.001; V = 0.141). Women comprised 30.1% of department heads and 36.1% of full professors. Women had lower odds than men of holding department-head versus other listed leadership roles (OR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33-0.64) and full versus assistant/associate professorships (OR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.73). Mean bibliometric measures were higher among men. These historical data cannot establish current representation or causal mechanisms. Gender inference, differing analytic denominators, unmeasured confounding and unaddressed institutional clustering limit interpretation. Updated longitudinal studies, interviews and validated surveys are needed. This national analysis examines gender representation in leadership, academic rank and scholarly productivity across Canadian universities and their affiliated medical schools.

items.title: AGNFormer. I: Reconstruction of active galactic nucleus spectra using a probabilistic transformer model
items.abstract: When analysing spectroscopic data to extract physical properties, emphasis is often placed on small portions of a spectrum (e.g. ionisation diagnostic diagrams, broad Hβ or Mg ii emission lines, etc.), potentially discarding a wealth of useful information. We explore how an uncertainty-aware transformer-based architecture can leverage information embedded across the entire observed optical spectra of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), focussing on the algorithm's ability to predict unseen or masked parts of luminous AGN spectra, providing a direct probe of the learnable correlations between AGN continua and broad lines. We introduce AGNFormer -1 $; missing halves), inputting rest-frame spectral fluxes and uncertainties across the entire redshift range of the SDSS DR16 Quasar Catalogue. We evaluate the performance of the model on both full (no S/N limit) and high-quality (S/N $> 10) spectral samples using the negative-log likelihood and via comparisons with existing ̧iv and łyman reconstruction algorithms. The model successfully reconstructs unseen AGN broad lines up to an error floor of ≈2-6% of the flux at S/N ≈ 40, while the predictive power for larger unseen halves diminishes with distance from the cut-off wavelength of the input spectrum. Predictions faithfully reproduce the broad AGN spectral diversity across the entire optical and UV quasi-stellar object (QSO) main sequence parameter spaces, including both Gaussian and Lorentzian profile regimes, complexes, and narrow emission lines. The performance is found to be similar or better compared to previous spectral reconstruction algorithms. The high precision of the broad-line region reconstruction demonstrates that the method successfully aggregates information across the spectrum and highlights how the AGN continuum as well as weaker lines and complexes have the potential to assist astronomers in the extraction of the entire wealth of information embedded in AGN spectra. items.title: Euclid. XI. A two-point correlation approach to diagnosing star-related systematics in the spectroscopic survey
items.abstract: The Euclid spectroscopic survey will measure galaxy clustering with unprecedented precision, which demands stringent control over observational and instrumental systematics. Among these, star-related effects may contaminate the spectroscopic images through photometric persistence and through imperfect masking of stellar images. We characterized the imprint of star-related effects in the spectroscopic exposures and quantified their impact on galaxy clustering analyses. If these effects produce characteristic angular features, they can be identified and characterized in the data, thereby enabling an assessment of their impact on cosmological measurements. We used angular and spatial auto- and cross-correlation statistics to quantify these effects. For the galaxies we used mock spectroscopic catalogues extracted from EuclidLargeMocks. We focused on a 330 region of the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS). For the stars, we considered the real Gaia and star catalogues in the same area. To simulate photometric persistence, we implemented a simplified detector-level model calibrated on spectroscopic measurements and modulated the strength of the effect to introduce varying fractions of `interlopers' into the mock galaxy catalogues. For the stellar mask, we modelled potential inconsistencies between the mask used to remove regions around stars in the data and the mask applied to the random catalogue used to quantify the survey selection function. We measured the star--star, galaxy--galaxy, and star--galaxy angular correlation functions using the Landy--Szalay estimator and quantified deviations from the expected null star–galaxy correlation with a dedicated metric. Finally, we evaluated the impact of these systematics on large scales using the 3D two-point correlation function (2PCF). Our results show that photometric persistence produces a characteristic feature in the star--galaxy angular cross-correlation at scales of order 100 consistent with the scale set by the Euclid dithering pattern and grism dispersion geometry. It also induces a spurious, positive cross-correlation signal that remains approximately constant in amplitude up to 1^̧irc. We find that star–galaxy cross-correlation analysis is a sensitive tool for detecting residual persistence and is capable of revealing spurious contamination levels as low as 10% in a Data Release 1-like spectroscopic catalogue. In contrast, mismatches in stellar masking produce strong small-scale angular signatures but do not significantly impact the large-scale 2PCF under realistic EWS conditions.

items.title: P2D - A Two-Dimensional Multi-Spacecraft Solar Wind Persistence Model
items.abstract: The background solar wind is a key component in space weather forecasting, as it contains geoeffective high-speed streams and provides the medium through which coronal mass ejections propagate and evolve in interplanetary space. Due to the solar rotation and the slow evolution of large-scale solar wind structures, solar wind properties exhibit an autocorrelation with a period of roughly 27 days, particularly at solar minimum. We made use of this property to develop a solar wind persistence model with input from multiple spacecraft (Solar Orbiter, Parker Solar Probe, STEREO-A, STEREO-B and the OMNI database). The model ballistically propagates in-situ data from the position of their measurement radially away from the Sun, as well as longitudinally with the solar rotation rate, producing 2D maps of solar wind parameters. These can be extracted at any point in the heliosphere for a solar wind reconstruction. From Earth’s perspective, the reconstruction performs with an MAE of 65.41 km~s$^{-1}$ and 3.51 $cm^{-3}$ for speed and density, respectively. During high-speed streams, the peak hit rate is 50\% and 48\% for speed and density. It performs best during times when there are spacecraft located between Earth and Lagrange point L5. During these times, the mean absolute error of the predicted solar wind velocity decreases by roughly 35\% in comparison to the benchmark 27-day persistence model. Therefore, future L5 missions like Vigil are expected to provide a robust basis for reliable persistence forecasts.

items.title: The ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST Survey: Investigating the role of interstellar dust, gas, and stars in high-z galaxies at kiloparsec scales
items.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of galaxy evolution requires a detailed analysis of gas and dust, including their distribution and evolution within galaxies. In this work, we analyse spatially resolved (∼,1-2,kpc) rest-frame C ii and dust continuum ALMA observations together with JWST/NIRSpec IFU data of a sample of six massive galaxies at z,∼,4-5. We focus on deriving and comparing the spatial distributions of atomic and molecular gas masses, dust and stellar masses, star formation rates (SFR), and metallicity. The oxygen abundance maps have median values in the range of 12+log(O/H),sim8.1-8.3 with variations of the order of 1,dex within the same galaxy. In four galaxies of our sample, the oxygen abundance shows a minimum at the peak of the Hα emission and an enhancement in the outer parts. The calibration used in this study to estimate the atomic gas mass in our galaxies seems to overestimate the atomic gas mass surface densities by up to one to two orders of magnitude. However, a calibration based on a spatially resolved C ii conversion factor gives a more robust estimation of the total gas mass. The dust-to-gas surface mass density ratio varies between łog Σ_ ̊m dust /Σ_ ̊m gas =-2.2 ^ +0.24 _ -0.19 and łogΣ_ ̊m dust /Σ_ ̊m gas =-2.69^ +0.21 _ -0.16 , while the dust-to-stellar surface mass density ratio ranges from łogΣ_ ̊m dust /Σ_ ̊m star =-2.01^ +0.13 _ -0.12 to łogΣ_ ̊m dust /Σ_ ̊m star =-2.91^ +0.13 _ -0.13 . A detailed analysis of the dust-to-stellar surface mass density ratio and the gas mass fraction versus metallicity revealed that galaxies exhibiting signatures of strong outflows have a lower dust-to-stellar surface mass density ratio and lower gas mass fractions than the galaxies with no outflow signatures. While the latter is consistent with these galaxies ejecting part of their gas reservoir to the circumgalactic medium, the low dust-to-stellar surface mass density ratios also suggest that part of the dust content is expelled outside the galaxy, which reinforces previous theoretical suggestions of dust removal by stellar feedback or radiation pressure to explain the high UV luminosities in galaxies at very high redshifts. Some galaxies of our sample have almost an order of magnitude higher ratios of dust-to-gas and dust-to-stellar surface mass density than galaxies in the local Universe, suggesting that a large dust reservoir has been built up already at timescales of sim1,Gyr in these galaxies.

items.title: Surveying for close binaries among lithium-rich giants
items.abstract: The existence of low-mass giants with high lithium (Li) abundances poses a challenge to our understanding of post-main sequence stellar structure and evolution. Li-rich giants are preferentially found in the red clump (RC) rather than on the first-ascent red giant branch (RGB). One of the scenarios proposed to explain this Li enrichment involves tidal interaction with a close binary companion, which, if dominant, predicts an enhanced binary fraction among Li-rich giants relative to Li-normal ones. We aim to test the binary interaction scenario for the origin of Li-rich giants by using multi-epoch radial velocities (RVs) in order to measure the close binary fraction of a statistically robust sample of Li-rich giants. The surveyed sample contains both RC and RGB targets, which allows us to examine potential differences in the binary fraction as a function of evolutionary stage. We monitored 70 giants (40 RC and 30 RGB) using the ESPRESSO spectrograph, 57 (32 RC and 25 RGB) of which already had four or more visits over a ∼7-month baseline. The analysis presented here is based on these latter targets. We first used a criterion based on surface gravity and the maximum observed RV difference within our data in order to discard RV variations attributable to intrinsic stellar jitter. For the targets with RV variation larger than this threshold, we performed Monte Carlo simulations over a grid of companion mass and orbital period, to estimate the probability that the observed RV variation is due to a stellar (P_SB) or substellar (P_SS) companion. After removing targets consistent with stellar jitter, 11 (34 ± 8%) RC and eight (32 ± 9%) RGB stars remained as binary candidates or stars with a companion. Of these, three targets (16 ± 8% of the filtered sample) are confirmed stellar binaries. The distributions of P_SB and P_SS are statistically indistinguishable between the RC and RGB samples. We find no evidence in our current data for a binary fraction for Li-rich giants (in either evolutionary stage) larger than that expected for a regular Li-normal population, which suggests that binary interaction is unlikely to be the dominant mechanism driving Li enrichment in this sample. Extending the RV baseline to probe longer orbital periods will be important to continue exploring the plausibility of this scenario.

items.title: The Pristine survey. XXIX. Data Release 2: Photometric metallicities for 15 millions stars down to G∼ 20.3
items.abstract: Tailored narrowband photometric observations are an efficient way to measure the metallicity of Milky Way stars. The Pristine survey has been mapping the northern sky since 2015 using narrowband CaHK photometry obtained with the MegaCam imager on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). The Pristine Data Release 1 (DR1) provided a high-precision absolute calibration of the survey observed before October 2022 using Gaia DR3 XP synthetic photometry, yielding photometric metallicities over ∼6500 deg2$, but was limited in depth to the availability of Gaia spectro-photometry ($G łesssim 17.65). We present the Pristine Data Release 2 (DR2) that includes all Pristine observations until January 2025, corresponding to an additional 1500,deg2$ of coverage, and including all faint sources down to $G This release aims to exploit the full depth of the Pristine observations to uncover the faint metal-poor halo. We process all images observed from the start of the survey in March 2015 through to January 2025 following the methodology presented in DR1. The core of the calibration utilizes the subset of bright stars with Gaia synthetic CaHK_ neural network. We then derive photometric metallicities using the established Pristine (CaHK, G, G_ magnitudes to train the PhotCalib ̊m BP , G_ ̊m RP ) to FeH model. The resulting catalog covers approximately ∼ 8000 deg 2 and provides photometric metallicities for 15 million FGK stars, which show good agreement with recently published independent Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) metallicities. With its increased coverage and access to a significantly fainter regime compared to DR1, DR2 significantly increases the volume of the survey. items.title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
items.abstract: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. 3 We developed a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fitted it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1,806,196,447 sources in 3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. 3 is essentially complete for G ∈ (5,19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ∼ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Our approach builds on previous efforts that use the understanding of the Gaia survey strategy to model the survey selection function. Our model does not rely on a precise knowledge of the Gaia scanning law, making it more robust, while retaining the capability of deriving an all-sky selection function without the need to extrapolate from limited external surveys providing `ground truth'. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. 3

items.title: Constraining dust properties along the minor axis of Andromeda
items.abstract: Previous studies of dust emission in the Andromeda galaxy (M31) based primarily on Herschel data have reported inconsistent radial trends in the dust emissivity index (β), partly due to limited wavelength coverage and the degeneracy between dust temperature (T_̊m dust) and β. We aim to improve the constraints of β determinations and obtain the spatial surface density and temperature distributions at giant molecular cloud scales in M31 by extending the spectral coverage into the millimeter regime and by quantifying the impact of wavelength coverage on the T_̊m dust–β degeneracy. We present the 1.15 mm continuum emission along the minor axis of M31 with the 30 m telescope of the Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique (IRAM). The map has an angular resolution of 11.6'', corresponding to approximately 40 pc at the distance of M31. We used these data with Herschel and 450 and 850 μm maps from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope to perform pixel-by-pixel single-component modified blackbody fitting. Including the 850 μm and 1.15 mm data helps reduce the T_̊m dust–β degeneracy and yields an average emissivity index of β ≈ 1.8, which is systematically lower than values derived from far-infrared–only analyses. Radial analysis shows higher β values in the 5 kpc ring compared to the 10 kpc ring. The elevated β values in the inner 5 kpc may be linked to changes in dust composition, potentially associated with enhanced starlight heating in this region. Millimeter wavelength coverage is important for improving β constraints in M31. The lower β values inferred from the 250--1150 μm spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting suggest possible variations in dust emissivity and highlight the importance of sampling the long-wavelength SED slope in nearby galaxies.

items.title: Impact of the large-scale environment on the baryonic scaling relations of disc galaxies: Insights from the GASP survey
items.abstract: The Tully--Fisher relation (TFR) and the specific angular momentum--mass relation (SAMR) link the baryonic content of a disc to its kinematics and dynamics. Hence, these scaling relations should bear the imprints of any process removing baryons or altering their kinematics, such as those acting in clusters of galaxies. We tested this scenario using the MUSE survey `GAs Stripping Phenomena in galaxies' (GASP), which targets field, group, and cluster members at z ≈ 0.05 and various stages of ram pressure stripping. For the 81 discs with favourable inclinations, we measured the distribution and kinematics of stars and ionised gas and their specific angular momenta. Within their scatter, the stellar and baryonic relations show no significant dependence on the large-scale environment. The TFRs have slopes of α ≈ 3.6 and ≈ 3.5 for any kinematic tracer, and the SAMRs have α ≈ 0.65--0.75, as predicted by tidal torque theory. The same holds for the ten S0-S0/as in our sample, consistent with the `faded spiral' formation scenario. Only the gas SAMR shows an environmental signature, with ram pressure stripped galaxies lying ≈ 0.16 dex below unperturbed ones. This offset is mostly due to their enhanced star formation rate and thus higher gas mass when inferred through the Schmidt-Kennicutt law rather than to kinematic perturbations or disc truncation. Our results suggest that within the area probed by MUSE (łesssim6 disc scale lengths), these discs have preserved the angular momentum acquired at formation not only from cluster processes and pre-processing in filaments but also from mergers and ejective feedback acting in any environment.

items.title: Mitigating variance shrinkage in multitask galaxy property inference from imaging data via statistical manifold alignment
items.abstract: Inferring photometric redshifts (z) and key stellar population properties (łog(M_*/ _⊙), D_n 4000, and mathrm M H δ_A) directly from multiband imaging is increasingly critical for spectroscopically limited large surveys such as LSST and CSST. However, conventional pointwise loss functions (e.g., mean squared error or Huber loss) employed in deep neural networks often induce ``variance shrinkage''---a regression-to-the-mean effect that contracts predicted variances, distorts nonlinear physical manifolds (such as bimodal distributions), and truncates heavy-tailed populations. Here, we present ViTMultiTask, a vision transformer framework that incorporates a multiscale maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss to enforce higher-order joint distribution alignment in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Trained on 83,846 galaxies from Subaru HSC five-band (g,r,i,z,y) imaging cross-matched with DESI Data Release 1 Bright Galaxy Survey spectra, the model achieves high point-estimate precision on an independent test set of 5,000 galaxies: σ_ NMAD = 0.020 for z, 0.169, for łog(M_*/ _⊙), 0.073 for D_n 4000, and 1.185, δ_A. Ablation experiments demonstrate that incorporating the MMD loss effectively mitigates variance shrinkage and more accurately reproduces the observed spectroscopic parameter distributions (including bimodal structures and heavy tails), while maintaining point-estimate accuracy statistically consistent with the baseline (with RMSE changes łe 3.5%) and catastrophic outlier rates fully comparable to the baseline. This kernel-based manifold alignment offers a statistically grounded and practical paradigm for comprehensive galaxy property inference in the deep imaging era. M for mathrm H

items.title: Inferring accretion bursts in intermediate-mass protostars from asteroseismic imprints
items.abstract: During star formation, objects may gain the majority of their final mass through regular and intense bursts of mass accretion. For burst events of the FU Orionis-type (FUor), accretion rates can climb as high as 10^ -3 in short windows of time, amounting to just a few percent of the main accretion phase. Some bursters had not been observed in the preceding quiescent stage, making their classification as FUors difficult. To study the occurrence of such events observationally, signatures of the current accretion bursts and tracers of recent bursts are crucial. In this work, we investigate the potential to identify current accretion bursts and detect recent bursts in protostars and pre-main sequence (pre-MS) stars of intermediate mass using asteroseismology. The aim is to characterize theoretical period-spacing diagrams of pre-MS gravity-mode (g-mode) pulsators that have undergone accretion bursts. We used the stellar structure and evolution code to evolve stellar models from the protostellar seed phase of 0.01 MESA and 1.5 ̊sun up to 4.0 with a constant accretion rate of 10^ -6 A single accretion burst was initialized during the accretion phase. The stellar oscillation code GYRE was employed to compute the resulting asteroseismic properties of the models. Accretion bursts of up to 10^ -3 are sufficient to cause the convective cores of the models to recede, leaving behind a chemical trace that is manifested in the form of quasi-periodic dips in the g-mode period spacing. This effect is strongest during the outburst, but also lingers for up to 475 years before the convective core is re-established and the dips are gone. Our experiment shows that a single accretion burst leaves an imprint in the deep interiors of protostars and pre-MS stars of intermediate mass and that this imprint can be captured with asteroseismology. Well-resolved g-mode pulsations of young stellar objects may therefore help identify current and recent accretion bursts. Our results are most conclusive for burst magnitudes greater than 1 -4 corresponding to FUor-type bursts.

items.title: The long-period central star of the planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455
items.abstract: A significant fraction of planetary nebulae have been shown to host short-period binary central stars, but longer-period central stars are scarcer. We characterise the central star of the planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455, which has previously been claimed to be an intermediate-period binary with a period of approximately 12 days. We studied archival and catalogue photometry to probe the previously reported photometric variability and binary spectral energy distribution. We used long-term high-resolution spectroscopic monitoring to measure the radial velocity curves of the two components of the central binary, and to derive their atmospheric parameters. We also undertook kinematical and chemical abundance analyses of the nebula itself. The orbital period of the central binary of exceeds five years and is highly eccentric. The binary comprises a relatively low-temperature sdO-type central star and a spun-up K-type giant companion. The Kiel mass of the central star is approximately half the dynamical mass derived from the radial velocities. While the systemic velocity and inclination of the nebula are consistent with the radial velocities of the binary, its abundance pattern adds support for a lower-mass progenitor that did not experience hot bottom burning (and is thus more consistent with the Kiel mass than the mass derived from the radial velocities). To the best of our knowledge, the central star of is only the fourth planetary nebula central star to have a spectroscopically confirmed orbital period longer than one year.

items.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
items.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. items.title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.

items.title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

items.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
items.abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

items.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
items.abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. items.title: EventDiffusion: Learning Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
items.abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.

items.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
items.abstract: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

items.title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
items.abstract: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
items.abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.

items.title: On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys
items.abstract: Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.

items.title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
items.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.

items.title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
items.abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.

items.title: Hybrid AI for AI-Native RAN Control: A Functional Perspective
items.abstract: AI-native radio access network (RAN) control involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales. Understanding how AI and conventional methods can jointly support these decisions requires a common basis for comparing their functional roles. This survey introduces a technique-agnostic taxonomy of RAN decision-making organized around four complementary capabilities: Representation and Reasoning, Prediction and Simulation, Adaptive Control, and Decision Synthesis. These capabilities are defined by their roles in the control process, independently of the techniques used to implement them. Through this perspective, we examine representative AI and model-based approaches, including foundation models, world models, reinforcement learning, and optimization. We then apply the taxonomy to representative RAN control solutions across slow, medium, fast, and cross-timescale applications to identify which capabilities they implement and how these capabilities are combined in hybrid AI systems. We also review datasets, benchmarks, simulators, digital twins, and experimental platforms according to their support for the decision-making process and reproducible evaluation. The review highlights a gap between the availability of resources for closed-loop experimentation and the standardization of tasks, metrics, and evaluation protocols needed for meaningful comparisons.Finally, we identify research directions for hybrid AI in AI-native RAN, including capability integration, multi-agent and cross-timescale coordination, constraint handling, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation. A curated list of surveyed works and evaluation resources is available at https://github.com/pegahani/Hybrid-AI-RAN-Survey.

items.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
items.abstract: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq

items.title: RecordRoute: Auditing Agent Failures with Localization-Guided Diagnosis
items.abstract: Auditing failed agent executions requires identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode. Representative supervised methods either focus on step localization or predict multiple attribution targets from shared trajectory representations. These methods do not use the localization result to select the text for mode diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose RecordRoute, which couples comparative localization with local diagnosis. Specifically, it represents each record with word and character features and learns to rank records through comparisons within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, while its text and metadata drive mode prediction. On controlled-injection Who&When Pro, RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon on all four official metrics. With actor and step predictions fixed, local diagnosis reaches 77.47% pooled joint accuracy versus 69.28% for full-trace diagnosis. On natural failures from TraceElephant and CatchBench POST, it outperforms these baselines and three open LLMs in localization.
