items.title: Acute physical effort enhances interoceptive accuracy without improving error awareness: evidence from the Heart Rate Discrimination Task.
items.abstract: According to Fechner's law, perceived sensations increase logarithmically with stimulus intensity. During exercise, rising physical effort is therefore accompanied by increasingly salient bodily signals such as heart rate. Interoception, the sensing of internal bodily states, supports adaptive responses to these changing demands, for instance, by guiding the regulation of exertion. Beyond physical regulation, interoceptive signals have also been proposed to inform higher-order monitoring processes, such as error detection. Yet it remains unclear whether acute exercise sharpens cardiac interoception and whether this would translate into greater awareness of errors. In a within-participant design, 36 healthy adults completed two tasks while cycling at low versus moderate intensity: a Heart Rate Discrimination Task assessing cardiac interoception and a Go/No-Go task measuring error awareness through post-error reports. Moderate effort reduced interoceptive bias, bringing participants' perceived heart rate closer to their actual heart rate, while discrimination precision remained unchanged. Confidence in interoceptive judgments increased under moderate effort, but this was not accompanied by improved metacognitive insight. In the Go/No-Go task, commission errors were more frequent at moderate intensity, whereas the proportion of detected errors was unchanged. Interoceptive performance did not reliably predict error awareness. These findings suggest that acute exercise recalibrates cardiac judgment bias rather than improving perceptual sensitivity or metacognitive monitoring. This recalibration did not extend to error awareness; however, given the temporal and reporting constraints of the task, the null effect cannot determine whether cardiac signals contribute causally to conscious error detection.

items.title: Sequential exposure to environmental chemicals and immune challenge leads to sex-specific changes in behavior, the hippocampal transcriptome, and thyroid signaling.
items.abstract: Individuals experience multiple environmental challenges through development that can set the trajectory for health and disease. Among these, both endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and infection/injury can alter neurodevelopment, leading to long-lasting behavioral changes. However, the interaction among EDCs, the immune system, and behavior remains poorly understood. We used a two-hit model to test the hypothesis that perinatal exposure to the known EDC Aroclor 1221 (A1221), a mixture of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), would alter neuroimmune pathways and the response to a later immune challenge, resulting in changes to social and anxiety-like behaviors. Pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats were orally administered A1221 or vehicle from embryonic day 8 through postnatal day (P) 4, and offspring were subsequently challenged with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or saline on P24. In females, A1221 and LPS exposure altered anxiety-like behavior and sociability outcomes, while in males, A1221 and LPS influenced anxiety-like behaviors, and A1221 alone increased preference for social novelty. Transcriptomic analysis of the hippocampal dentate gyrus revealed LPS treatment induced changes in synapse, cell adhesion, and myelination/glia related genes that were absent in rats exposed to A1221 prior to LPS treatment. Because these pathways are associated with thyroid hormones, we measured serum thyroid hormones, revealing LPS decreased circulating thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in males. Thyroid hormone reporter gene assays demonstrated that A1221 is a TRα antagonist but did not have an appreciable effect on TRβ. Together, these findings indicate that developmental PCB exposure alters neuroimmune and endocrine responsiveness to later immune challenge, resulting in enduring sex-specific behavioral changes.

items.title: Cumulative herpesvirus exposure is associated with reduced cerebellar volume in adolescents with and without early-onset psychosis.
items.abstract: Background Adolescence is a critical period of brain maturation, during which neuroimmune processes involved in neural circuit refinement may heighten sensitivity to effects of environmental exposures. Neurotropic herpesviruses such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) have been linked to structural brain differences in adults with severe mental illness, but little is known about similar associations in adolescents with early-onset psychosis (EOP), or in healthy youth. Methods We examined associations between CMV serostatus, HSV-1 serostatus, viral burden (0, 1, or 2 seropositive pathogens), and brain structure in 95 adolescents aged 12-18 years (34 with EOP, 61 healthy controls). Viral serostatus was determined using solid-phase immunoassays, and cortical and subcortical brain metrics were derived from T1-weighted MRI. Separate general linear models tested associations between each viral predictor and brain metric, adjusting for age, diagnostic group, sex, and intracranial volume, with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Higher viral burden was significantly associated with smaller cerebellar volume across all participants, independent of diagnostic status (F = 6.011; p = 0.004; pFDR = 0.029; η 2 p =0.120). In particular, individuals seropositive for both viruses displayed smaller cerebellar volumes than those seronegative (p = 0.001) or seropositive for one virus (p = 0.007). No significant associations were observed between individual viral serostatus and other brain measures after correction. Conclusions These findings identify the combined viral burden of HSV-1 and CMV as a potential contributor to individual differences in adolescent brain development, and underscore the need for longitudinal studies to clarify timing, mechanisms, and clinical relevance.

items.title: Pathogen, Commensal, Contaminant: The Context-Dependent Pathogenicity of Mycoplasmas
items.abstract: Background: Mycoplasma and its mollicute relatives appear as respiratory and urogenital pathogens, oral commensals, and cell-culture contaminants, three literatures that have largely evolved separately. Methods: We review the taxonomic and mechanistic literature and present an illustrative re-analysis of 24 representative species from public reference genomes (16S rRNA neighbor-joining and whole-genome protein k-mer clustering), together with bibliometrics of a curated three-theme dataset of 1,997 records. Results: The evidence reveals an asymmetric pattern in which adhesins differ at the protein-family level whereas host receptors are conserved molecules that differ in distribution and modification. Respiratory surface colonization evolved independently in three clades (M. pneumoniae, M. pulmonis, and M. hyopneumoniae), and the same species distributes measurably across pathogen, colonizer, and contaminant roles. Conclusions: Mycoplasma pathogenicity is a context-dependent property of the species-niche-host combination, a thesis that links tropism mechanisms, oral microbial ecology, and contamination control, and that exposes persistent receptor-assignment gaps.

items.title: Gradients of Pyrophytism in Obligate Seeders: Towards a Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum
items.abstract: Persistent soil seed banks are a defining feature of many obligate-seeding species in Mediterranean-type ecosystems, yet the extent to which fire-related germination responses vary among taxa remains poorly quantified. We propose a methodological framework to detect and measure gradients of pyrophytism within obligate seeders and evaluate whether such gradients can be interpreted within a broader Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum. Using raw germination, dormancy, and viability data for ten Cistaceae species from five genera exposed to eight heat treatments (25–120 °C), we reformulate the coupled germination–viability assay as a probabilistic diagnostic test in which germination is conditional on seed viability. From contingency-table metrics, we derive ROC-point distances and F1 scores as germinability descriptors that avoid limitations associated with the biological impossibility of false-positive germination events. We then introduce the Global Minimum Dispersion of Germinability (GMDG), a variance-based metric inspired by Markowitz portfolio theory, to quantify interspecific variation in heat-triggered germination responses. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity among species traditionally classified as obligate-seeding pyrophytes. Species rankings change across the heat-treatment gradient, and several taxa exhibit responses more consistent with opportunistic exploitation of favorable post-fire conditions than with strict fire adaptation. Ordination based on GMDG identifies a continuum ranging from highly heat-responsive species to comparatively opportunistic strategists. We argue that these patterns support the existence of a Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum linking fire ecology, bet-hedging theory, life-history evolution, and plant economics frameworks through alternative evolutionary investments in establishment versus temporal seed persistence.

items.title: Kick-Net Versus eDNA: Year-Round Methodological Comparison of Benthic Macroinvertebrate Community in an Alpine River.
items.abstract: In Alpine rivers, rapid melting of glaciers will lead to changes in aquatic ecosystems, yet their current state remains poorly known. Benthic macroinvertebrates have been a primary focus of monitoring in such ecosystems because they are highly sensitive to environmental disturbances. Traditionally, monitoring involves physical sampling such as using the kick-net method. Yet, such monitoring can be challenging or unfeasible due to harsh climatic conditions. Environmental DNA (eDNA) has been proposed as an alternative approach, as samples can be obtained without direct access to the river. However, the year-round feasibility of this technique, especially during winter months, and differences relative to kick-net sampling have not yet been fully assessed. Here, we compare kick-net and eDNA sampling as year-round tools to monitor alpine benthic communities. We sampled these communities every 2 months with both methods and examined the results in relation to the physicochemical parameters of the river (sediment load, temperature and conductivity). We found a significant correlation between the proportion of kick-net individuals and their detectability using eDNA, but this correlation was not as clear when using the relative read abundance of sequences instead of the binary detection of taxa. Among the key bioindicator groups, Diptera and Ephemeroptera showed significant positive correlations between eDNA and kick-net estimates, whereas Plecoptera and Trichoptera did not. As for kick-net data, we did not find a direct link between sediment load and a decrease in the number of individuals recovered. Overall, our results suggest that eDNA may serve as a year-round alternative to kick-net sampling, while also highlighting the need for further research to elucidate technique-specific biases among macroinvertebrate groups.

items.title: Soil eDNA Metabarcoding of Vascular Plants: Global Patterns in Marker Use and Reference Database Coverage.
items.abstract: Soil environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding has emerged as a promising tool for plant biodiversity monitoring, providing a scalable and minimally invasive complement to traditional vegetation surveys. However, its application to vascular plants remains constrained by methodological limitations, particularly limited species-level taxonomic resolution. Here, we present a global review of soil eDNA metabarcoding studies targeting vascular plants, focusing on marker choice, primer selection, and reference database coverage, with particular attention to underrepresented regions such as Africa. A systematic literature search identified 25 relevant studies. We analyzed patterns in marker use, habitat coverage and geographical distribution, and evaluated coverage of commonly used markers in the Barcode of Life Data System (BOLD). Both taxonomic and spatial representation of vascular plant barcodes were assessed. Research effort is concentrated in Europe, whereas reference database coverage was highest in North America and parts of Asia, especially China. Tropical regions, particularly Africa, remained poorly represented in both research activity and reference databases. Contrary to early expectations that rbc L and ITS2 would become the dominant markers for plant eDNA monitoring, the plastid trn L P6 loop and ITS2 were the most frequently used markers. The short trn L P6 loop facilitates amplification from degraded soil DNA, but this practical advantage comes at the cost of reduced taxonomic resolution. Markers such as ITS2 generally provide higher species-level resolution but remain limited by amplification biases and incomplete reference databases. Our review reveals a substantial mismatch between markers most commonly used in soil eDNA studies and those best represented in barcode databases. Future progress will depend on coordinated advances in marker selection, primer development, and, most importantly, the expansion of regionally representative reference libraries. Addressing these challenges will be particularly important in biodiversity-rich but underrepresented regions such as Africa, where eDNA metabarcoding has considerable potential for large-scale biodiversity monitoring and conservation.

items.title: Mitogenomic Evidence of Host Plasticity and Strict Phylogeographic Restriction in the Avian Malaria Parasite Plasmodium collidatum.
items.abstract: Avian malaria parasites ( Plasmodium spp.) are globally distributed pathogens that significantly affect host evolution and biodiversity. The rapid expansion-cancelation cycles that are characteristic of invasive lineages are well documented. However, the mechanisms maintaining the stability of endemic generalists remain poorly understood. This study aimed to resolve the evolutionary history and population genetics of Plasmodium collidatum (lineage pFANTAIL01) across three regions in Thailand with the use of a mitogenomic approach incorporating a 3315-bp concatenated dataset of cytb , cox1 , and cox3 . Phylogenetic reconstruction confirmed that P. collidatum was a robust monophyletic clade with substantial divergence (5.6%-5.7%) from its sister taxon ( P. ashfordi ). Results revealed a distinct phylogeographic paradox. In particular, although P. collidatum exhibited a high host plasticity across taxonomically diverse avian orders (Galliformes, Columbiformes, and Gruiformes), this genetic structure was strictly partitioned by geographic distance. The haplotype network analysis identified three site-specific haplotypes, indicating that the regional gene flow was constrained by localized vector communities rather than by host species barriers. The genetic diversity indices ( pi = 0.00072, Hd = 0.80) and the non-significant neutrality tests (Tajima's D = 1.64, Fu's Fs = 0.952) showed a state of neutral equilibrium, thereby reflecting long-term demographic stasis and endemic integration. Based on these findings, P. collidatum maintains a stable endemicity via local ecological exploitation rather than via contemporary range expansion. This study underscores the need for high-resolution mitogenomic markers to elucidate the fine-scale transmission dynamics of generalist parasites. Further, it provides an important molecular baseline for avian conservation biosecurity in Southeast Asia.

items.title: Longitudinal Patterns in Predator Diets Reveal Juvenile Chinook Salmon Predation Is Concentrated Upstream.
items.abstract: At the southern extent of their range, Chinook Salmon ( Oncorhynchus tshawytscha ) in California's Central Valley face myriad challenges, including altered hydrology, habitat degradation, and introduced species, that have led to poor survival during juvenile emigration and declining stocks. Predation by nonnative sport fish is considered a major source of mortality, but patterns in consumption have not been investigated over the entire migration corridor to understand where and when juvenile salmon are consumed. We used distribution and diet data from nonnative Striped Bass ( Morone saxatilis ) and black bass ( Micropterus spp.), collected over 130 km, from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta (Delta) to a major upstream tributary, to quantify and characterize predation on juvenile Chinook Salmon. Nonnative predators were distributed throughout the study area but relatively more abundant in the Delta than in the upstream tributary. Predated salmon were frequently observed in the upstream tributary, with none observed in the Delta. Environmental covariates and habitat attributes (e.g., discharge and bank armoring) typically thought to influence predation risk were not associated with longitudinal predation patterns, but distance downstream and predator size were, likely reflecting a prey availability gradient. The spatial pattern of predated salmon indicates that predation mortality occurs as soon as juvenile Chinook Salmon enter the migration corridor. Management actions taken in tributary reaches instead of downstream reaches may reduce predation mortality, complementing benefits from ongoing habitat restoration efforts to improve overall survival.

items.title: Physiology and the Co-Occurrence of Competing Carnivores: The Diet and Digestive Enzymes of Fishers (Pekania pennanti) and Martens (Martes americana and Martes caurina) in the Forests of the Great Lakes and the Sierra Nevadas.
items.abstract: The order Carnivora largely consists of predators of vertebrates, yet many have retained the ability to consume foods other than meat. The digestive capabilities of omnivory among carnivorans remain understudied. Fishers ( Pekania pennanti ) and martens ( Martes americana and M. caurina )-related and competing carnivores in forests across North America-are considered carnivorous, but some populations consume plants, insects, and fungi. We investigated the digestive capacity of both species from two regions: the Sierra Nevada, where fishers consume a range of diet items and the Great Lakes region, where both species are predominantly meat-eaters. We first demonstrated using zymography-based proteomics that both species produce trehalase, the enzyme required for digesting the principal carbohydrate in fungi and insects. We then tested whether fishers and martens had different digestive hydrolase (trehalase, maltase, sucrase, and aminopeptidase-N [APN]) profiles reflecting different dietary niches. Fishers and martens ( M. americana ) in the Great Lakes as well as martens ( M. caurina ) in the Sierra Nevadas were primarily meat eaters; however, fishers in the Sierra Nevadas consumed fungi and insects in similar proportions to meat. As predicted, we found that the investment in the activities of trehalase and maltase but not sucrase, relative to APN, was higher in fishers compared to martens. Consistent with the phylogenetic inertia hypothesis, fishers in the Sierra Nevadas did not differ in their investment in trehalase or maltase compared to fishers in the Great Lakes. These findings suggest that while both species possess some ability for diet and digestive flexibility, fishers constitutively produce higher trehalase and maltase activities in their small intestine than martens, which would allow them to have greater spare capacity to digest non-meat dietary items. This difference in digestive capacity may explain why fishers, despite being the dominant competitor, switch diets more readily than martens when they co-occur.

items.title: Life in the Fastlane-Circannual Spatio-Temporal Interactions Between Three Sympatric Shrew Species Reveals Dynamic Relationships.
items.abstract: Competition and niche segregation are fundamental processes shaping species coexistence in animal communities. While these dynamics are well studied in large mammalian predators, far less is known about how micro-predators, such as shrews, partition resources to promote coexistence. We investigated spatio-temporal interactions among three sympatric shrew species-common shrew ( Sorex araneus ), pygmy shrew ( S. minutus ), and water shrew ( Neomys fodiens ) in Denmark-using data collected using Double-Mostela camera trap boxes and a spatio-temporal multispecies occupancy model. We assessed dominance by modeling subordinate detection intensity conditional on the putative dominant species, comparing alternative dominance directions using AIC. We found the larger water shrew was dominant over common shrew and pygmy shrew, with the common and pygmy shrew dominance hierarchies varying across seasons. Spatial overlap was high, suggesting competitive exclusion was unlikely. Subordinate species tended to change activity patterns when sharing space with dominant species and/or temporarily avoided sites recently used by dominant species. These shifts are consistent with temporal niche partitioning and were especially apparent during energetically costly periods (i.e., breeding season and winter). Specifically, subordinate species shifted activity patterns to more diurnal in summer and more nocturnal in winter in response to a dominant species, which may expose them to greater temperature extremes. Although pygmy shrew and common shrew tended to co-occur in autumn and winter, pygmy shrew temporarily avoided sites recently used by common shrew representing an additional strategy for pygmy shrew to avoid direct competition with common shrew during a time of food scarcity. Our findings point to temporal partitioning, rather than spatial segregation, as a primary mechanism enabling coexistence of shrews under strong interspecific competition, highlighting the importance of time as a critical axis of niche differentiation in small mammal communities.

items.title: Same City, Different Fates: A Nature-Based Solution to Reducing Human-Bird Conflict in Urban Roosting Birds.
items.abstract: Roosting birds in cities often conflict with humans through droppings and noise. In this study, two sites of large aggregations of roosting birds only 1.4 km apart in Dongfang City, Hainan, south China, were surveyed and compared. One site, on the Donghai Road of the urban center, was used by barn swallows ( Hirundo rustica ) (more than 4600 individuals) and white wagtails ( Motacilla alba ) (more than 3000 individuals) and roosting in roadside trees at dusk (ca. 18:50-19:20 PM), coinciding with peak local human activity. Heavy droppings on pavements and shops triggered loud shouting, stamping, and severe branch cutting. In contrast, a small reed bed within the wetland site held large aggregations of red-billed starlings ( Spodiopsar sericeus ) (more than 21,000 individuals) roosting over water. A small water body acted as a natural barrier; droppings fell into the water, residents were not disturbed, and no conflict occurred. Thus, human-bird conflict depended not on spatial proximity but on effective physical buffers. We urge urban planners to incorporate offshore roosting habitats (islets, peninsulas, or floating islands) from pedestrian paths. These low-cost, proactive designs can prevent expensive post-conflict measures and achieve a win-win situation: safe bird refuges and humans enjoying nature without nuisance.

items.title: Climatic and Anthropogenic Drivers of Amphibian Richness and Vulnerability in Nigeria.
items.abstract: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group, yet broad-scale patterns of diversity, environmental sensitivity, and extinction risk remain poorly understood across tropical Africa. Nigeria supports high amphibian diversity at the interface of forest and savanna systems, but uneven survey coverage limits understanding of diversity patterns, environmental drivers, and climate risks. In this study, we assessed the patterns and drivers of amphibian species richness and species vulnerability, as well as the projected impacts of climate change on amphibians distributed across Nigeria. To do this, we analyzed 1110 spatially filtered occurrence records representing 119 species across the country. We combined multi-scale species richness analyses, boosted regression tree modeling, vulnerability assessments, climate projections for 25 sufficiently sampled species, and evaluations of projected changes in species richness inside and outside protected areas. Results showed that observed species richness was concentrated in southern forests and montane regions. However, more than 95% of grid cells lacked occurrence records, revealing substantial sampling gaps that limit robust inference at the national scale. Our study revealed the important role of Human Footprint Index in shaping amphibian species richness patterns in Nigeria. Results also showed that a subset of environmental variables such as isothermality, precipitation of the warmest quarter, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, mean diurnal range, and distance to the nearest river influenced the amphibian species richness patterns. Furthermore, 40 species (33.6%) were classified in the highest vulnerability category, particularly range-restricted taxa with narrow elevational ranges and high anthropogenic exposure. In addition, our study revealed spatial redistribution of species richness due to climate change, with projected species richness losses consistently greater outside protected areas. In sum, our study identifies southern forests and montane regions as priority areas for amphibian conservation under climate change while also revealing major gaps in knowledge of amphibian distributions across Nigeria. We recommend expanded surveys in poorly sampled regions to determine whether additional diversity remains undocumented and to strengthen national conservation planning for amphibians. Moreover, protecting Nigeria's amphibians will require conservation action beyond existing protected areas, particularly in unprotected landscapes where future species richness losses are projected to be greatest.

items.title: Optimizing Wildlife Survey Design: Simulating Drone and Helicopter Surveys for Moose Detection and Population Estimation.
items.abstract: Estimating population sizes is crucial for wildlife management, but conventional crewed aerial surveys are expensive and pose safety risks. Drone platforms offer a effective alternative, yet optimal survey designs remain unclear. This simulation study examined the influence of survey design, camera configuration, and moose ( Alces alces Linnaeus, 1758) density on the accuracy, precision and efficiency of drone surveys (fixed-wing and quadcopter) compared to helicopter surveys, using line-transect distance sampling with density surface models. Simulations used existing moose survey data from five wildlife management units in Alberta, Canada (2132-12,034 km 2 ). Systematic, zigzag and segmented grid transects for fixed-wing drones and systematic transects for quadcopters were compared to the helicopter's segmented grid design at equal survey effort. All simulated designs produced unbiased density estimates. Precision depended mainly on the assumed camera configuration rather than on the platform or the area covered: drones with a gimbal-mounted camera covered about 40% of each area but matched the precision of the helicopter, which covered 88% (coefficient of variation 0.07-0.08 vs. 0.08), whereas the narrow two-camera and nadir configurations increased the coefficient of variation by 60%-90%. Survey design influenced efficiency but not accuracy: zigzag designs achieved the highest proportion of on-transect flight (95%), and concentrating effort in subplots performed as well as spreading it across the whole area. Quadcopters were limited by low efficiency and the logistics of surveying many small subplots rather than by accuracy. These results are conditional on the simulated designs and assumed detection functions, and suggest that, if comparable drone detection is achieved in the field, fixed-wing drones with wide-swath cameras could provide an alternative to helicopter surveys. Field validation of drone detection for moose is needed, as canopy cover, snow, temperature and animal movement, which were not simulated, may affect real-world performance.

items.title: Recommendations for Integrating Non-Overlapping Legacy Data Into Mitogenome Studies: A Case Study of cox1 Data for Resolving Phylogenetic Relationships in Onthophagus (Scarabaeidae: Scarabaeinae: Onthophagini).
items.abstract: DNA barcoding initiatives have led to the generation of millions of cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 ( cox1 ) sequences, yet this resource remains underutilized for phylogenetic inference due to single-gene limitations. C ox1 barcodes can be integrated with genomic backbones to expand taxon sampling, but the phylogenetic consequences of heterogeneity within barcode datasets are unclear. Legacy datasets predominantly consist of the 5-P Folmer region, while other initiatives have increasingly sequenced 3-P fragments, both of which exhibit minimal overlap and differ in their evolutionary properties. The effects of fragment choice, partitioning strategy, and alignment trimming on phylogenetic accuracy are similarly unclear. We addressed these questions using the dung beetle genus Onthophagus Latreille, 1802. We augmented a previously published mitogenomic phylogeny by mining mitogenes from ultraconserved element (UCE) data and evaluated phylogenetic performance across 15 matrices representing four base datasets that vary in taxon sampling, alignment length, and partitioning scheme. Trees retaining the mitogenomic scaffold outperformed those trimmed to reduce missing data. Trees supplemented with 3-P fragments only generally recovered more clades and had higher nodal support. However, this pattern was concentrated in clades with disproportionate 3-P sampling and not consistently present in balanced clades, suggesting that fragment effects are likely lineage-specific. Combining 3-P and 5-P fragments resulted in the poorest tree performance overall. We applied this framework to evaluate the state of systematics for Western Hemisphere Onthophagus , finding broad support for existing species-group hypotheses. Our results provide empirical guidance for integrating heterogeneous cox1 barcode data into a phylogenomic framework.

items.title: Parent-Offspring Conflict Drives Selection for Integrated Egg Traits in the Male-Incubated Emu Egg.
items.abstract: Optimal early-life phenotypes, including those of the amniote egg, may differ for the parent and their offspring. Understanding the optimal offspring phenotype requires testing at the level of parent and offspring for all integrated traits, though this is rarely addressed in studies of avian egg evolution. Here, we use an uncommon avian system, the Australian emu ( Dromaius novaehollandiae ), with male-only parental care and polyandrous mating, to estimate selection for optimal egg phenotypes for offspring/mothers and for incubating fathers. Selection on multivariate egg traits was estimated, including the colour, shape and size. We found that the form of selection on these traits differed for the offspring/mother compared with the father. For offspring, linear selection favoured larger, elongated eggs of a dark, dull green colouration (i.e., lower brightness and saturation values), which may have functions in thermoregulatory or camouflage. For incubating males, significant negative linear selection was found for smaller nests which may occur if fathers are unable to cover and incubate extremely large nests that can contain more than 30 eggs, resulting in poor hatching success. Here, egg phenotype was shown to be the outcome of selection via the paternal, maternal and offspring phenotype that collectively influence the 'optimal' egg phenotype.

items.title: Sex-specific cumulative effects of inbreeding on lifetime fitness in purple-crowned fairy-wrens.
items.abstract: Complex environmental and genetic factors can cause inbreeding depression to vary across different life-history stages. However, disentangling inbreeding effects over the full lifespan remains challenging, as the required combination of detailed genomic, individual and ecological information is rarely available in natural populations. Here, we assess the effect of genomic inbreeding on fitness in the purple-crowned fairy-wren (Malurus coronatus coronatus), an endangered tropical passerine. Our study population has unusually accurate lifetime fitness measures for both sexes acquired during two decades of intensive individual-based study. We found evidence of more frequent inbreeding in the population than we would expect, given behavioural inbreeding avoidance. There was no evidence for a relationship between inbreeding and survival in the first year of life, despite our large sample size and ability to control for known environmental factors important in early-life. However, we found a negative relationship between inbreeding and the probability of breeding position acquisition as well as lifespan, resulting in substantially reduced lifetime fitness. Structural equation models identified an additional direct negative effect of inbreeding on lifetime reproductive success that was present in males only, despite very similar investment in offspring care by both parents. Overall, our results suggest pervasive, late-acting or cumulative effects of inbreeding that are partly sex-specific. Our findings emphasise that inbreeding depression in wild populations may be underestimated if cumulative lifetime impacts of inbreeding cannot be quantified. Additional study of inbreeding load and environmental interactions would be valuable in further understanding the mechanisms of inbreeding depression and the genomic and ecological factors underlying the sex difference. This is particularly important given the large reduction in lifetime fitness associated with realised levels of inbreeding in this population and the ongoing anthropogenic threats it is facing.

items.title: Linking predator-prey diel activity to predation patterns.
items.abstract: Time is a key ecological resource, and the partitioning of time among species can stabilize ecological interactions, including predation. Over ecological and evolutionary time scales, predator-prey interactions shape the diel activity patterns of both actors, and in turn, predator and prey activity drive patterns of predation. Recent methodological advances have facilitated the quantification of fine-scale animal temporal activity patterns. In response, there is growing interest in understanding patterns of diel overlap among predators and prey, with the assumption that temporal overlap translates into interaction frequency. However, the degree to which predator-prey diel overlap is correlated with the timing of predation should vary with predator and prey traits and environmental context. Here, we discuss the factors that should mediate the relationship between diel activity overlap and predation, including mobility, predator hunting and sensory modes, prey anti-predator defences, and diel variation in habitat selection. To formalize and visualize our hypotheses, we present the results from a simple agent-based model that highlights the context dependency of the link between overlap and predation. We contend that a core assumption underlying the study of temporal predator-prey dynamics-that overlap in activity translates into predation timing and frequency-is largely untested. Further, our agent-based model highlights key contributors to the decoupling of timing overlap and predation frequency, including predator sensory mode, predator and prey mobility, and, importantly, the predilection of predators to hunt while stationary or to hunt stationary prey. We suggest that future efforts quantify not only temporal overlap but also the timing of predation events, guided by the hypotheses presented here, to better understand the role of diel activity in predator-prey interactions. These insights may also shed light on the ecological implications of altered activity and overlap patterns under human disturbance.

items.title: Belowground Activity of the Entomopathogenic Nematode-Bacterium Complex Modulates Context-Dependent Associational Effects in Quercus robur.
items.abstract: Tree species diversity reduces herbivore damage through associational resistance, yet the cross-compartment mechanisms driving these effects remain unresolved. Beyond altering plant defences and herbivore host-finding, diverse plant communities reshape associated trophic networks. However, the role of belowground organisms in modulating these aboveground dynamics has received little attention. Entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) are key soil-dwelling organisms that induce systemic physiological changes in plants through chemical cues released by infected insect cadavers. These responses can alter plant growth, defensive allocation, and interactions with aboveground herbivores. We manipulated tree neighbourhood composition and exposure to Steinernema carpocapsae-infected larvae in a field experiment to assess effects on leaf phenolics, volatile emissions, herbivory, and biomass in Quercus robur saplings. Our results revealed contrasting responses among defensive traits: tree neighbourhood composition primarily determined constitutive phenolics, whereas VOC emissions were more plastic and depended on interactions between neighbourhood composition and exposure to EPN-infected cadavers. Specifically, sesquiterpene emissions declined when trees were exposed to infected cadavers in specific tree mixtures, potentially altering aboveground signalling. Although no significant overall effects on herbivory were detected, planned comparisons revealed more severe chewing damage in four-species mixtures under exposure to infected cadavers. This variation in herbivory was not accompanied by corresponding changes in structural biomass, a functional decoupling potentially consistent with a tolerance-like response, although tolerance was not directly quantified. Overall, our results suggest that belowground biotic interactions may modify aboveground associational effects by linking neighbourhood-dependent variation in plant chemistry, herbivory, and biomass allocation.

items.title: Renal histopathological alterations and elemental profiles in wild Mus musculus chronically exposed to a volcanic environment.
items.abstract: Volcanically active environments expose resident organisms to complex mixtures of gases, particulate matter, and geogenic elements, yet the renal effects of chronic residence in such settings remain poorly understood. We assessed renal histomorphometric alterations in wild Mus musculus from Furnas, a hydrothermally active area on São Miguel Island, Azores, using Rabo de Peixe as a reference location. Kidneys were examined by conventional histology, quantitative histomorphometry, and mercury-selective autometallography (AMG). Whole-tail tissues were additionally combined into location-specific composite samples and analysed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to characterise elemental profiles. Mice from Furnas showed a significantly enlarged Bowman's space, a narrower distal convoluted tubule lumen, and greater distal epithelial height, whereas proximal tubular parameters did not differ significantly. AMG revealed a significantly greater density of renal vascular mercury deposits in Furnas mice. Pooled whole-tail samples from Furnas had higher mean concentrations of Hg, Pb, Cr, Ni, and Cd, whereas Ba, Co, Sr, Ti, and V were higher in Rabo de Peixe. These findings demonstrate selective glomerular and distal tubular alterations, greater renal vascular mercury deposition, and a distinct multielemental profile in mice chronically inhabiting the Furnas volcanic environment. Although the contribution of individual elements cannot be resolved, the results support a renal biological response to chronic volcanogenic exposure and reinforce the value of wild mice as sentinels of environmental health.

items.title: Global patterns of cultivated plant diversity and their implications for invasion.
items.abstract: People have cultivated plants for their wide-ranging services for millennia, introducing thousands of species to new regions through human migration and trade. By increasing the number and abundance of introduced species and selecting for particular traits, cultivation likely promotes the self-sustained establishment (naturalization) of alien species. Using a recently collated database of 3050 lists of vascular plant species cultivated around the world, we characterized the global cultivated flora and explored the role of cultivation in naturalization. The global cultivated flora is highly diverse, comprising about a quarter of all known vascular plant species. Species richness and phylogenetic richness of cultivated plants were highest in temperate, species-rich regions. Most species were alien to the regions where they were cultivated and were climatically suited to these regions. The majority (84.6%) of species that have naturalized world-wide are cultivated, and alien cultivated species richness strongly predicted naturalization within regions. This suggests that global regional patterns of naturalization are most directly shaped by the human-mediated introduction of plants for cultivation. Our findings provide a broad description of cultivated plant diversity and demonstrate the tight coupling of cultivation and naturalization at the global scale.

items.title: A 2027 horizon scan of biological conservation issues.
items.abstract: We present our 18th horizon scan of issues that may impact global biodiversity conservation in the next decade. Issues are either novel (largely unknown) or represent a substantial step-change in impact. The initial list of 96 issues was scored by 28 scientists, practitioners, and policymakers. The 35 highest-ranked issues were discussed at a workshop and then rescored to identify the 15 top-ranked issues. Activities in space feature prominently this year with mirrors that could affect nocturnal wildlife and interrupted satellite data affecting global environmental monitoring. We highlight an increase in data manipulation for financial gain and a disconnect between temperature increases at the sea surface and the seafloor. Raising awareness of these issues could provide early opportunities to mitigate foreseeable impacts on biodiversity conservation.

items.title: A brief stocktake of the leaf economics spectrum centred on leaf lifespan and specific leaf area.
items.abstract: The leaf economics spectrum (LES) was proposed as an analogy linking leaf construction, physiology, lifespan, and ecological strategy. Two decades later, its value lies both in relation to broad-scale trait correlations and to questions those correlations continue to generate. We revisit the LES with emphasis on the leaf lifespan-specific leaf area relationship, a direct expression of the investment-duration trade-off at the heart of leaf economics. Subsequent work has revealed scale dependence from leaves to ecosystems and exposed persistent misunderstandings, such as the assumption that fast-return leaves necessarily imply fast-growing adult plants. Future advances need targeted leaf lifespan data, stronger cost-benefit theory, and more comprehensive tests of how LES relationships shift across environments, ontogeny, and organisational scales.

items.title: Phylogenomic analyses shed new light on the phylogeny and historical biogeography of the water lily genus Nymphaea (Nymphaeaceae).
items.abstract: Nymphaea is the most species-rich, geographically widespread, and phenotypically diverse genus in the basal angiosperm order Nymphaeales. Species of this genus possess considerable ornamental, cultural, medicinal, and ecological value. However, phylogenetic relationships among species and the biogeographic history of this genus remain incompletely understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive phylogenomic study of Nymphaea using cytoplasmic (plastid and mitochondrial) and nuclear genomic sequence data. Our phylogenetic analyses supported the merger of the genera Victoria and Euryale into Nymphaea. The significant phylogenetic discordance detected within Nymphaea was attributed to both incomplete lineage sorting and reticulate evolution. Moreover, network analyses suggested that hybridization and "ghost introgression" have likely been widespread throughout the evolutionary history of the genus. Molecular dating and biogeographic analyses indicated that Nymphaea originated in the Oriental region during the mid-Cretaceous and subsequently dispersed to other regions, where multiple centers of diversification were established. Long-distance dispersal and vicariance appear to have jointly shaped the intercontinental distribution of the genus. These findings provide new insights into the phylogeny and evolutionary history of Nymphaea.

items.title: Slow-release carbon source of zoned in-situ fermentation for enhancing advanced nitrogen removal in anammox system: microbial structure enhancement and carbon-nitrogen synergistic mechanism.
items.abstract: The process of anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) frequently encounters challenges associated with nitrate accumulation and limited total inorganic nitrogen (TIN) removal efficiency, primarily due to the activity of competing nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) and the production of NO 3 - as a metabolic byproduct. This study introduced an Integrated Anammox and Zoned In-situ Fermentation (IAZIF) process designed to enhance anaerobic ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AnAOB) activity and facilitate NO 3 - removal. Over 198 days of continuous operation across five stages, the IAZIF system increased the TIN removal efficiency from 48.6% to 85.7% and reduced the average effluent NO 3 - concentration from 20.99 mg/L to 5.56 mg/L. Batch tests demonstrated that fermentation liquid promoted AnAOB activity and facilitated denitrification. Metagenomic analysis indicated an enrichment of fermentation bacteria and an increase in the abundance of genes encoding key enzymes involved in the degradation of polysaccharides, proteins, and fatty acids. Furthermore, the abundances of functional genes associated with partial denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium increased, suggesting an enhanced genetic potential for NO 3 - conversion to NO 2 - or NH 4 + . Meanwhile, the activity of AnAOB increased, consolidating the dominant position of AnAOB. The relative abundance of Candidatus Brocadia in the reaction zone rose from 0.57% to 3.28%, while the relative abundance of NOB decreased from 3.84% to 1.45%. IAZIF system not only improved anammox performance and maintained a low relative abundance of NOB but also promoted efficient NO 3 - removal. This study provided a valuable theoretical insight for mitigating NO 3 - accumulation and enhancing the anammox process to achieve advanced nitrogen removal.

items.title: Mechanisms of iron-mediated nitrogen removal under contrasting carbon-to-nitrogen ratios: Enhanced nitrate reduction and potential coupling with ammonium oxidation.
items.abstract: The roles of iron in nitrogen removal through iron-mediated denitrification and anaerobic ammonium oxidation coupled to Fe(III) reduction (Feammox) under contrasting carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratios remain unclear. Under carbon-sufficient conditions (chemical oxygen demand (COD)/NO 3 - -N = 16.9-18.7), NO 3 - -N removal increased with iron concentration. At 12 h, removal efficiencies were 71%, 83% and 92.3% in the low-, intermediate- and high-Fe(II) groups, respectively (initial Fe(II): 198.6, 305.5 and 393.6 mg/L). Under carbon-limited conditions (COD/NO 3 - -N = 0.85-1.07), intermittent NO 3 - -N addition promoted Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycling and accelerated NO 3 - -N and NH 4 + -N removal at higher iron concentrations (initial Fe(II): 47.6, 103.2 and 157.4 mg/L). On day 30, relative to the low- and intermediate-Fe(II) groups, the high-Fe(II) group showed respective reductions of 25% and 18% in residual NO 3 - -N concentration, 30.9% and 18.3% in residual NH 4 + -N concentration. The detection of iron-oxidizing/reducing microorganisms and 29 N 2 / 30 N 2 , together with the undetectable nitrifiers and anaerobic ammonium oxidation bacteria/genes, suggested that NH 4 + -N was most likely removed by Feammox. At both C/N ratios, iron likely enhanced nitrate-dependent ferrous oxidation (NDFO)-mediated NO 3 - -N reduction to NO 2 - -N, followed by Fe(II)-driven chemodenitrification of the resulting NO 2 - -N. This interpretation was consistent with the enrichment of potential NDFO genera, nitrate reductase genes, and Fe(II)-oxidation-associated genes, alongside decreased nitrite reductase gene abundance at higher iron concentrations. These suggested that Fe(II) accelerated nitrate removal through iron-mediated denitrification involving NDFO and/or chemodenitrification under both carbon-sufficient and carbon-limited conditions, while generating Fe(III) potentially available for Feammox. The study demonstrates distinct roles of iron in enhancing nitrate removal and potentially coupling nitrate and ammonium removal for low-C/N wastewater.

items.title: Source population identity predicts success better than environmental matching in stickleback introductions.
items.abstract: Species introductions and transplants offer powerful contexts to understand evolutionary patterns and processes, and they are increasingly critical for conservation. However, introduction success varies widely, and predicting outcomes remains challenging. Using multiple source populations should increase the chance of introduction success, while also providing an opportunity to explore the factors that predict success of individual source populations in the same environment. We used replicated, mixed-population introductions of >12,000 threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) to test whether source population success could be predicted by environmental matching between source and recipient environments and/or by source population characteristics. We introduced four to eight source populations of stickleback into each of nine natural lakes with no other stickleback and tracked their relative success over the following 2 years (up to two generations). Source population success was largely consistent across lakes, despite divergent environmental conditions. These results point to the importance of consistent source population differences rather than environmental matching in determining introduction success in natural settings. Source populations that were consistently successful tended to have greater stress tolerance and higher genetic diversity, though these relationships were not conclusive. Our study highlights the value of considering factors that generate fitness differences independent of environmental context when predicting ecological and evolutionary dynamics and planning conservation programs.

items.title: PBPK-based prediction of human health risks from cadmium-contaminated shellfish under ocean warming and acidification.
items.abstract: Climate-driven changes in seawater temperature and acidification may alter Cd bioaccumulation in shellfish and associated human health risks. We integrated a generalized additive model, dietary data, a physiologically based pharmacokinetic model, and Monte Carlo simulations to assess Cd exposure in Taiwanese adults aged 19-65 years under current conditions (20.1 °C, pH 8.1) and a hypothetical 2100 scenario under SSP5-8.5 (23.7 °C, pH 7.7). Urinary Cd concentrations were simulated after 46 years of exposure, and hazard quotients (HQs) were evaluated using a conservative screening value of 0.2. Under the 2100 scenario, the geometric mean shellfish Cd concentration increased from 0.11 to 0.59 μg/g. In the whole group (WG), median urinary Cd concentrations increased from 0.021 to 0.069 μg/g creatinine in males and from 0.023 to 0.097 μg/g creatinine in females; corresponding 90th-percentile (P90) HQs reached 0.235 and 0.351. The consumer-only (CO) group had higher predicted exposure, with P90 HQs reaching 0.780 in males and 1.163 in females. These scenario-specific findings indicate potential renal health concerns requiring further assessment, particularly in the CO group. Future food safety regulations should incorporate climate change projections and an acceptable-risk framework when establishing or reviewing Cd limits in shellfish.

items.title: Coupling relationship and threshold calculation between forest degradation/improvement and carbon-water use efficiencies in Northeast Asia.
items.abstract: Carbon use efficiency (CUE) and water use efficiency (WUE) are key parameters of terrestrial carbon-water cycling that strongly influence forest degradation and improvement. Previous studies have mainly focused on the independent spatial-temporal dynamics of CUE and WUE, while the coupling relationships, ecological thresholds, and coordinated responses between CUE-WUE and forest degradation/improvement remain insufficiently explored. Focusing on the temperate-boreal transition zone of Northeast Asia, this study constructed an analytical framework integrating MK-Sen trend analysis, coupling coordination degree, and ROC analysis-based threshold identification to examine relationships between forest degradation/improvement and the long-term evolution of carbon-water use efficiencies between 2001 and 2021. The results showed that CUE in Northeast Asia exhibited a declining trend, while WUE showed an increasing trend, with 31.08% and 50.78% of the forest area experiencing increase trend, respectively. The coupling coordination degrees between forest degradation/improvement and carbon-water use efficiencies were 0.711 and 0.663, indicating moderate coordination. Moreover, the CUE and WUE spearman's correlation coefficient are -0.0231 (-0.0234--0.0228, 95% CI, P < 0.001***) and -0.0270 (-0.0273--0.0267, 95%CI, P < 0.001***), indicating the weak negative correlation. When the CUE trend exceeded 0.0005 and the WUE trend surpassed -0.005, forests shifted toward improvement. Approximately 51.54% of improved forests were driven by WUE increases, while 21.11% of the region showed degradation risks. This study advances the understanding by linking CUE-WUE trajectories with forest degradation/improvement processes and identifying critical ecological thresholds associated with forest transition risks., offering carbon-water efficiencies-based evidence for identifying areas at risk of forest degradation as well as supporting the assessment work for SDG 15.3.1 (Land Degradation Neutrality, LDN).

items.title: Ecosystem multifunctionality responses to post-restoration grazing in seeded versus fenced alpine grasslands on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau.
items.abstract: Current grassland restoration assessments largely focus on vegetation and soil improvements during grazing exclusion, yet the long-term trajectories and plant-soil regulatory mechanisms of ecosystem multifunctionality (EMF) following grazing resumes remain unclear. We constructed a 13-year post-restoration grazing experiment on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau (QXP), integrating field vegetation surveys, multi-index soil measurements, Bayesian regression, structural equation modeling and driver-EMF correlation analysis to compare EMF sustainability between seeded grasslands (SG) and fenced grasslands (FG). Our results demonstrated FG maintained significantly higher EMF than degraded grasslands over the full 13-year period, declining at a slow annual rate. This stability was sustained by a streamlined cascade centered on vegetation height that connects native species richness and soil nitrate nitrogen. Weak linear coupling between individual drivers and EMF endows naturally restored FG with sufficient functional redundancy to buffer sustained grazing pressure. By contrast, SG achieved striking EMF elevation during the first three years of re-grazing, however, it experienced rapid functional degradation, falling below the degraded grassland (DG) reference level by year nine. SG's multifunctionality relies on a strongly coupled, ammonium-dominated network; grazing-induced reductions in vegetation height, soil moisture, species abundance, and mineral nitrogen availability, driving rapid functional decline that, within the 13-year observation window, reduced EMF below the reference degraded level, despite minor compensatory effects from nitrate pools. A unified critical intervention window spanning 3-5 years after grazing resumption was identified, during which Bayes factors provided anecdotal evidence (<3) for EMF divergence between restoration modes and soil nitrogen cycling remained intact. Synthesising our mechanistic findings, we reveal that fenced grasslands sustain long-term EMF via a streamlined height-nitrate-species richness cascade with consistently weak driver-EMF coupling, whereas seeded grasslands exhibit a strongly coupled, ammonium-dominated multi-pathway network that delivers short-term productivity gains but undergoes rapid functional decline after five years of grazing. These contrasting plant-soil functional frameworks provide a mechanistic basis for designing differentiated post-restoration management strategies on the QXP.

items.title: Rethinking broad diet breadth as a sign of scarcity: A 50,000-y record of subsistence from northwestern Australia.
items.abstract: The prey choice model, widely applied in archaeological reconstructions of Pleistocene diet, predicts that people will initially focus on a narrow suite of high-ranked prey before broadening their diet to include lower-ranked species as necessitated by subsistence needs. However, evidence from arid and semiarid northern Australia challenges this assumption. Archaeological faunal records demonstrate that a broad diet was established early and persisted through the Holocene. We argue that these diverse diets do not indicate resource scarcity, but rather represent an ideal strategy for exploiting abundant, low-risk hidden, or cryptic prey, as well as high-risk, conspicuous prey within an environment characterized by unpredictable rainfall. This pattern also necessitates reconceptualizing traditional notions of prey rank and dietary breadth. Rather than adhering to static prey rankings, northern Australian peoples skillfully adapted their hunting strategies in response to fluctuating nutritional content and pursuit costs of different species. The most successful subsistence strategy in this region was therefore one of high responsiveness and flexibility, manifesting as a consistently broad diet. This case study suggests that the relationship between human dietary breadth and resource abundance is more nuanced in situations of abundant, cryptic prey.

items.title: Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama's anchoveta fishery and its exports.
items.abstract: In 2025 the seasonal upwelling of the Gulf of Panama failed. Net primary production fell by 64% across the Gulf and industrial anchoveta landings dropped to 11% of the average, the lowest since the fishery became fully exploited in 1966. Anchoveta caught per purse-seine set fell to under a third of the normal rate while total catch per set stayed within its normal range. Landed fish carried about half their usual lipid content, and fish oil exports fell by 88% in both volume and value. The effects of one failed season reached international trade within months. Seasonal upwellings like this are common across the tropics yet far less studied than the large eastern boundary systems. The very strong El Niño now under way makes the 2027 season more uncertain.

items.title: Phase coding supports neuronal replication and enables combinatorial problem solving.
items.abstract: Darwinian neurodynamics posits that the brain searches large solution spaces through iterated cycles of variation and selection on competing neural representations. Testing this hypothesis requires a biologically plausible neural replicator: a mechanism that copies spatiotemporal signals faithfully enough to cumulatively improve good solutions, yet loosely enough to allow exploration. We show that phase-coded spike patterns constitute such a replicator. Spike timing referenced to a local field oscillation is compressed into a transferable spike train and reconstructed by coincidence with the receiver's own field, without synaptic plasticity or a shared code key. As replication noise rises, the system crosses two thresholds. Below the first, faithful copying sustains patterns as dynamic memory. Between the two thresholds, pattern populations evolve. On two hard combinatorial benchmarks, the traveling salesman problem and NK fitness landscapes, neural replication remains competitive with standard search methods at a matched evaluation budget. Beyond the second, an Eigen-like error threshold, inherited information collapses. The network architecture tunes the exploration-exploitation balance: high-degree lattices, where local competition is stronger, exploit smooth landscapes, while low-degree lattices, where weaker competition preserves diversity, search more broadly on rugged landscapes. The framework predicts phase-locked information transfer and phylogenetic structure in replay, as well as a selective loss of combinatorial problem solving beyond the error threshold. These results indicate that a single neurobiological substrate can support memory, variation, and selection, and point to evolutionary dynamics as a candidate computational principle for cognition.

items.title: Genetic architectures of floral pigment and patterning in hybrid monkeyflowers.
items.abstract: Coloration in living organisms varies in hue, saturation, and pattern. Here we use genetic mapping to investigate all three elements in monkeyflowers Mimulus luteus var. variegatus and M. cupreus, whose flower petals differ in both yellow carotenoid and magenta cyanidin (anthocyanin) pigmentation and whose hybrids exhibit anthocyanin pattern variation not seen in either parent. We report two QTLs associated with carotenoid intensity, and show that lighter yellow petals accumulate relatively high proportions of beta-carotene at the expense of downstream carotenoids. We propose that the derived loss of carotenoid saturation in M. l. variegatus is due to a function-reducing mutation in a Beta-Carotene Hydroxylase candidate gene, possibly coupled with a reduction in the availability of carotenoid-storing chromoplasts influenced by the ORANGE candidate gene. We next identify five QTLs associated with the spatial patterning of anthocyanin pigment. Two QTLs, 9b and 23, each contain genes in the anthocyanin-activating subgroup of the MYB family. We hypothesize that MYB5a/NEGAN, at QTL-9b, activates spot formation in hybrids as part of a Turing-type reaction-diffusion system, while a MYB at QTL-23 activates solid, non-Turing-type anthocyanin pigmentation and may also be able to activate the variegatus allele of MYB5a/NEGAN. In addition to the apparently stochastic placement of most spots (consistent with a Turing mechanism), some pattern aspects - such as spots at the petal tips - appear to conform to a positional specification model in which spot location is predetermined. Collectively, this work begins to identify how combinations of yellow and red hues, shifts in carotenoid intensity, and two cryptic patterning systems all contribute to the complexity of color divergence between two close relatives.

items.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
items.abstract: When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation-selection-drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

items.title: Safety collaborative prevention and control technology for coal mining beneath oil pipelines.
items.abstract: Coal mining beneath oil pipelines requires a balance between resource recovery and the control of mining-induced pipeline deformation. Using coal seam at Haichatan Coal Mine and the Jingbian-Yulin refined-oil pipeline as a case study, a coupled analysis framework was developed to link ground movement, relative pipe-soil displacement, and pipeline equivalent stress. The probability integral method was used to predict ground subsidence, tilt, horizontal strain, and curvature. The three-dimensional ground-displacement field was then applied to a nonlinear Winkler foundation model implemented in ANSYS. Sixteen scenarios were defined by combining two pipeline branches, two mining scales, and four mining-thickness levels. For full-thickness extraction of three panels, the maximum predicted ground subsidence along the western and eastern branches was 1 480 and 1 634 mm, respectively. The corresponding maximum pipeline equivalent stresses were 728 and 946 MPa, with strength-utilization ratios of 2.79 and 3.62. Reducing the effective mining thickness to 0.2M decreased these stresses to 255 and 227 MPa; however, the western branch remained close to the adopted limit, with a strength-utilization ratio of 0.977. Effective mining thickness strongly influenced the predicted response within the scenarios examined. A candidate control strategy combining a 2.3 m mining-thickness limit with trench excavation, pressure reduction, and pipeline lifting where necessary was proposed. Its safety requires further verification because the thickness limit alone does not establish compliance. A monitoring framework integrating InSAR, ground surveys, pipeline strain measurements, and trench-displacement measurements was also proposed to support model calibration and staged intervention. The framework provides a basis for assessing coal extraction beneath long-distance pipelines in areas with overlapping coal and petroleum resources.

items.title: A review: efficient microbial remediation technologies for petroleum-contaminated soils under the concept of ecological civilization.
items.abstract: Petroleum-contaminated soils have become a global environmental concern, posing significant risks to ecosystem integrity and human health. This review systematically analyzed 1105 publications from 2011 to 2026 (with 2026 partially indexed) to summarize the research progress and engineering applications of microbial remediation technologies for petroleum-contaminated soils. Keyword clustering and evolutionary analysis suggested that microbial remediation has evolved from early biostimulation and single-strain bioaugmentation toward the construction of microbial consortia, remediation with functional materials, plant-microbe synergistic strategies, and the integration of multiple technologies. Patent evolution analysis further indicated shifts in technological development and identified potential technology gaps and challenges in engineering applications. The application scenarios and enhancement strategies have continuously expanded. Laboratory, pilot-scale, and field studies indicate that microbial remediation promotes petroleum hydrocarbon degradation through microbial metabolism and cometabolism; however, its application remains constrained by high contaminant concentrations, aging effects, limited bioavailability, insufficient colonization stability of functional microorganisms, and challenges in large-scale field implementation. Combining microbial remediation with biochar, biosurfactants, electrokinetic remediation, and chemical oxidation can further improve remediation performance by optimizing microbial environments, enhancing contaminant bioavailability, and promoting electron transfer. Nevertheless, adaptation to extreme environments, precise regulation of remediation processes, and the establishment of green and low-carbon evaluation frameworks remain key challenges. This review provides theoretical insights and technical references for effective, green, and sustainable remediation of petroleum-contaminated soils.

items.title: Ultra-high hydrostatic pressure combined with tea saponin micelles enhances naringin extraction from pomelo peel.
items.abstract: Pomelo peel is a citrus-processing by-product rich in naringin, a high-value bioactive flavonoid, but its dense tissue matrix and naringin's limited aqueous solubility constrain efficient extraction. We therefore developed an aqueous process combining ultra-high hydrostatic pressure (UHHP) with tea saponin micelles to address both tissue disruption and solubilization. Conductor-like screening model for real solvents (COSMO-RS) calculations, followed by experimental screening, identified tea saponin as the most suitable candidate among the tested surfactants. Response surface methodology gave optimal conditions of 293 MPa, 80.8 mg/mL tea saponin, a liquid-to-solid ratio of 25 mL/g, three pressure cycles, and a holding time of 4.45 min per cycle. Under these conditions, mean naringin recovery and extraction yield reached 80.3% and 9.58 mg/g, respectively. In a laboratory-scale comparison with ethanol maceration and ultrasound- and microwave-assisted extraction, the UHHP-micellar process gave the highest yield and shorter treatment time, together with lower calculated energy use and CO 2 emissions within the laboratory-scale comparison. Scanning electron microscopy indicated marked disruption and increased porosity of the peel matrix, while Fourier transform infrared spectra showed no new major bands attributable to naringin degradation. Density functional theory calculations supported hydrogen-bonding and van der Waals interactions between naringin and the modeled tea saponin structure, and molecular dynamics simulations suggested pressure-induced micellar compaction and retention of naringin after decompression. The enhanced extraction performance is attributed to complementary contributions from tissue disruption, micellar solubilization, and noncovalent association. These findings provide a basis for further scale-up, downstream purification, and life-cycle evaluation of an aqueous route for recovering poorly soluble flavonoids from citrus-processing by-products.

items.title: Lead bioaccumulation in urban wall lizards (Podarcis muralis).
items.abstract: Lead (Pb) has toxic effects on wildlife and humans including anemia, delayed development, and reproductive failure. Anthropogenic land use introduces risks of soil Pb contamination from industrial activity and automobile traffic. Few studies have examined heavy metal toxicokinetics in reptiles, and whether soil Pb concentrations can be used to predict the Pb concentration of reptile tissues. In this study, we examined the Pb content of soils and tissues from common wall lizards (Podarcis muralis) from three sites with differing urban infrastructure in Cincinnati, Ohio (USA). The highest Pb concentrations were observed in soil and lizard blood from a site with elevated vehicle and railroad traffic. Juvenile lizards had lower blood Pb concentrations than adult females, though blood Pb concentrations were not correlated with body size or body condition. Pb concentrations were not correlated among oviductal eggs, blood, and livers within individuals, but blood and livers exhibited higher Pb concentrations than eggs. These results suggest that female lizards may be accumulating Pb, or excreting Pb using pathways besides vitellogenesis. We advocate the need for further study of Pb toxicokinetics in reptiles, including additional tissues that are infrequently examined, such as kidneys, brains, and bones. Reptiles can serve as bioindicators and reveal environmental Pb contamination that could be harmful to wildlife, pets and humans.

items.title: The Self-Powered Nanofiltration Membrane Driven by Pulsed Pressure for Efficient Selective Separation of Na<sup>+</sup>/Ca<sup>2</sup>.
items.abstract: Enhancing electrostatic repulsion against divalent cations in the selective layer is effective in improving monovalent/divalent cation separation in nanofiltration. However, conventional grafting and coating strategies are limited by insufficient reaction sites or poor coating stability, both of which restrict further improvements in monovalent/divalent cation selectivity. Herein, a positively charged nanofiltration membrane with a piezoelectric response (PQNF) was designed via reverse thermally induced phase separation (RTIPS) coupled with interfacial polymerization (IP). RTIPS endowed the poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) substrate with a sponge-like pore structure, a narrow pore-size distribution, and a high β-phase content. Subsequently, the PQNF membrane was prepared via IP, quaternization, and corona poling. Under pulsed pressure operation, a periodic in situ voltage of 0.4 V was generated, which contributed to the 98.7% Ca 2+ rejection and a Na + /Ca 2+ separation factor of 89.6. The membrane also maintained stable separation performance over 144 h and showed enhanced antifouling performance under pulsed pressure operation in a 14 h fouling test. Finally, an "electrostatic-piezoelectric synergistic enhancement" separation mechanism was proposed and supported by molecular dynamics simulations.

items.title: Evolutionary relatedness is a partially reliable predictor of host-associated microbiome composition.
items.abstract: Multicellular animals emerged into a microbial world, and they continue to be influenced by sympatric bacterial species. Host-associated microbiomes are recognized as critical contributors to their living domicile's success. Detailing how microbiomes are assembled and maintained by their hosts has important implications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and biodiversity interventions across the tree of life. Tens to 100s of bacterial genera are frequently detected in animal microbiomes, with some being uniquely and consistently detected in specific host species. Such discoveries have informed theories like phylosymbiosis that assert that host-associated microbiomes often reflect host species relatedness. We explored the predictive limits of this theory by performing a multi-scale dissimilarity-based comparative analyses using publicly available microbiomes drawn from 113 insect species spanning 14 insect orders. We detected a moderate inter-order phylosymbiotic signal (Mantel test: r = 0.392, P r = 0.173, P < 0.001) when the Blattodea were excluded from the analysis. Intra-order level phylosymbiotic signals varied widely for lepidopteran, hymenopteran, hemipteran, and blattodean host species microbiomes. Strong signals were often explained by obligate endosymbionts and/or nestmate-acquired gut bacteria, rather than by the total microbiomes. In short, host species-defining bacterial genera often represented a small fraction of the total observed microbial diversity in their respective insect host species, and these genera were well-integrated into host behaviors and/or physiologies that facilitated reliable intra- and inter-generational transmission. In contrast, microbiome compositional variability was so high in some insect orders that attempts to reflect host speciation events using their microbiomes were impossible.IMPORTANCEWhile all animals have microbiomes, the principles determining their composition remain an incomplete story. We leveraged the diversity of Insecta, arisen from 400 My of evolution, to evaluate if microbiome evolution is synchronized with the evolutionary history of their associated hosts. We found that host evolution plays a limited role in predicting microbiome composition, particularly due to the non-uniformity of host-microbial symbioses across insects. This result is in stark contrast to studies of similar scope in vertebrate organisms that spanned much less evolutionary time (i.e., up to 50 My). While insects of the order Blattodea, in particular, harbor exceptionally diverse microbiomes, many insect microbiomes are characterized by few bacterial genera. Our results suggest that host evolutionary history is but one of many factors, including differences in microbiome transmission modality, influencing insect microbiome evolution.
