items.title: Cats in the dark: A review of our current knowledge of the deep-sea catshark genus Apristurus.
items.abstract: The deep-sea catsharks in the genus Apristurus (Pentanchidae) constitute one of the most species-rich yet least resolved elasmobranch lineages. Herein, we utilised a systematic literature search to synthesise current knowledge on their diversity, morphology, phylogeny, distribution, ecology, reproduction and threats, and outline priorities for research aligned with the UN Decade of Ocean Science. The genus currently comprises 43 described extant species and three extinct taxa. Morphologically, Apristurus species share cephalic dorso-ventral compression, broad spatulate snouts and diagnostic labial-furrow states; meristics (including vertebral counts) and egg-capsule morphology provide additional taxonomic signal. Morphological ratios and fin shapes are also valuable for identification. Phylogenetic evidence generally supports monophyly of the genus and recovery of three species groups (brunneus, spongiceps, longicephalus), although some recent morphology-led hypotheses warrant further genomic testing. Apristurus is circumglobal (excluding polar seas and the Mediterranean), occupies depths ca. 24-2652 m and functions primarily as a generalist mesopredator, with region- and species-specific trophic specialisation. Reproductive ecology is oviparous; egg capsules commonly aggregate on structurally complex substrates (e.g., sponges and corals) where local hydrodynamics likely enhance embryonic ventilation. Fossil egg cases at cold seeps indicate long-standing associations with complex deep-sea habitats. Major threats to the genus arise from deep-sea trawl bycatch and emerging seabed industries. Threats are exacerbated by genus life-history traits (prolonged development, low fecundity) which imply high sensitivity, though many species remain listed as Least Concern owing to a paucity of data due to the depths at which the genus lives. Key research gaps identified include the need for a robust, integrative taxonomy; publicly accessible genetic reference libraries; in situ behavioural and life-history observations; quantification of bycatch and post-release mortality; and assessment of climate and mining impacts on nursery habitats. We provide a consolidated baseline of information to assist with accelerated discovery, identification and conservation of Apristurus across its global range.

items.title: Assessing Guidance and Counseling Needs of Iranian Dental Students: A Cross-Sectional Study in Kerman University of Medical Sciences.
items.abstract: Background Upon admission to the university, students encounter a range of personal, emotional, academic, and occupational challenges that impact their mental health and overall efficiency. This study aimed to evaluate the guidance and counseling needs of dental students at Kerman University of Medical Sciences. Methods This cross-sectional descriptive-analytical study was conducted among dental students at Kerman University of Medical Sciences in 2021. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling, and data were collected from 173 students through the Counseling Needs Assessment Questionnaire, which assesses demographic characteristics as well as guidance and counseling needs. The questionnaire items are scored employing a four-point Likert scale, which spans "no need = 0" to "urgent need = 3." Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27. Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t -tests, one-way analysis of variance, and multiple linear regression were used for data analysis. Results The average score for students' guidance and counseling needs was 40.06 ± 15.75. Occupational counseling had the highest mean score (9.34), whereas family and marriage counseling had the lowest (6.99). The students' scores for guidance and counseling needs did not reveal any significant differences regarding age, marital status, place of residence, or academic level ( p > 0.05). Meanwhile, female participants achieved significantly higher scores on guidance and counseling needs than male participants ( p B = - 7.262, β = -0.231, 95% CI = -11.985 to -2.540, p = 0.003). Conclusion Dental students needed counseling services most frequently for their occupational needs but least frequently for their marital issues. Moreover, their guidance and counseling needs were associated with their gender.

items.title: The Epidemiological Profile of Major Depressive Disorder Among a Nationally Representative Sample in Saudi Arabia.
items.abstract: Aims Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading contributor to global disease burden, and national data on its epidemiology in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region remains scarce. This research therefore aimed to estimate the prevalence, sociodemographic correlates, comorbidities, and impairment associated with MDD in Saudi Arabia. Methods A cross-sectional, nationally representative survey was conducted using a validated diagnostic instrument based on DSM-IV criteria. Lifetime, 12-month, and 30-day prevalence estimates of MDD were reported. Associations with sociodemographic factors, age-of-onset, psychiatric comorbidities, functional impairment, and treatment utilization were examined. Results Lifetime prevalence of MDD was 6.0%, with a 12-month prevalence of 3.8% and a 30-day prevalence of 1.3%. Women exhibited higher prevalence (8.9%) compared to men (3.1%). The mean age-of-onset was 20.4 years. There were higher odds for MDD among youth, women, respondents who are employed and with lower education, urban residents, and those who were previously married. MDD showed strong comorbidity with anxiety and substance-use disorders and was associated with significant role impairment, with 71% reporting role impairment. Despite the substantial burden, treatment utilization was low, particularly among the severely impaired. Conclusions MDD is a prevalent and impairing condition in Saudi Arabia, with early onset, marked gender disparity, and strong comorbidity. The findings underscore the urgent need for early detection, targeted prevention, and expansion of accessible mental health services.

items.title: Study demands, self-critical perfectionism and dropout intentions among undergraduates: A six-wave study of weekly within-person associations.
items.abstract: Background Study Demands-Resources theory suggests that study demands and personal demands such as self-critical perfectionism can weaken persistence. However, evidence on their links with dropout intentions comes mostly from between-person comparisons, and little is known about week-to-week processes within students. Aims This study examined reciprocal within-person associations among study load, cognitive demands, self-critical perfectionism and dropout intentions. Sample Participants were 266 first- and second-year undergraduates (73.7% women) in teacher education programmes at a Turkish state university. Methods Six weekly assessments at the end of a semester were analysed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, alternative specifications and design-sensitivity analyses. Hypotheses were tested with cross-lagged paths pooled across intervals. Results Within students, none of the hypothesized cross-lagged associations was statistically significant. The 95% confidence intervals excluded effects larger than about .13 for the paths between self-critical perfectionism and study demands and from study load to dropout intentions, but not for most paths involving dropout intentions. Between students, dropout intentions were significantly correlated only with study load (r = .25), and self-critical perfectionism was correlated with study load and cognitive demands (r = .28 and .35). Conclusions The hypothesized weekly lagged associations were not detected, although the design could reliably detect only unusually large effects. Larger samples are needed to assess typical effects, and measurement intervals should match the timescale of the hypothesized processes. The reported variance decomposition and sensitivity estimates provide design parameters for future studies.

items.title: Barriers to Help-Seeking for Psychological Distress and Wellbeing Among Nurses, Midwives, and Nursing Students: A Convergent Parallel Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Aim To identify barriers influencing help-seeking behaviours among nursing/midwifery professionals/students experiencing psychological distress. Design Convergent parallel mixed-methods systematic review. Data sources Six databases (CINAHL, PsycINFO, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched between December 2023 and January 2024, with regular updates. The final search was completed in April 2025. Methods Two researchers independently screened and synthesised data following EPPI-Centre methods. Included populations were nurses, midwives, health visitors, and nursing/midwifery students. Eligibility encompassed 12 prespecified mental health and occupational wellbeing domains. All research study designs were eligible; reviews were excluded. Results Twenty studies met inclusion criteria: five quantitative, nine qualitative and six mixed-methods. An empirically-informed logic model highlighted six barriers to help-seeking: (1) perceived career threats, (2) stigma, judgement, and expectations, (3) perceptions of manager and informal support, (4) perceived need for support, (5) availability, accessibility, and adequacy of formal support, and (6) time and workload constraints. Various demographic and occupational factors emerged as potential influencers. Conclusions This review shows how personal, interpersonal, and organisational factors interact to shape help-seeking. The resulting logic model offers a strengthened and integrated explanation linking workplace culture, concerns about professional consequences, and difficulties accessing support to help-seeking barriers among nurses and midwives, bringing together formal and informal pathways that are rarely examined in a single framework. Implications for profession and/or patient care Findings can inform targeted workplace wellbeing interventions and support positive mental health cultures. Future research should test the models' practical applications. Impact The review generated a comprehensive, empirically informed logic model, representing an important step toward consolidating the evidence base, although further testing is required before the model can inform policy or strategy. Reporting method Conducted in accordance with the SWiM and PRISMA guidelines. Patient and public contribution A seven-member nursing/midwifery advisory group informed barrier identification and model development. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD42024518783 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?RecordID=518783).

items.title: A comparison of Japanese, Taiwanese, and U.S. Normative score patterns on the WISC-V: proposed cultural and educational influences.
items.abstract: Cultural context shapes neuropsychological test performance through interrelated influences of education, language, and test-taking conventions. Building on adult cross-national profile findings, this descriptive and hypothesis-generating study examined whether similar normative score patterns are evident in children using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fifth Edition (WISC-V). Normative data were obtained from the US English, Japanese, and Taiwanese WISC-V manuals. For Japan and Taiwan, raw score ranges corresponding to a local scaled score of 10 were identified within each age band and converted to US-norm-referenced scaled scores; index scores and FSIQ were derived from the converted subtests. One-sample t-tests compared converted scores with US expectations, and associations with schooling were evaluated across age bands. Both East Asian cohorts showed strengths in processing speed, visual spatial reasoning, and working memory, with Japanese also demonstrating strengths in fluid reasoning. Relatively weaker performances were demonstrated on verbally mediated measures and Picture Concepts, with country-specific weaknesses on Comprehension (Japan) and Similarities (Taiwan). Education-related increases were strongest for verbal and processing speed measures, and East-West differences attenuated from early childhood to adolescence. Overall, the results generate hypotheses regarding possible cultural, linguistic, and educational contexts that may contribute to WISC-V normative score patterns across development.

items.title: Annual Research Review: Ecological momentary assessment in child and adolescent psychopathology - insights, challenges, and future directions.
items.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) is a powerful method for understanding daily-life processes associated with the etiology and phenomenology of child and adolescent psychopathology. The present review synthesizes recent work using EMA to reveal novel insights - as well as unique challenges - associated with this methodology across child and adolescent diagnostic categories and domains of psychopathology. We highlight the strengths of EMA for illuminating dynamic, within-person, contextualized processes contributing to the onset, maintenance, and ultimately amelioration of youth psychiatric distress. We identify pressing areas for ongoing research, as well as opportunities to advance the science of EMA through multimodal ambulatory assessment, experimental designs, and the development of ecological momentary interventions.

items.title: The role of ageism, aging anxiety, and death anxiety in understanding psychology trainees' therapeutic expectations for and interest in providing end-of-life care.
items.abstract: Objectives Few psychologists specialize in geropsychology, and even fewer work in the subspecialty of end-of-life care for older adults, despite a growing need for these services. No known research has investigated factors that might predict psychology trainees' therapeutic expectations for and interest in providing end-of-life care. This study examined ageist attitudes, aging anxiety, and death anxiety as potential predictors. Method A sample of 197 doctoral psychology trainees completed survey measures online. Structural equation modeling was used to test the hypothesized relations of ageist attitudes, aging anxiety, and death anxiety with therapeutic expectations and interest in end-of-life care with older adults. Results More aging anxiety related significantly to poorer therapeutic expectations for clients at end-of-life and less interest in providing end-of-life care. More ambivalent ageist attitudes unexpectedly related to greater interest in end-of-life care. Death anxiety did not relate to either therapeutic expectations or interest in end-of-life care. Conclusion These findings suggested that doctoral psychology training programs and early clinical opportunities should consider the role of aging anxiety, as well as ageist attitudes, on trainees' interests and perceptions towards working with older adults living with life-limiting illness.

items.title: Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation of the arabic tokophobia assessment questionnaire (TAQ-Ar) among egyptian pregnant women.
items.abstract: Background Tokophobia, a severe and multidimensional fear of childbirth, is associated with adverse maternal psychological outcomes and increased preference for elective cesarean delivery. Although the Arabic version of the Tokophobia Assessment Questionnaire (TAQ) has recently been psychometrically validated among Jordanian women, independent evidence supporting its application in other Arabic-speaking populations remains limited. Therefore, further validation is needed to strengthen confidence in its broader applicability. This study aimed to independently translate, culturally adapt, and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Tokophobia Assessment Questionnaire (TAQ) among Egyptian pregnant women. Methods A cross-sectional psychometric study was conducted with 426 pregnant women recruited from antenatal clinics and online platforms in Egypt (September 2025-January 2026). The TAQ underwent forward-backward translation and pilot testing. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring with oblimin rotation was conducted, with factor retention guided by parallel analysis and Velicer's MAP. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using WLSMV estimation based on polychoric correlations compared competing models. Reliability was assessed using McDonald's omega. Known-groups validity and multivariable linear regression were conducted to examine discriminative capacity and independent predictors. Results EFA supported a refined 21-item, three-factor structure representing (1) inability to address physical and social needs, (2) fear of childbirth, and (3) avoidance of pregnancy, explaining 75.49% of total variance. CFA demonstrated excellent model fit for the three-factor model, whereas one-factor and six-factor models were rejected. Internal consistency was excellent (ω_total = 0.98; ω_subscales = 0.90-0.96). Bifactor analysis indicated a strong general factor (ωh = 0.94), supporting interpretation of the total score as the primary indicator of severity. Lack of previous pregnancy (primiparity) and the presence of chronic medical conditions were independently associated with higher tokophobia scores (R² = 0.106). Conclusions The TAQ-Ar demonstrates strong structural validity, reliability, and discriminative capacity, supporting its use as a culturally appropriate tool for research applications and structured clinical assessment in Egyptian maternal health settings.

items.title: Differential Efficacy of a Psychoeducational Intervention for Older Adults Across Face-to-Face and Synchronous Online Modalities: A Doubly Robust Quasi-Experimental Analysis.
items.abstract: Objectives This study evaluates the efficacy of a multicomponent psychoeducational program, Improving Your Strengths and Quality of Life , based on Positive Psychology and the FRAG model (Perceived family Functioning, Resilience, Experiential avoidance and acceptance-related responding, and Gratitude), delivered through face-to-face and synchronous online formats. Methods A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 143 participants (M age = 68.4). Conditions included face-to-face ( n = 42), synchronous online ( n = 29), and a waiting-list control group ( n = 61). To address nonrandom attrition (13.4%) and baseline imbalances, a Double Robustness framework was applied, integrating Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW) with ANCOVA using Huber-White heteroscedasticity-consistent estimator type 3 (HC3) robust estimators. Results Both intervention modalities significantly reduced anxiety and depression versus controls. The online format was associated with greater gains in resilience and gratitude than the face-to-face format. Conversely, the face-to-face modality showed greater adjusted posttest scores in QoL and experiential avoidance and acceptance-related responding. A significant decrease in control/ autonomy was observed in the online group, tentatively suggesting a potential reevaluation of perceived personal agency, an interpretation requiring further replication. Conclusions Multicomponent interventions are effective in both formats. Online format optimizes personal strength-building, whereas face-to-face interaction remains critical for holistic well-being. These findings support dual-access services to optimize older adults' mental health care. Clinical implications Dual formats optimize care: online for internal resources; face-to-face for quality of life.

items.title: Epigenetic clocks and adverse childhood experiences: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Epigenetic clocks predict biological age from DNA methylation patterns, providing insight into cellular aging. Different clocks capture distinct aspects of aging, and their relevance to research areas may vary - including early-life stress (ELS) and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). This meta-analysis evaluates which clocks are most associated to biological consequences of ELS and ACEs. A systematic search was conducted following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO registration: CRD420251047805) to identify studies assessing associations between ACEs or ELS and epigenetic age acceleration (EAA). Eligible human studies used validated ACE or ELS measures and reported DNA methylation-based age from peripheral tissues. Data were extracted and pooled using inverse-variance random-effects models to generate beta coefficients and 95% confidence intervals (RevMan 5.4). Seventeen studies (n = 10,940) met inclusion criteria and used 8 epigenetic clocks: Horvath's, Hannum's, PhenoAge, GrimAge, DunedinPACE, DunedinPoAm, Skin & Blood and PedBE. Amongst these, GrimAge and DunedinPACE demonstrated the strongest, most consistent associations with total ACE counts and subdomains including abuse (total, physical, sexual), neglect (total), and household dysfunction (total, socioeconomic impact). Only DunedinPACE demonstrated robust associations across strata, with significant age differences and no sex effects. This meta-analysis highlights variability in how clocks capture the biological imprint of early adversity. Later-generation clocks like GrimAge and DunedinPACE, integrating physiological and mortality-related methylation signatures, show the most consistent with cumulative effects of ELS and ACEs. These findings emphasise the need for careful clock selection and rigorous study design in stress-biology research, with implications for identifying individuals at risk for EAA and stress-related disorders.

items.title: Aligning episodic memory scores from different time points.
items.abstract: To measure episodic memory, recall of sentences or words with or without cues or enactment is commonly used. In longitudinal studies, participants may join at different points or drop out, yet comparison of episodic memory is still desired. The aim of this study is to explore different methods of linking scores obtained at different time points, to allow for comparability between scores from various test administrations. When the same instrument is used across timepoints, a possibility is to use a test equating method to link the scores by aligning scores from different versions or instruments on the same scale. While equating and linking is well researched for knowledge tests, few studies have applied it to health or psychology instruments, and in those cases mainly used an assumption of equivalent groups and equipercentile equating. This paper differs by focus on different methods to compare scales either within the same test group, or by using collateral information about the participants. The results showed that both proposed approaches are useful and which one to use depends on the assumptions on the data at hand.

items.title: Sleep Health Interventions Among Indigenous Peoples: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Objectives Given the disproportionate burden of sleep problems such as insomnia among Indigenous Peoples, we sought to examine the literature on sleep interventions in these populations. In this scoping review, we aimed to describe traditional Indigenous sleep improvement practices as well as non-Indigenous behavioral sleep interventions (e.g. cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, CBT-I) that have been adapted for and/or tested with Indigenous communities. Method We searched eight health sciences and Indigenous Peoples databases for articles that described or tested sleep health practices or interventions among Indigenous adolescents or adults located in North America, New Zealand, Australia or the Pacific Islands. Articles were screened and reviewed independently by two reviewers. Results Twenty articles met inclusion criteria. None described Indigenous-specific sleep practices. No articles focused on insomnia, and none mentioned CBT-I. Two articles described sleep health interventions with Indigenous Peoples. The remaining articles described recommendations for sleep health interventions based on their original research findings. Conclusions This review underscores the limited published research on sleep health programs among Indigenous populations and the absence of insomnia-specific interventions, including CBT-I. The scarce literature possibly reflects a misalignment of the research questions and strategies with Indigenous views of sleep, rather than an absence of relevant knowledge. Overall, our findings highlight the need for approaches that address sleep health and insomnia among Indigenous populations. These approaches should be based on holistic frameworks nested in Indigenous worldviews that consider socio-economic inequities, community capacity, and culture.

items.title: Exploring the Experience of Receiving Comprehensive Risk Estimates and Genetic Counseling for Substance Use Disorders.
items.abstract: The study team has built a platform that integrates genomic, behavioral, and environmental data to generate comprehensive risk estimates for substance use disorders (SUDs). We conducted a qualitative study to explore how people respond to this information and the role that genetic counselors may play in its communication. We explored the experiences and perceptions of adults who had received comprehensive risk estimates and genetic counseling related to SUDs as part of a larger randomized controlled trial. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 12 participants and used interpretive description to develop a conceptual model of participants' experiences. Overall, participants demonstrated a good understanding of their results and generally described positive experiences, with individual responses shaped by lived experience. While most participants viewed receiving the comprehensive risk results as the primary benefit of the experience, all participants acknowledged the added value of genetic counseling and identified populations they believed would benefit from it. Although no long-term behavioral changes were described, some participants reported reduced anxiety after receiving their results. It was also suggested that receiving comprehensive risk information alongside genetic counseling could help reduce stigma in the population surrounding SUDs.

items.title: Enterochromaffin cells as sensory hubs of the gut-brain axis.
items.abstract: The mucosal epithelium of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract forms one of the largest exposed surfaces of the body, providing a unique interface through which environmental stimuli are integrated and modulate physiological processes. This review focuses on enterochromaffin cells (ECCs), a rare subtype of enteroendocrine cells comprising <1% of all intestinal epithelial cells. ECCs are excitable cells that express a variety of ion channels and receptors, allowing them to react to varied chemical and mechanical stimuli. Recent studies have shown that ECCs are major players in GI epithelial sensing and affect a variety of physiological and pathophysiological states, such as secretion, GI motility, GI sensory afferent nerve hypersensitivity, satiety, nausea, and visceral pain. This review highlights the diverse functions of ECCs, the peripheral 5-hydroxytryptamine they release, and the nerves they interact with.

items.title: Nonlinear association between daily rest period and psychological distress among Japanese public school teachers: a mixed-effects spline analysis.
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined the association between daily rest period (DRP) and psychological distress among Japanese public school teachers. Data were obtained from a nationwide survey conducted in 2022. After applying the eligibility criteria and complete-case analysis, 13,754 teachers were included. DRP was calculated as the average interval between the end of one workday and the start of the next across four weekday intervals. Psychological distress was assessed using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6). Linear mixed-effects models with school-level random intercepts were used. A natural cubic spline model examined the nonlinear association between DRP and K6 score, and sequentially adjusted models examined changes after adjustment for post-clock-out work, job stress, and total sleep time. Shorter DRP was associated with higher K6 scores. The spline model showed a better fit than the linear model and indicated that predicted K6 scores decreased as DRP increased, with the slope becoming more gradual around 13 h. Approximately 13 h was interpreted as a descriptive feature of the spline curve rather than as a statistically identified threshold. These findings suggest that avoiding shorter DRPs and securing sufficient post-work recovery time may be important for teachers' mental health.

items.title: Gut microbiota profiles and neurodevelopmental symptoms in children from a prenatal-risk enriched birth cohort: findings from the PREDO study.
items.abstract: Background Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are common neurodevelopmental conditions whose early-life biological correlates remain incompletely understood. Children's gut microbiota may represent a biological pathway through which immune-metabolic and gut-brain signalling links early-life adversity with neurodevelopment. We examined gut microbiota profiles associated with ADHD and ASD symptoms in children from the Prediction and Prevention of Preeclampsia and Intrauterine Growth Restriction (PREDO) birth cohort. Methods We analysed data from 323 Finnish children assessed at a mean age of 8.6 years. Stool microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing and differential taxonomic abundance was assessed using MaAsLin2. ADHD and ASD symptoms were mother-rated using the Conners' Parent Rating Scale-Revised and Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire. Results Clinically relevant ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with metric-specific reductions in alpha diversity, whereas beta diversity did not differ between groups. Male children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae_FCS020_group, Subdoligranulum, Fusicatenibacter, and Anaerostipes (ps ≤ 0.049). Female children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed a distinct profile, including higher Negativibacillus and Faecalibacterium (p ≤ 0.018). Children with clinically relevant ASD symptoms showed lower abundance of six genera, including Anaerostipes and Lachnospiraceae_ND3007_group (p ≤ 0.001). Conclusions In this prenatal-risk enriched cohort, ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with distinct gut microbiota profiles, including alterations in taxa implicated in short-chain fatty acid metabolism, immune regulation, and gut-brain signalling. These findings support microbiota-immune-brain pathways as a hypothesis-generating framework for future longitudinal and multi-omics research.

items.title: Beyond clinical symptoms: A psychosocial and machine learning approach to understanding suicidal ideation.
items.abstract: Background Suicide is a major public mental health challenge, and many individuals experiencing suicidal ideation do not meet diagnostic criteria for psychiatric disorders or disclose symptoms during clinical encounters. This limits the effectiveness of symptom-based screening commonly used in mental health services. From an epidemiological and social psychiatry perspective, identifying psychosocial risk and protective factors beyond psychopathology is essential for population-level prevention and early intervention. This study examined whether suicidal ideation can be predicted using psychosocial measures and identified socially and developmentally meaningful risk and resilience markers through explainable machine learning models with external validation. Methods Data were obtained from a mixed clinical and community-based sample of 190 adults. Suicidal ideation was defined using self-reported endorsement of suicide-related thoughts. Predictors consisted exclusively of validated psychosocial measures relevant to social psychiatry and life-course epidemiology, including chronic and perceived stress, childhood adversity, personality traits, attachment styles, coping strategies, and emotion regulation capacities. Five supervised machine learning algorithms were implemented using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. To reduce demographic confounding and address class imbalance, analyses were conducted on both the full dataset and a demographically matched subsample (n = 110) matched on age, gender, education level, and income status, although some residual imbalance remained, notably in income. Hyperparameter optimization targeted both area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) to ensure relevance for low-prevalence outcomes. Predictive performance was estimated using fully nested cross-validation, in which predictor selection, standardization, and hyperparameter optimization were repeated within each training fold. Model generalizability was assessed using an independent external validation sample of university students (n = 84). Model interpretability was examined using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results Random Forest models showed the most robust and generalizable performance. In the matched sample, nested cross-validation yielded an AUC of 0.820 ± 0.131 (mean ± SD) with an F1-score of 0.778 ± 0.137 (F1-optimized) and an AUC of 0.825 ± 0.114 with an F1-score of 0.736 ± 0.078 (AUC-optimized). External validation of the F1-optimized model yielded an AUC of 0.792 (95% confidence interval (95%CI): 0.677-0.896). Explainable analyses consistently identified perceived loneliness as the strongest predictor of suicidal ideation, followed by childhood emotional abuse, limited access to emotion regulation strategies, and low perceived self-efficacy. Higher conscientiousness and extraversion were consistently associated with lower predicted probability of suicidal ideation. Conclusion Self-reported recent suicidal ideation can be predicted using psychosocial and developmental indicators, which may provide information complementary to traditional psychiatric symptom-based approaches, although their incremental predictive value beyond psychiatric symptom measures remains to be established. These findings identify loneliness and emotion regulation as candidate modifiable targets and personality-related factors as potential resilience markers, whose relevance for prevention and risk stratification requires prospective evaluation. Integrating such markers into mental health services and surveillance frameworks may help enhance early identification beyond diagnostic approaches, though this remains to be tested.

items.title: Attitudes to HTLV-1 antenatal screening among women and non-binary individuals in the UK: HTLV Antenatal Screening Survey 2025.
items.abstract: Objectives With targeted HTLV-1 antenatal screening under review in the UK, and no existing evidence on public opinion, we conducted a survey to assess perspectives on HTLV antenatal screening in the UK. Methods Non-pregnant women and non-binary individuals, aged 17-54 years living in the UK were sampled via Prolific into three equal groups, born in: (1) HTLV endemic countries (GRP1), (2) the UK and of Black ethnicity (GRP2), and (3) non-endemic countries of other ethnicities (GRP3). A co-designed questionnaire collected views on screening. Universal versus targeted screening and anticipated anxiety were compared using paired t-tests and one-way ANOVA. items.title: From Relief to Relief and Back Again: Placebo Hypoalgesia Induced by Operant Conditioning with Negative Reinforcement.
items.abstract: Operant conditioning has been shown to induce placebo hypoalgesia using verbal, token-based, or social reinforcement. However, in clinical contexts, the most relevant reinforcement appears to be pain relief. This study investigated whether pain relief as reinforcement increases the likelihood of placebo choice and leads to placebo hypoalgesia, while also examining differences between medical and non-medical placebos. Participants were divided into four groups: two experimental (medical and non-medical placebo) and two corresponding controls. During conditioning, pain intensity decreased contingent on placebo choice in experimental groups, whereas in the control groups, pain relief was delivered randomly and was unrelated to placebo choice. In testing, the intensity of all stimuli remained unchanged. Results suggested that operant conditioning contributed to placebo hypoalgesia with both medical and non-medical placebo, as reflected by self-reported pain ratings. However, some differences emerged in response patterns. Unexpectedly, participants in the medical placebo control group chose the placebo more often than those in the experimental group, with no such pattern for the non-medical placebo. Pain expectations shifted over time in the medical placebo experimental group. Psychophysiological findings were inconsistent and offered limited support for operant placebo learning. These findings support the hypothesis that pain relief may function as a negative reinforcer contributing to placebo hypoalgesia within an operant conditioning framework, highlighting patient agency as a potentially important factor and providing a basis for future research on reinforcement-based placebo mechanisms in pain management. PERSPECTIVE: The present study provides evidence that pain relief may function as a negative reinforcer contributing to placebo hypoalgesia induced by operant conditioning. This effect was observed for both placebo types (medical and non-medical) and was not fully explained by expectations, suggesting that reinforcement processes may contribute to placebo hypoalgesia alongside expectancy-related mechanisms.

items.title: Psychological and Clinical Factors Associated With School Refusal Across Educational Stages in Adolescent Psychiatric Outpatients: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: IntroductionThis cross-sectional study examined clinical and psychological factors associated with school refusal across educational stages in adolescent psychiatric outpatients.MethodsWe evaluated 417 outpatients: 254 middle schoolers (aged 12-15) and 163 high schoolers (aged 15-18). School refusal was operationalized as ≥ 30 annual absence days. Participants completed the HQ-25 (hikikomori), TACS-22 (modern-type depression), BRS (resilience), and QIDS-SR (depression).ResultsIn multivariable regression (N=417), an ICD-10 F4 diagnosis and HQ-25 Isolation independently predicted school refusal, while depressive severity and resilience did not. Educational stage significantly interacted with TACS-22 Avoidance of Social Roles. In middle schoolers (n=254), Isolation was the primary associated factor, with marginal trends for female sex and physical comorbidity. Conversely, in high schoolers (n=163), Avoidance of Social Roles independently predicted school refusal, whereas ADHD diagnosis was associated with lower odds.ConclusionsFactors associated with school refusal transition from middle school somatic distress and isolation to high school social role avoidance. Stage-specific screening integrating withdrawal traits and neurodevelopmental profiles is recommended.

items.title: Prelimbic neurons represent diverse danger-modulated behaviors and veridical threat probability structure.
items.abstract: Prelimbic cortex activity is known to promote fear expression, yet its specific representational function within the fear circuit remains unclear. We recorded prelimbic single-unit activity in rats undergoing probabilistic fear discrimination and identified three complementary levels of representation. Prelimbic neurons represented diverse danger-modulated behaviors, not just freezing, such that the initiation and cessation of five behaviors could be accurately decoded from ensemble firing. Behavioral representations were embedded within a veridical representation of the environmental threat structure, in which the majority of prelimbic neurons tuned cue firing to learned threat probability-regardless of behavior coding. This threat probability representation supported precise decoding of learned cue identity and partial decoding of threat cue timing, both of which were degraded when discriminative responding was poor. Prelimbic outcome firing was dominated by inhibition to predicted shock. Together, these results reveal that prelimbic cortex firing is organized around threat at multiple levels, from rich representations of danger-modulated behavior to veridical probabilistic threat predictions and predictive outcome signals.

items.title: The perinatal window of opportunity: Translating biopsychosocial mechanisms of perinatal vulnerability into maternal and infant mental health care.
items.abstract: Perinatal mental health is commonly approached through symptom-based, maternally focused, and discipline-specific frameworks. Although clinically useful, these approaches may underestimate the extent to which pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum constitute a dynamic period of psychological, biological, relational, and developmental reorganisation for mothers, infants, and families. In this statement paper, developed within the ECNP Perinatal Psychiatry Network, we propose a body-brain-dyad-environment framework for understanding maternal mental health across pregnancy and postpartum and its implications for maternal and offspring outcomes. We position the perinatal period as a window of both vulnerability and plasticity, while emphasising that pregnancy and postpartum are clinically and biologically distinct phases with partly different risks, mechanisms, and treatment considerations. We outline key pathways linking maternal psychopathology to maternal and child outcomes, including neuroendocrine and neurosteroid adaptation, immune-inflammatory signalling, placental and foetal programming, caregiving, and dyadic co-regulation. We then consider how interacting biological, psychological, relational, and contextual processes may contribute to heterogeneous clinical phenotypes, trajectories, and intervention needs, supporting longitudinal, multidimensional, interpretable, and equitable approaches to risk stratification. Finally, we highlight the translational gap between mechanistic knowledge and real-world care across Europe. We call for integrated biopsychosocial models that move from episodic symptom detection to longitudinal formulation, from maternally focused symptom reduction to dyadic, developmental, and family-sensitive support, and from fragmented care pathways to stratified, context-sensitive, and equitable systems of prevention and care. By framing perinatal mental health as an emergent property of interacting systems, this framework supports more precise, developmentally informed, and equitable research and care.

items.title: PRISM-MP: Psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal learning for cross-musician emotion recognition during musical performance.
items.abstract: Emotion classification during active musical performance is challenging because neural activity, cardiac dynamics, and acoustic expression provide complementary but non-equivalent evidence of intended emotional communication and self-reported affect. This study presents PRISM-MP, a psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal framework for cross-musician emotion recognition. We analyzed a publicly available dataset comprising synchronized electroencephalography, electrocardiography, and musical audio recordings from 11 experienced musicians who performed excerpts intended to communicate happiness, sadness, anger, or relaxation. PRISM-MP integrates dynamic frequency-specific electroencephalographic functional graphs with affine-invariant tangent-space covariance representations, models multiscale physiological dynamics, and applies class-conditional source-domain alignment to reduce musician-specific distributional differences. The physiological and acoustic pathways receive auxiliary supervision from felt and communicated valence-arousal ratings, respectively. Their contributions are dynamically adjusted according to signal quality, predictive uncertainty, and cross-modal disagreement. Under nested source-only leave-one-musician-out evaluation, PRISM-MP achieved a musician-macro-averaged performance-level accuracy of 92.14%, balanced accuracy of 91.82%, macro-F1 of 0.910, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.892, and expected calibration error of 0.041. Against the strongest recent source-only EEG baseline evaluated under the same protocol, the corresponding gains were 3.91 percentage points in balanced accuracy and 0.037 in macro-F1. The framework remained robust when electrocardiography or audio was unavailable and under partial electroencephalographic channel loss. A systematic leave-one-channel-out analysis across 29 EEG electrodes revealed nonuniform channel sensitivity. Removing C3, Cz, C4, and F3 produced the largest balanced-accuracy reductions of 2.22, 2.05, 2.02, and 1.90 percentage points, respectively, while removal of several other channels produced minimal changes. Computational profiling indicated 3.46 million trainable parameters and processing times of 74 ms with GPU-supported audio embedding and 312 ms on a desktop CPU, while physiological encoding and fusion required 18.7 ms after feature preparation. These timings exclude the 30-s observation period and do not represent end-to-end interactive latency. A secondary post hoc within-recording calibration analysis increased macro-F1 to 0.946 using a lightweight residual adapter. These findings support reliability-aware physiological-acoustic modeling as a computational foundation for future musician-centered affective interfaces.

items.title: When the WRENCH fails to turn heads: Task relevance determines the fate of unexpected semantic information.
items.abstract: Inattentional blindness (IB) is the failure to perceive a fully visible, unexpected stimulus when attention is engaged elsewhere. Two experiments examined how expectation violations and semantic relatedness affect the allocation and suppression of attention. Participants named primary-task pictures from one semantic category and ignored distractor pictures from another category. On the critical trial, a six-letter unexpected word (21-point Arial) was presented at fixation simultaneously with the pictures. In Experiment 1, expectation violations involved replacing primary-task insect pictures with unexpected tool pictures. Participants were more likely to report the word BEETLE, semantically related to the task-instructed category insects, than WRENCH or VIOLIN. Participants were also more likely to report the word WRENCH, semantically related to the unexpected tool pictures, than VIOLIN. In Experiment 2, expectation violations involved replacing either primary-task insect pictures or distractor fruit pictures with pictures from an unexpected picture-category. The unexpected word was semantically related to the unexpected picture-category. Participants were less likely to report the word when expectation violations involved the distractor picture-category than when they involved the primary-task picture-category. Together, the findings suggest that attentional control settings operate at the level of semantic categories. Experiment 2 further showed that when primary-task goals were disrupted because the primary-task pictures were unexpectedly replaced and no insect stimuli remained, attentional priorities updated to include unexpected semantic information. Yet, when primary-task goals were uninterrupted because the distractor pictures were unexpectedly replaced and insect pictures remained in the display, suppression of attention extended broadly across semantic categories unrelated to the task goal.

items.title: Prospective associations between emotion regulation flexibility components and psychotic-like experiences: A one-year two-wave study.
items.abstract: Objective Emotion regulation (ER) flexibility is theorized to buffer against the development of psychopathology, but its longitudinal relationship with psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) has not been tested bidirectionally. This study expanded prior research by examining whether baseline individual differences in ER flexibility components prospectively predict follow-up CAPE frequency scores after adjustment for baseline scores, and whether baseline CAPE frequency scores prospectively predict follow-up ER flexibility. Methods Participants (N = 192; M age = 47.38, SD age = 14.35) completed measures of ER flexibility and PLEs at two time points one year apart. Three components of emotion regulation flexibility were assessed: context sensitivity, perceived expressive flexibility (a limited proxy for the implementation component), and feedback responsiveness. These are self-report and vignette-based instruments, and their mapping onto the evaluation, implementation, and monitoring stages is heuristic but not a direct measurement of real-time regulatory processes. Psychotic-like experiences were indexed using the CAPE total and positive frequency scores; CAPE negative and depressive frequency scores were examined as additional dimensions that may capture broader affective, motivational, or interpersonal difficulties. Bidirectional associations were tested using cross-lagged panel models (CLPM). Results All variables showed significant autoregressive effects, suggesting relative stability over time. Across 24 focal paths in the primary models, only two survived false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment: baseline CAPE negative frequency predicted lower follow-up perceived expressive flexibility (β = -0.184, p = .002, q = 0.024), and baseline CAPE depressive frequency predicted lower follow-up feedback responsiveness (β = -0.210, p Conclusions The primary FDR-adjusted findings were confined to baseline CAPE negative and depressive frequency predicting lower follow-up flexibility components; they did not support associations in both directions. These exploratory findings warrant replication. Because the design is observational and two-wave, and because the CAPE was administered with lifetime wording, the results do not establish within-person change, a reciprocal mechanism, or intervention targets. Future research should replicate these findings in individuals at elevated risk for psychosis (e.g., those in the prodromal phase or at clinical high risk) and in intensive longitudinal designs.

items.title: Mother-infant interactions live and online: A large-scale, longitudinal study employing the functional architecture of maternal mirroring and marking.
items.abstract: Maternal mirroring and marking are core components of early face-to-face interaction, and have been proposed as key mechanisms supporting the emergence of infant social expressiveness. In a seminal study, Murray et al. (2016) proposed a functional architecture account, arguing that mothers respond to infant behaviours in structured and behaviour-specific ways, and that these responses, particularly mirroring and positive marking, play a critical role in shaping early social development. However, although influential, this proposal was based on a relatively small in-person sample of 20 dyads, raising questions about robustness, generalisability, and replicability. The present study is the first to test the theory with a substantially increased sample size and via online observational methodology. The study had two complementary aims: first, to provide a large-scale replication of the functional architecture account, and second, to examine whether this interactional structure could be captured using online observational methodology. We compared longitudinal observations of mother-infant (N = 131 dyads) face-to-face interaction collected remotely via synchronous video calls at 5, 7, and 9 weeks postpartum with home visit data of Murray et al. (2016), employing the same second-by-second micro-analytic coding scheme. Mixed-effects models were used to examine developmental trajectories in infant behaviours and maternal responses, as well as the specificity of maternal mirroring and marking to different infant behaviours. Across both datasets, we observed strong and consistent developmental trends, including increases in infant social behaviours and maternal mirroring and marking, alongside decreases in biological events and negative affect. In both studies, maternal mirroring and marking were selectively directed towards infant social behaviours more than non-social or biological behaviours, replicating the behaviour-specific interactional patterns reported by Murray et al. (2016). Only minor quantitative differences emerged between studies, without altering the overall pattern of results. These findings provide robust support for the functional architecture of maternal mirroring and marking and demonstrate that its structure is replicable across methodological contexts. The study also shows that online observational methods can be used to scale and replicate subtle in-person interactional research without undermining theoretical validity.

items.title: Microbiota-gut-brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Mechanistic Insights, Experimental and Clinical Evidence, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
items.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by marked biological and clinical heterogeneity, arising from an interplay of genetic vulnerability, immune, metabolic, and gastrointestinal dysfunction, and neurobiological alterations. The bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the brain via neural, immune, endocrine, and microbial- metabolite pathways may contribute to ASD pathophysiology. We conducted a literature review by searching PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science, emphasizing studies published since 2022 and integrating mechanistic, experimental, and clinical evidence. Alterations in gut microbial ecology have been associated with impaired metabolite production, compromised intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurotransmitter imbalances. Findings from germ-free models, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and targeted microbiota modulation suggest that gut microorganisms can influence ASD-related behaviors. However, human studies are limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneous designs and are confounded by gastrointestinal symptoms, diet, and medication. It also remains uncertain whether microbiota alterations are a cause or a consequence of ASD. Clinical studies of probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, dietary interventions, FMT, and emerging microbiome-engineering strategies suggest that these interventions may improve gastrointestinal symptoms and selected behavioral outcomes in certain populations. However, the results are inconsistent, and these interventions require further investigation. This review discusses the limitations of the current evidence and the opportunities and challenges for microbiome-based therapeutics. Future priorities include stratified clinical trials, standardized outcome measures, and longitudinal cohorts.

items.title: Molecular fingerprint insights into microplastic‑derived dissolved organic matter mediating phosphate immobilization on microplastic‑goethite complexes.
items.abstract: Microplastic‑derived dissolved organic matter (MP‑DOM) is pervasive in aquatic systems, yet its polymer‑specific controls on nutrient cycling remain poorly understood. This study investigated orthophosphate adsorption on pre-synthesized MP-goethite complexes in the presence of MP-DOM leached from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polylactic acid (PLA). Batch experiments showed that MP-DOM competed with orthophosphate for goethite adsorption sites, with PET-DOM exerting a stronger inhibitory effect (60.0% adsorption reduction) than PLA-DOM (57.1%). Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry results revealed preferential depletion of lignin-, protein-, and lipid-like molecular formulas, reflecting distinct compositional traits: PET-DOM is enriched in carboxyl-rich protein and lipid components, whereas PLA-DOM is dominated by tannin-like and condensed aromatic constituents. Mechanistic fraction‑based tests confirmed that DOM components enriched in oxygen‑containing groups, potentially including carboxyl‑ and phenolic‑hydroxyl‑related structures, may exhibit stronger competitive effects for phosphate adsorption on goethite. Beyond site competition, MP-DOM reduces surface Fe(III) and induces goethite amorphization, with more significant mineral alteration under PET-DOM exposure. This study provides molecular‑level insights into how MP‑DOM alters phosphate retention in the sediments, highlighting that polymer‑driven MP‑DOM effects should be considered when assessing internal phosphorus loading in MP‑polluted aquatic systems.

items.title: Responses of particulate carbon and nitrogen to a mild oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) in the Zhenbei Seamount waters of the South China Sea.
items.abstract: Low-oxygen conditions in oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) influence particulate organic matter degradation and transport, yet particulate carbon and nitrogen dynamics in mild OMZs and seamount effects remain poorly understood. We investigated hydrography and distributions of particulate organic carbon (POC), particulate nitrogen (PN), the POC/PN mass ratio, δ13C-POC, and δ15N-PN at Zhenbei Seamount, South China Sea. We examined the mild OMZ within a common 450-2050 m analysis interval, with a regional dissolved oxygen (DO) reference of 3.2 mg/L and a minimum DO of 2.31 mg/L near 750 m. From 0 to 100 to 100-450 m, POC and PN decreased by 50.50% and 54.85%, respectively. Both continued to decline in the upper OMZ but changed little in the lower OMZ, consistent with continued transformation and variable particle replenishment. Below this analysis interval, DO increased without increases in POC or PN, while mean POC/PN was higher. None of the four paired interlayer POC/PN changes was significant after Holm correction. DO was related to POC and PN across the whole water column, but neither relationship remained significant within the OMZ. The greater relative loss of PN likely reflected preferential degradation of nitrogen-rich labile components. Neither isotope showed a monotonic trend, suggesting combined effects of initial isotope composition, microbial alteration, and source mixing. Local density-surface and particle heterogeneity near the summit and slopes was consistent with physical redistribution. Together, the concentration, POC/PN, and isotope observations distinguish stage-dependent particle transformation from local seamount-associated heterogeneity in a mild OMZ.

items.title: Wetland mitigated excessive N 2 O concentrations for urban river-wetland continuum.
items.abstract: Urban waters are potent sources of N2O. The mechanism by which interconnected wetlands and rivers (i.e., river-wetland continuum) regulate N2O dynamics in urban waters remains unclear. This study investigated the spatiotemporal patterns and microbial mechanisms underlying N2O dynamics within the urban river-wetland continuum (URWC) in Guangzhou, China, across wet and dry seasons. Excessive N2O concentrations (ΔN2O) were generally higher in urban rivers (UR) than in urban wetland rivers (WR), with a wider range of seasonal medians in UR (31-63 nmol L-1) than in WR (23-33 nmol L-1). UR generally exhibited higher concentrations of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3N), and ammonium nitrogen (NH4N) than WR. Isotope-based source partitioning identified bacterial denitrification (bD) as the dominant N2O-producing pathway in the URWC, with a greater relative contribution in UR (60.7%) than in WR (51.6%). In contrast, genes involved in NH4+ assimilation (gltB/D/S, gdhA, and glnA) and NO3- assimilation (narA/B, nasA/B/D/E, and nirA/B) were significantly more abundant in WR than in UR. Although the nosZ/(nirS + nirK) ratio did not differ significantly between UR and WR, isotope-derived estimates indicated a higher N2O reduction fraction in WR (91%) than in UR (87%). These findings suggest that nitrogen availability and microbial N2O production and reduction processes may jointly influence ΔN2O in the URWC. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining urban wetlands and controlling external nitrogen inputs to limit N2O accumulation and potentially mitigate emissions in connected urban waters.

items.title: Estimations for strong and weak hot Jupiter magnetism. A Python package with interpolators and scaling laws
items.abstract: Hot Jupiters (HJs) are commonly thought to host the strongest dynamo-generated magnetic fields among exoplanets, exceeding Jupiter's by up to an order of magnitude, which can potentially induce observable star--planet interaction (SPI) and planetary radio emission. However, while several indirect, model-dependent estimates of HJ magnetic fields have been reported from SPIs and recent transmission spectroscopy diagnostics, no unambiguous direct (radio) detection has yet been achieved. We aim to provide a range of magnetic field estimates for HJs, considering at the same time the mechanisms responsible for inflation and the convective flux that enters into the magnetic field scaling law. Given that their dynamos operate in the fast-rotating regime (Rossby number łesssim 0.1), we combined one-dimensional evolutionary interior models with magnetic field scaling laws under two limiting heating scenarios within the convective zone: deep and shallow energy depositions. Using interpolators built from the simulated data output, we provide magnetic field predictions for the HJ population. The deep-heating scenario maximizes convective heat flux in the dynamo and predicts strong magnetic fields of up to ∼100 G, whereas shallow heating, which is arguably more realistic for most proposed physical mechanisms, weakens convection and yields much weaker fields of $ ̧al O (1)$ G. The strong field scenario is compatible with indirect SPI detections, and the weak field scenario is in agreement with recent atmospheric constraints. We derived easy-to-use scaling law relations based on observables, i.e., planetary mass, radius, and/or incident stellar flux, that roughly reproduce the magnetic field estimates of our interior models: B_ ̊m strong = 19 , ̊m P ^ 0.6 R_ ̊m P ^ 1.7 G and B_ ̊m weak = 0.8 , M_ ̊m P ^ 1.5 R_ ̊m P ^ -1.2 G. With this range of magnetic field estimates for the current observed HJ population, our predictions provide a framework for interpreting future atmospheric wind measurements, SPI signatures, and radio observations, which may ultimately discriminate between competing interior-heating scenarios.

items.title: How to Measure Victimhood and Moral Judgment with the Theory of Dyadic Morality
items.abstract: The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) argues that moral condemnation revolves around intuitive perceptions of victimization. We provide a curated collection of items for measuring moral judgment and perceived victimization, organized around one question: “From someone’s perspective, who is victimizing whom, how, and to what extent?” Each part of the question connects to a core element of our moral psychology, including the dyad itself (an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim), the continuum of perceived victimization (mild to severe), different kinds of victimization (e.g., physical violence versus spiritual suffering), and the important worldviews that shape perceived victimization (e.g., cultural and politics). We show how classic paradigms, from moral dilemmas to moral dumbfounding, can be measured with TDM, and we outline future directions, including how TDM can align artificial intelligence with human moral judgment.

We show how classic paradigms, from moral dilemmas to moral dumbfounding, can be measured with TDM, and we outline future directions, including how TDM can align artificial intelligence with human moral judgment.

items.title: Scientists in conservation advocacy: moving beyond the lab and taking protagonism in activism in Brazil
items.abstract: The global environmental crisis threatens human health, ecosystem functioning, and the economy. Scientists are essential in providing evidence-based solutions and informing public policy. However, many feel unprepared or hesitant to engage in activism or political processes. Here, we discuss how scientists can bridge the gap between research and policy implementation through dialogue with policymakers and society, public engagement, and active participation in biodiversity conservation. Scientists can enhance the science-policy interface and influence conservation decisions by actively participating in public engagement. Collaboration, political commitment, and active involvement as citizen scientists are critical to addressing environmental issues. Scientists should be encouraged to recognize their expertise as valuable contributions to public policies and advocate for change, despite the challenges of balancing research demands and societal spheres. By gradually engaging in the political process, advocating for change, and disseminating high-quality information, scientists can significantly impact biodiversity conservation and environmental sustainability.

items.title: Reward sensitivity is associated with gambling participation, and financial vulnerability with problem gambling in U.S. adults
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of legal and online gambling in the United States has renewed public-health concern about gambling participation and gambling-related problems. These outcomes may have partly distinct correlates, yet they are rarely examined together within a single sample. We therefore tested whether demographic, contextual, financial, and psychological factors differentiated non-gamblers, recreational gamblers, and participants classified as problem gamblers. A nationally recruited, cross-sectional sample of 726 U.S. adults aged 18–80 completed measures of gambling behavior and symptoms, socioeconomic and financial vulnerability, mental health, loneliness, risk-taking, reward sensitivity, and neighborhood conditions. After adjustment for age and gender, reward sensitivity differed across all three groups, with the lowest scores among non-gamblers and the highest among problem gamblers. In adjusted models, reward sensitivity distinguished gamblers from non-gamblers. Among gamblers, socioeconomic deprivation and financial-exploitation vulnerability distinguished problem from recreational gambling, whereas reward sensitivity did not. In exploratory analyses, financial-exploitation vulnerability was more strongly associated with symptom severity among problem gamblers than among recreational gamblers after correction for multiple comparisons. Evidence for a similar group difference in socioeconomic deprivation depended on the scoring method. Reward sensitivity was positively associated with symptom severity at both low and high loneliness, with a stronger association at high loneliness. These findings suggest that gambling participation and problem gambling have partly distinct correlates: reward sensitivity distinguished gamblers from non-gamblers but not problem from recreational gamblers in fully adjusted models, whereas socioeconomic and financial vulnerability more clearly differentiated problem from recreational gambling.

items.title: Motoric signatures to detect original authorship versus cognitive effort in instructed motor responses of an emerging speaker with ASD
items.abstract: There is at present no objective, agnostic method to track levels of message authorship and agency in non-speakers who rely on assisted typing to communicate. Part of the problem is that nuances in spontaneous gestural movements of the typer transpire largely beneath awareness of both the typer and the communication-regulation-partner. Such spontaneous movements co-occur with the intentional ones producing the typed messages but are currently not considered part of the communication system. We introduce an assay that probes various levels of cognitive loads in an ecologically valid environment. Then, in collaboration with an emerging speaker-typer and his communication-regulation-partner, we empirically estimate motoric stochastic signatures during both independent and assisted typing. Under varying levels of cognitive loads, the assay and biometrics distinguish motoric patterns in spontaneous typing of phrases in response to open-ended questions from those in instructed typing of the same phrase. The non-dominant bodily motions, co-occurring with the dominant (typing) side reveal not only levels of cognitive mental effort and agency of the typer but also levels of creative thoughts through motoric preambles present only in open-ended mode. This level of semantic authorship is detectable in both the geodesic paths along the manifold representing the Gamma stochastic parameters of the motions fluctuations and those of the physical 3D spatial trajectories. The head and facial micro-motions capture these non-dominant-body nuances, offering a personalized motoric metric of cognitive effort, agency, authorship and a comprehensive suite of assays to open new research avenues for assisted typing with haptic support.

items.title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding
items.abstract: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.

items.title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
items.abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

items.title: Predicting the Orbital Retention of Habitable-Zone Planets Following Stellar Flybys Using Machine Learning
items.abstract: Stellar flybys can significantly alter the orbital configurations of planetary systems, potentially displacing planets initially located within the habitable zone (HZ) of their host stars. In this study, we investigate the dynamical effects of stellar encounters on HZ planets using a large suite of three-body N-body simulations. We examine how the properties of the host star, passing star, planetary orbit, and encounter geometry influence the final orbital configuration. A planet is considered to retain an HZ orbit only if it remains bound to its original host and its entire final orbital range, from periastron to apastron, lies within the HZ boundaries. Based on the simulation results, we develop an XGBoost classifier to predict the final HZ status of planets following stellar encounters. The model achieves an accuracy of 0.90, an ROC-AUC of 0.97, and a PR-AUC of 0.97 on the test set. Feature importance analysis identifies the encounter-impulse parameter as the dominant predictor of the outcome. The classifier provides a computational speedup of approximately 74 compared with direct N-body simulations. We further evaluate the model using an independent dataset representing a globular-cluster environment, where approximately 20 per cent of planets retain HZ orbits. Despite the naturally imbalanced class distribution, the model achieves an accuracy of 0.87, an ROC-AUC of 0.92, and a PR-AUC of 0.77. These results demonstrate the potential of machine learning for efficiently predicting the dynamical retention of HZ planets following stellar encounters and for investigating their outcomes in dense stellar environments.

items.title: Rethinking Discovery Research with AI: The promise of transdisciplinarity and the danger of reductionism
items.abstract: In theory, transdisciplinary research focuses on solving real-world problems without being constrained by disciplinary boundaries and methodologies. In practice, doing so is challenging, as recognized by the phrase "The world has problems; universities have departments." As a powerful integrative tool, AI may help overcome traditional reductionist approaches and enable genuine transdisciplinarity. In this essay, we discuss how this could happen and why, within the current system of incentives, it is not happening.

items.title: Political Orientation and Participation in Prediction Markets: Large Stakes Converge, Small Stakes Diverge
items.abstract: Prediction markets offer a way to study collective expectations and beliefs: people express their views on various events and, by putting money behind their predictions, take on the risks of their judgments. As a result, the scale of investment can reveal additional dimensions of individual behavior and beliefs. In this study, we use a complex network approach to examine the structure of user participation, drawing on roughly 1.14 billion transaction records from the Polymarket platform, covering more than 3.1 million wallet addresses and 764,000 prediction events. To do this, we build a bipartite network of users and events and analyze patterns of investment concentration, connections between topics, and the network's community structure. Our findings show a highly skewed distribution of financial participation: 1\% of events account for 64\% of total transaction volume, while 1\% of wallets account for 79.2\% of total financial participation. We also examine how investment scale and political orientation shape user participation patterns. Focusing on the 2024 U.S. presidential election, we compare users who invested exclusively in a Trump victory or exclusively in a Harris victory, grouping wallets by purchase size rather than by retail or institutional status. The results show that among large-scale investors, capital allocation patterns across topics are more similar between the two political groups; in contrast, these patterns diverge more and vary more among small-scale investors. This result holds across six different ways of representing and comparing the networks, and four of these differences are also statistically supported.

items.title: Pharmacy stock and post-earthquake access to medicines in Tokyo: modeling choices that change recovery judgments
items.abstract: Community pharmacies sustain access to medicines after an earthquake only while open, staffed and stocked. Accessibility models rarely represent stock depletion, and the assumptions this requires may change conclusions about recovery. We examine these assumptions for over-the-counter (OTC) medicines supplied by 4,748 registered pharmacies in Tokyo's 23 wards during the first week after a magnitude-7.3 scenario earthquake. A two-step floating catchment area model computes walking accessibility for 2,651 grid cells (500 m) under 10,000 sampled combinations of stock duration, staffing, operation and demand. Results are expressed as Retention: post-disaster accessibility divided by the same cell's pre-disaster accessibility. First, the assumed link between stock and service, the supply a pharmacy can still provide, determines the recovery verdict. If service falls in proportion to remaining stock, mean Retention declines from 0.479 (days 2-3) to 0.273 (days 4-7). If service is maintained until stock falls below one quarter, the mean rises instead, although low-end (10th-percentile) outcomes still decline. Measuring at the start of each period rather than averaging over it also reverses the trend. Second, a simple model that rescales a fixed map by citywide supply and demand reproduces citywide patterns but cannot evaluate where pharmacies close or where capacity is added; a spatial model run once on average inputs can. Third, four floating catchment methods agree on overall rankings (rank correlation 0.81), but their lowest-ranked 10% of cells overlap only partially (Jaccard index 0.56). Disaster assessments should report stock assumptions and low-end outcomes, and treat local priority areas as method-dependent.

items.title: Hyperbolic network embedding via dimensional annealing and Barnes--Hut approximation
items.abstract: Common features observed in complex networks from various domains can be explained by network geometry in hyperbolic space. Inferring the latent coordinates of nodes enables efficient navigation, link prediction, and geometric renormalization. However, the loss landscape of the hyperbolic model is extremely rugged due to the topological constraints of the low-dimensional embedding space. To overcome this, we introduce the dimensional annealing framework, which bypasses these constraints by introducing an auxiliary dimension. We show that dimensional annealing achieves higher-quality embeddings than existing energy-based embedding methods. Additionally, we incorporate the Barnes--Hut approximation for computational scalability.
