items.title: Anisotropic field suppression of charge order reveals orbital-selective Kondo hybridization in UTe 2
items.abstract: UTe 2 is a rare correlated quantum material where unconventional density-wave orders, Kondo physics, spin-triplet pairing, and reentrant superconductivity coexist. Because superconductivity emerges from a strongly correlated normal state, identifying and controlling intertwined normal-state orders are essential for understanding the electronic landscape where superconductivity arises. Here, using scanning tunneling microscopy in a vector magnetic field, we uncover a staggered charge density wave (CDW) in high-quality UTe 2 crystals. This CDW exhibits a strong directional field response: It is completely quenched by a modest 1.7-tesla magnetic field along the quasi–one-dimensional uranium-chain direction while remaining robust against fields along other crystallographic axes. This anisotropy suggests an orbital-driven field-tuned quantum phase transition. Unexpectedly, the same field orientation concurrently suppresses the 5f Kondo resonance. Modeling indicates a switch in the dominant hybridization channel from Te 5 p- U 5 f to U 6 d- U 5 f coupling, suggesting an intimate interplay between CDW and the Kondo effect.

items.title: Inspiral test of the Kerr hypothesis beyond the quadrupole with GW241011
items.abstract: All multipole moments of a Kerr black hole are uniquely determined by its mass and spin. Gravitational wave observations can test this prediction by measuring spin-induced multipole moments imprinted on the inspiral phase of compact binary mergers. In this Letter, we show that the recently reported compact binary coalescence GW241011 enables a simultaneous test of deviations in the spin-induced quadrupole and octupole moments of the binary components from their black hole values. We find no evidence for deviations from the Kerr prediction and place the first constraints on spin-induced octupole moments of the compact binary. This approach complements tests of the Kerr nature of compact binary merger remnants based on quasinormal mode measurements in the ringdown phase.

items.title: EP250302a: Violent Shell Collision in a Soft-X-Ray-selected Gamma-Ray-burst-like Transient
items.abstract: The Einstein Probe (EP) opens a previously unexplored soft X-ray window onto gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), filling a critical observational gap in the soft X-ray coverage of their prompt emission. In this Letter, we present EP250302a, a soft-X-ray-selected, GRB-like transient at z = 1.131 detected by the EP. Follow-up observations from X-ray to radio reveal a narrow X-ray flare at ∼1.1 ks and subsequent achromatic optical and X-ray rebrightening. These features challenge a standard single-component afterglow model and indicate the need for multiple ejecta components. A violent collision between a late relativistic shell and the decelerated leading blast wave provides a plausible interpretation: the flare arises from internal dissipation of the late ejecta, while the rebrightening is powered by the shocked emission produced in the collision. Quantitative modeling constrains the kinetic energy ratio between the late shell and the initial ejecta to E k,iso,2 / E k,iso,1 ∼ 5 (with E k,iso,2 ∼ 10 53 erg and E k,iso,1 ∼ 2 × 10 52 erg), as well as the Lorentz factor contrast to Γ 2,0 /Γ 1,0 ≈ 0.98–2.27, required to reproduce the observed flare luminosity and rebrightening amplitude. Such an energetic late shell can be launched in a radiatively inefficient second episode of central-engine activity. Thanks to the well-sampled, early-time multiband coverage facilitated by the EP trigger, EP250302a provides a valuable case to test the physical connection between central-engine activity and shell collisions.

items.title: Are Nucleosynthetic Yields Universal? Interpreting the Multielemental Abundances of Quiescent Galaxies over Cosmic Time Using Milky Way Stars
items.abstract: The detailed abundance patterns of quiescent galaxies offer powerful constraints on their formation and evolution. Yet physical insight remains elusive, as nucleosynthetic yields are notoriously uncertain. We introduce a framework that circumvents this problem by using Milky Way abundance trends as empirical proxies for initial mass function (IMF)-averaged yields. Applied to quiescent galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( z ∼ 0), LEGA-C ( z ∼ 0.7), and JWST/SUSPENSE ( z ∼ 2), our approach recovers the α - and Fe-peak abundances with a median offset of ∼0.05 dex across 10 elements, compared to ∼0.23 dex for theoretical yields. Systematic residuals of up to ∼0.1–0.2 dex remain for some elements in galaxies with the highest velocity dispersions. The largest discrepancies arise in N, Sr, Ba, and (at z ∼ 2) C, all of which depend on asymptotic giant branch enrichment, a channel we do not explicitly model. We explore the impact of a top-heavy IMF and find that it can shift the IMF-averaged core-collapse supernova yields by ∼0.05–0.2 dex in a direction that reduces the systematic residuals. Surprisingly, the predictions succeed without modeling the full chemical-evolution history of a galaxy: Mg and Fe alone are sufficient to predict the remaining α - and Fe-peak elements. Combined with previous results in dwarf galaxies and the Milky Way disk, this success suggests that the IMF-averaged nucleosynthetic yields of α - and Fe-peak elements are largely universal. This predictability makes the empirical yields immediately useful: embedding them in stellar population synthesis models will improve inferences on stellar populations and star formation histories, while incorporating them into cosmological simulations will produce more observationally motivated predictions.

items.title: Assessing the imprint of eccentricity in GW signatures using two independent waveform models
items.abstract: The gravitational wave signal from merging compact binaries encodes information about their orbital and intrinsic properties. Over the last few years, state-of-the-art waveform models have begun to incorporate the effects of orbital eccentricity into their estimated signal. Over a similar period, many groups have applied these waveforms to characterize whether the imprint of eccentricity is present and, if so, measure this time-evolving property (at a suitably-defined reference point). In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of 162 confident sources identified in the O3 and O4a observing runs of the International Gravitational Wave Network (LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA). Using the RIFT parameter inference engine, we employ two independently implemented waveform models (SEOBNRv5EHM and TEOBResumS-Dali) which account for orbital eccentricity and the effects of aligned compact object spins. Using these two waveforms, we find consistent conclusions that disfavor the eccentric hypothesis. Unlike previous work, among binary black hole candidates, we find potential evidence for eccentricity in three events: GW200129, GW231001, and GW231123. For the latter two events, the evidence for eccentricity is ambiguous, with different degrees of support from different waveforms. Consistent with previous work, we find conclusions obtained about GW200129 can be sensitive to analysis settings, as expected, given the nonstationary noise present.

items.title: Reconstruction of Reionization Histories from 21 cm Power-spectrum Evolution with Artificial Neural Networks
items.abstract: We investigate whether the redshift evolution of the fixed- k dimensionless 21 cm power spectrum, Δ 21 2 ( k , z ) , contains sufficient information to reconstruct reionization histories x HI ( z ) with artificial neural networks. Using semi-numerical realizations generated within a restricted three-parameter 21cmFAST model family, we train a compact feed-forward network to learn the inverse mapping from power-spectrum trajectories to the neutral-fraction history on a 97-point redshift grid spanning 6 ≤ z ≤ 15. For k = 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 h Mpc −1 , representative tests on an independent test set show that the midpoint redshift z 50 is recovered more accurately than the duration Δ z = z 75 − z 25 in terms of dimensionless relative errors: z 50 is reconstructed with MAE = 0.0046 and RMSE = 0.0100, whereas Δ z yields MAE = 0.0302 and RMSE = 0.0378. This result indicates that fixed- k power-spectrum evolution carries stronger information about the timing of reionization than about the detailed width of the transition within the adopted prior. We further test an idealized foreground-free SKA1-Low-like thermal-plus-sample-variance noise model and find that the reconstruction remains stable in the favorable signal-to-noise regime considered here. These results demonstrate that neural networks can serve as prior-dependent inverse mapping for reconstructing reionization histories from 21 cm power-spectrum evolution.

items.title: A framework for modelling Population III stars in cosmological simulations
items.abstract: Population III (Pop III) stars are the first generation of stars to form in the universe, emerging from primordial gas composed mainly of hydrogen and helium. In this work, we present a comprehensive framework for modelling Pop III stars in cosmological simulations. This includes: (1) an enhanced thermochemical network that tracks the equilibrium abundances of $\rm {H_2^+}$ and $\rm {H^-}$ which catalyses $\rm H_2$ formation in primordial gas; (2) detailed stellar spectra of Pop III stars computed from MESA evolutionary tracks and TLUSTY NLTE atmosphere models; and (3) comprehensive supernova feedback, including both Core-Collapse and Pair-Instability supernovae, with detailed elemental yields. We implement these improvements in AREPO-RT and test them using cosmological zoom-in simulations of a 1.07 × 1010M⊙ halo at z = 3 with varying Pop III IMF. Our results show that Pop III stars form at z > 13 and are under 1 percent of new stars by z ∼ 5. Their Lyman-Werner radiation raises the local LW flux by two orders of magnitude at z ≈ 16, and their feedback lowers the star formation rate at z > 5.5. The new chemistry more than doubles the mass fraction of cool, dense pristine gas, while Pop III feedback creates photo-heated diffuse gas and drives distinct metal enrichment patterns at 10 20 Å) comparable with JWST observations from a galaxy at z ∼ 11.

items.title: Density fluctuations in pseudo-streamer and helmet streamer: Generation, propagation and comparison with Metis observations
items.abstract: Recent white-light observations from the Metis coronagraph on board Solar Orbiter have shown the presence of propagating density fluctuations with a period of ∼5 minutes, particularly in the observationally bright regions of helmet streamers and pseudo-streamers. These density fluctuations have been shown to originate from magnetohydrodynamic wave modes – slow and fast modes can directly compress the plasma, whereas AlfvÃ©n waves generate density fluctuations via a non-linear coupling with the slow and fast modes. In general, in low plasma β regions, slow modes contribute more towards the generation of density fluctuations, whereas in high β regions, there are significant contributions from both slow and fast waves. In this work, we investigate the propagation of (non-linear) AlfvÃ©n waves and the associated density fluctuations using a 2.5D axisymmetric global solar wind model that includes two distinct magnetic field topologies – a helmet streamer and a pseudo-streamer. Key differences in these magnetic configurations give rise to differences in the wave behaviour due to, for example, the presence of a current sheet in the helmet streamer and an X-type null point in the pseudo-streamer, and the structure of the β = 1 layer in both magnetic field configurations. This leads to the possible creation of prominent interference patterns along the helmet streamer axis, which do not appear along the pseudo-streamer axis. Unlike in the streamer region, we also find that along the pseudo-streamer axis, the contribution to the density fluctuations is due to the fast waves only, despite being in a low β plasma.

items.title: Primordial black holes from vector-induced curvature perturbations sourced by primordial magnetic fields
items.abstract: Generating an appreciable abundance of primordial black holes (PBHs) requires a substantial enhancement of primordial curvature perturbations on small scales. In this Letter, we propose a new post-inflationary mechanism in which such an enhancement arises during a stiff, or kination, epoch. The mechanism is driven by metric vector perturbations sourced by the vector component of the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor associated with primordial magnetic fields (PMFs). Since these first-order vector modes remain approximately constant during kination, they act as persistent nonlinear sources for second-order scalar perturbations. We show that the resulting vector-induced curvature perturbations are amplified toward the infrared cutoff of the kination band and exhibit the characteristic scaling PR(k) k^{-5}. As a concrete realization, we consider PMFs generated in a Ratra-type magnetogenesis scenario and find that the induced curvature perturbations can produce PBHs with an abundance large enough to constitute a substantial fraction of the dark matter.

items.title: Multiparameter two-photon polarimetry approaching the quantum limit
items.abstract: Photonic quantum metrology has demonstrated advantages in precision and resource efficiency for a wide range of applications, with several schemes approaching the fundamental quantum Cramér-Rao precision bound (QCRB). However, the intrinsic incompatibility of quantum measurements represents a hurdle in extending these advantages to the simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters. In this paper, we present an experimental protocol approaching the QCRB simultaneously in two polarisation parameters, across a wide range of the parameter space, with as few as $\sim 200$ photon pairs, offering advantages for polarimetric sensing for dim sources such as in X-ray astronomy or photosensitive samples.

items.title: Design and Performance of the Carruthers Geocoronal Imager
items.abstract: The GeoCoronal Imager (GCI) onboard the Carruthers Geocorona Observatory is the primary scientific instrument of the mission. It is designed to measure far ultraviolet light at 121.6 nm Lyman- $\alpha $ α (Ly- $\alpha $ α ) emitted by hydrogen (H) atoms in Earth’s exosphere with the sensitivity, accuracy and precision to meet the mission’s scientific objectives regarding the nature of terrestrial exospheric structure and dynamics on both global and regional scales. The GCI is comprised of two co-aligned UV imaging systems. The Narrow Field Imager (NFI) acquires nearly continuous images of exospheric Ly- $\alpha $ α radiance near and above the Earth’s limb at relatively high spatial and temporal resolution, while the Wide Field Imager (WFI) uses relatively higher optical sensitivity and a wider field of view to detect faint Ly- $\alpha $ α emission from the exosphere’s outermost extent. Both imaging channels feature identical active pixel sensor cameras, gain-intensifiers, and 6-position optical filter wheels. This paper outlines the instrument design requirements, informed by mission science goals, as well as its performance as measured in the vacuum ultraviolet laboratory test and calibration.

items.title: Combining gravitational wave search pipelines to find subthreshold signals in GWTC-5.0
items.abstract: The detection of transient gravitational wave signals relies on independent search algorithms that analyse detector data and assign significance measures to candidate events. However, varying performance complicates their interpretation. We use supervised machine learning combined with conformal prediction, a framework to quantify uncertainties, to merge multi-pipeline information into well-calibrated confidence scores. We demonstrate that this approach is robust across different classifier architectures and remains stable when trained on different simulated datasets. When applied to events across the GWTC catalogue up to and including the second part of the fourth observing run, the framework identifies several subthreshold candidates with elevated confidence, including the binary neutron star candidate GW200311_103121. We examine the reliability of these up-rankings, finding evidence that high-confidence predictions correspond to signal-like events. This framework enables simplified systematic candidate assessment for gravitational wave catalogues and real-time alerts by providing a single, well-calibrated confidence measure per candidate.

items.title: A two-platform blueprint for modeling human brain development.
items.abstract: No single experimental system spans human neural-plate induction through late-stage circuit maturation. Brain organoids have transformed human developmental neuroscience, yet a decade of progress has clarified their intrinsic limitations: they cannot fully recapitulate neural induction driven by embryo-scale developmental signals, nor achieve the degree of circuit maturation that requires an in vivo physiological context. Stem cell-based embryo models are positioned to provide mechanistic access to peri-gastrulation and early neurulation, whereas interspecies chimeras provide the physiological milieu to study myelination, pruning and circuit-level function. Here we propose a two-platform roadmap that integrates stem cell-based embryo models to decode developmental logic with interspecies chimeras to study functional maturation. We outline reproducibility and reporting standards, including rigorous benchmarks for neural-tube formation and closure, and present a milestone-based oversight framework anchored to verifiable developmental landmarks. Together, these complementary platforms enable causal interrogation of human neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease while remaining responsive to ethical and technical constraints.

items.title: Dynamic visualization of cell adhesion molecule interactions using reversible split-HaloTag labeling in living cells.
items.abstract: Critical for diverse cellular functions, cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) interact to transduce information from the external environment to drive coordinated intracellular responses. However, direct visualization of CAM interactions in living cells and organisms remains a major challenge. Recent developments in split-HaloTag technology present a promising strategy for chemical labeling of protein-protein interactions. Here, we apply this method to dynamically monitor CAM interactions in living HEK293T cells using split-HaloTag-CAM fusion proteins. With high specificity, we visualized trans-cellular interactions between known adhesion pairs natively found in neuronal and immunological synapses. To expand the system's versatility, we adapted a modified split-HaloTag component (cpHaloΔ N272H ) that enables reversible dye exchange and facilitates rapid time-lapse imaging of CAM interactions. Leveraging fluorogenic HaloTag dyes, split-HaloTag-CAMs measured the real-time disassembly and reassembly of Ca 2+ -dependent CAM junctions in live cells. These tools enabled imaging long-term changes in surface contacts mediated by CAM binding, thus providing a robust platform for dissecting the spatiotemporal dynamics of CAM interactions in cellular and organismal contexts.

items.title: Ketamine promotes strategic and efficient approach-avoidance conflict resolution.
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires flexibly balancing approach and avoidance in risky or threatening environments, a flexibility disrupted in depression and other disorders marked by excessive avoidance. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam broadly dampen neural excitability and synaptic plasticity, whereas ketamine may enhance both. We therefore asked whether ketamine promotes more strategic and efficient motivational behavior. In this completed randomized crossover study, 34 healthy participants with no lifetime neurological or psychiatric disorders and no regular medication use were assessed at the University Medical Center Freiburg (DRKS00025471). Participants completed three visits separated by seven days: a control visit without medication, followed by intranasal ketamine (50 mg) and oral lorazepam (1 mg) in randomized, counterbalanced order. Threat probability and loss magnitude were varied independently in a dynamic approach-avoidance conflict task conducted after ketamine's acute dissociative phase. Reported behavioral outcomes were net token gain, approach behavior, and approach and withdrawal latencies. Behavioral assessors were blinded to condition; participants and physicians were not. Mixed-effects models were used. All 34 randomized participants completed each condition and were analyzed. Ketamine yielded 57% higher token gains than control (β = 0.09, 95% confidence interval 0.05 to 0.13; p < 0.001) and 33% higher gains than lorazepam (β = 0.05, 0.01 to 0.09; p = 0.009). Behavior following ketamine was more strongly guided by outcome value than threat probability and showed faster approach and withdrawal responses. Lorazepam produced a less selective increase in approach behavior. No unexpected adverse events occurred. In healthy participants, ketamine was associated with more efficient and value-sensitive approach-avoidance behavior than control and lorazepam.

items.title: Integrating behavioral and molecular biomarkers reveals neurotoxic effects of common insecticide in big brown bats.
items.abstract: While foraging in croplands, bats are exposed to pesticides that can be neurotoxic even at low concentrations, affecting their physiology and behavior. These sublethal effects are often assessed using molecular biomarkers in isolation, with limited insights into ecological consequences. Here, we used an integrative approach to assess the sublethal effects of chlorpyrifos, a common neurotoxic insecticide, on big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus). We combined behavioral experiments with molecular biomarkers that could reveal the mechanisms underlying observed changes. We orally exposed bats to chlorpyrifos and evaluated their associative memory in a crawling Y-maze, and their stereotyped flight trajectories. To understand the mechanisms behind these behavioral changes, we quantified brain cholinesterase (ChE) activity and used non-targeted proteomics to identify cellular and molecular biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Exposed bats did not change their flight consistency, but were less explorative, had a slower reflex response, and made more incorrect choices in the Y-maze. Exposed bats had a significant reduction in their ChE activity and showed dysregulation of proteins involved in neurological processes like memory, learning, and sound perception. Our results not only provide a comprehensive understanding of the different ways in which pesticides affect individual performance, they also provide a broad description of the underlying cellular and molecular processes, increasing our mechanistic understanding of these effects. Moreover, our results support the sensitivity of behavior as an ecologically relevant biomarker of toxicity and the importance of considering multiple levels of organization to elucidate the mechanisms underlying altered behavior in wildlife due to human activities.

items.title: Brain variation underlying genetic factors linked to psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.
items.abstract: Background Psychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions have both shared and distinct symptomatology, but the brain mechanisms underlying diagnostic similarities and differences remain unclear. Methods Using genome-wide association data, we analyzed 12 psychiatric disorders and four neurodegenerative diseases, assessing polygenic overlap, shared loci, and genetic causal relationships linking their genetic latent factors with 3,935 brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDP). Results Using genomic structural equation modeling, we identified an internalizing factor (F1), an addiction factor (F2), a factor related to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (F3), a neurodevelopmental factor (F4), and a factor related to Alzheimer's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (F5). These showed shared transcriptomic enrichments for frontal and anterior cingulate cortical regions, while F1-specific depletion in substantia nigra and F3-specific enrichment in nucleus accumbens appeared to be specific. Fine-mapping identified 99 variants, including shared loci (e.g., VRK2: F1, F2, F3; TSHZ3: F1, F2; TCF4: F1, F3) and factor-specific loci (e.g., DRD2-F2; SCN2A-F3; FOXP2-F4; TNIP1-F5). The brain-wide analysis of fine-mapped loci identified 1,480 IDP associations (false discovery rate q 400 brain IDPs (mostly related to cortical area, cortical grey-white contrast, cortical thickness, and regional and tissue volume). Similarly, MOBP rs1768190 related to F5 was associated with >200 brain IDPs, with about half of them related to cortical thickness. Conclusions The present study provides new insights into cross-diagnostic mechanisms linking genetic variation and molecular changes to the brain structural and functional variation across psychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions.

items.title: The Association between Physical Activity and Higher Corticolimbic Synaptic Density is Independent of Body Mass Index.
items.abstract: Background Regular physical exercise has been linked to biomarkers of slowed biological aging, including brain aging, though the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. Exercise may enhance neuroplasticity and attenuate synaptic decline; however, evidence supporting these effects has largely been limited to animal and postmortem studies. Whether physical activity is associated with synaptic density in the living human brain remains unknown. Methods We used positron emission tomography (PET) with the radiotracer [ 18 F]SynVesT-1 to quantify synaptic density in vivo in 51 individuals (61% female). Participants were classified as physically active or insufficiently active, and group differences in synaptic density across corticolimbic regions were examined. Additional regression and mediation analyses assessed associations among physical activity, synaptic density, body mass index (BMI), and depressive symptom severity. Results Physically active individuals exhibited significantly higher synaptic density across corticolimbic regions compared to insufficiently active individuals (F 6,44 =2.41, p=0.042). These effects remained marginally significant after adjusting for BMI and depressive symptom severity (F 6,42 =2.33, p=0.050). Region-specific regression analyses further demonstrated positive associations between physical activity and synaptic density. Mediation analyses indicated that BMI did not account for the observed relationships. Conclusions These findings provide the first known in vivo evidence that physical activity is associated with higher synaptic density in the living human brain, particularly within prefrontal circuits. Results suggest that exercise may support synaptic integrity through mechanisms partially independent of BMI. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine causality, characterize temporal dynamics, and evaluate whether physical activity may serve as a scalable intervention to preserve synaptic health.

items.title: Flow-induced endothelial lipid dysregulation in ischemic stroke: from mechanotransduction to therapeutic implications.
items.abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) induces significant and sustained alterations in cerebral hemodynamics, which extend beyond the acute phase and actively contribute to post-stroke cerebrovascular remodeling. Accumulating evidence suggests that endothelial cholesterol and neutral-lipid homeostasis is a critical determinant of vascular integrity, whereas its dysregulation may promote endothelial inflammation, and vascular remodeling. Abnormal shear stress, particularly low and oscillatory shear stress, may connect post-stroke hemodynamic changes to endothelial lipid dysregulation by regulating lipid uptake, intracellular lipid processing, cholesterol efflux, and lipid storage through mechanotransduction pathways. Although direct evidence demonstrating that altered shear stress drives endothelial lipid accumulation in the cerebral vasculature remains limited, findings from endothelial studies and mechanobiology suggest a functional "flow-lipid axis" implicated in post-stroke vascular pathology. In this review, we summarize the hemodynamic alterations following IS and how abnormal shear stress may regulate endothelial cholesterol and neutral-lipid homeostasis through mechanosensors and downstream pathways, including AMPK, mTOR, SREBP, and lipophagy. We further identify the existing gap in causal evidence connecting post-stroke hemodynamics to cerebral endothelial lipid accumulation, and propose targeted translational research avenues aimed at facilitating the development of hemodynamic- and metabolism-based therapeutic strategies for IS.

items.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces for Traumatic Brain Injury and Spinal Cord Injury: Lesion-Pattern Matching, Functional Restoration, and Clinical Translation.
items.abstract: Background Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly being developed for clinically relevant assessment, communication, rehabilitation, and functional restoration after central nervous system injury. However, their clinical roles differ substantially across injury types. This narrative review examines BCI applications in traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) using an injury-pattern-guided framework that links residual neural architecture with clinical tasks, interface selection, and outcome assessment. Main body In SCI, motor intention and cortical activity may remain accessible despite disruption of descending pathways, supporting motor-intention decoding, brain-controlled functional electrical stimulation, neuroprosthetic control, and brain-spine interfaces. In TBI, diffuse and heterogeneous network dysfunction shifts the clinical emphasis toward detection of covert consciousness, assisted communication, neurofeedback, and multimodal rehabilitation. We compare non-invasive, endovascular, electrocorticographic, and intracortical recording approaches; summarize evoked-response, motor-imagery, and continuous decoding paradigms; and distinguish functional substitution from closed-loop restoration of an individual's own movements. Recent invasive systems have supported the restoration of grasping, standing, and walking in selected individuals with SCI, whereas evidence in TBI remains concentrated on brain-state assessment and low-bandwidth communication. Conclusion Clinical translation will require careful candidate selection, stable long-term recordings, effective bidirectional feedback, clinically meaningful real-world outcomes, ethical oversight, and sustained technical support. Disease-specific translational pathways, rather than a universal BCI model, are likely to provide the most practical route to routine clinical use after central nervous system injury.

items.title: Validation and reliability of the Epilepsy Self-Stigma Scale (ESSS) in Italian.
items.abstract: Self-stigma is the interiorization and acceptance of prejudicial beliefs of one person's culture of origin. Higher levels of self-stigma in epilepsy negatively affect quality of life and outcome. We investigated self-stigma in people with epilepsy (PwE) in Italy, by translating, culturally adapting and validating the Italian version of the Epilepsy Self-Stigma Scale (ESSS). For psychometric validation, the scale (together with GAD7, NDDI-E, QOLIE31 and RSES) was filled-in by 87 adult PwE anonymously and voluntarily participating to an online survey broadcasted on "Fondazione Epilessia LICE ETS" social media. Clinical and demographic data were collected. Internal consistency was good (Cronbach's α = 0.74). Reliability was high (Omega Total = 0.87). Higher stigma scores were moderately associated with greater anxiety (GAD-7; ρ = 0.43, p < 0.001) and depressive symptoms (NDDI-E; ρ = 0.39, p < 0.001). Negative correlations were observed with self-esteem (RSES; r = -0.45, p < 0.001) and quality of life (QOLIE-31; ρ = -0.42, p < 0.001). Individuals with lower levels of independence showed higher stigma scores. The 8-item Italian version of ESSS is valid and reliable. The findings suggest self-stigma is closely associated with quality of life through psychological factors, particularly self-esteem, although relationships should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design.

items.title: Intelligent chemical production mode occupational health risk identification, assessment and intervention study.
items.abstract: The intelligent transformation of the chemical industry has reshaped petrochemical production workflows and altered occupational-health risk landscapes. This paper delineates four typical operating scenarios for intelligent chemical manufacturing and develops a four-tier hierarchical risk indicator system covering objectives, criteria, factors, and measurable indicators. A hybrid entropy-weighted Bayesian-network evaluation model is established, where entropy weights calibrate prior probabilities of root-node inputs while conditional-probability tables are retained to characterize risk-coupling behaviors. Model performance is validated via time-series partitioning, multi-model benchmark comparisons, and cross-validation using Monte-Carlo simulations. An entropy-weighted TOPSIS multi-criteria decision-making method is adopted to rank intervention-target priorities, and discrete time-series analysis quantifies outcomes from a six-month closed-loop intervention program. Results demonstrate that human-machine interaction, psychological, and managerial risks dominate occupational-health hazards within intelligent chemical-production contexts. Three highly sensitive critical drivers are identified: operating-instruction error rate, risk-monitoring gap duration, and information-overload frequency. Multi-criteria decision analysis further reveals that high-sensitivity risk factors do not inherently represent optimal intervention targets. The proposed model achieves 88.2% prediction accuracy on time-series test datasets, and statistically significant overall-risk reduction is observed post-intervention. This work offers theoretical support for risk identification, equipment retrofitting, and worker-health protection for smart petrochemical sites, facilitating the synergistic advancement of chemical-industry intelligent modernization, operational safety, and employee occupational-health outcomes.

items.title: Restorative plein-air environments and academic self-efficacy among fine arts students:A PLS-SEM-fsQCA study.
items.abstract: Plein-air painting is a core component of fine arts education, yet its educational value is often framed primarily in terms of artistic skill development rather than students' psychological learning outcomes. Drawing on Attention Restoration Theory, this cross-sectional survey examined associations between four perceived restorative qualities of plein-air environments and fine arts students' academic self-efficacy, including statistical indirect associations through fine-arts involvement. Data from 386 fine arts students with plein-air painting experience were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). The PLS-SEM results showed that Being Away and fine-arts involvement were positively associated with academic self-efficacy, whereas Fascination, Compatibility, and Extent had no statistically significant direct associations with the outcome. All four restorative qualities were positively associated with fine-arts involvement, and each showed a significant positive indirect association with academic self-efficacy through fine-arts involvement. The fsQCA identified five equifinal configurations associated with high academic self-efficacy. Taken together, the findings position restorative plein-air environments as conditional learning resources while not establishing temporal or causal relationships.

items.title: Development and preliminary psychometric evaluation of a Narrative Comprehension Assessment (NCA) for Indian children.
items.abstract: Narrative comprehension requires children to understand explicitly presented information and integrate events to derive implicit meanings. Despite its developmental and educational importance, English-language narrative assessments developed within the Indian cultural context remain limited. This study developed and conducted a preliminary psychometric evaluation of the Narrative Comprehension Assessment (NCA), a picture-based assessment for Indian children aged 4-8 years. The NCA was developed across three phases. An initial set of 27 comprehension questions was refined through expert review to 20 items comprising 9 literal and 11 inferential questions. The final assessment used two wordless picture narratives and four sequential components: Picture Walk, Retelling, Prompted Comprehension, and Guided Story Narration. Preliminary evaluation was conducted with 80 typically developing children, equally distributed across four age groups from 4-5-7-8 years. Content validity was high (S-CVI/Ave = 0.93), and internal consistency was high for both narratives (α = 0.97 and 0.96). Significant age-group differences were observed across major NCA components for both narratives (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Literal comprehension exceeded inferential comprehension across all age groups (p < 0.001). Guided Story Narration yielded higher overall scores than Prompted Comprehension for both narratives (p < 0.001). Three-week test-retest reliability was good (ICC = 0.89 and 0.91). The findings provide preliminary evidence for the NCA's content relevance, internal consistency, developmental differentiation, and temporal stability. Larger and more diverse samples are required to further establish broader psychometric, cultural, and clinical validity and to support future normative development.

items.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions.
items.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine/threonine kinase essential for brain development and function. Mutations in CDKL5 cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired synapse formation and function. However, how CDKL5 mutations disrupt synaptic function remains unclear. Here, we show that the major neuronal isoform of CDKL5 contains a C-terminal PDZ domain-binding motif that mediates direct binding to PSD-95 and SHANK PDZ domains and recruits CDKL5 to the postsynaptic density. Disrupting this motif mislocalized CDKL5, reduced dendritic spine density, and impaired spine maturation. We also show that the CDKL5 kinase domain binds the R8 rod domain of the mechanosensitive scaffold talin. Mutation of the talin-binding interface or reduced cellular contractility altered CDKL5 positioning relative to focal adhesions. These findings define how CDKL5 is targeted to synapses, suggest that talin mechanoswitching may position CDKL5 kinase activity, and highlight the importance of C-terminal anchoring for interpreting pathogenic truncations.

items.title: The Role of U.S.-Based Professional Societies in Advancing and Creating Space for Global Psychological Science.
items.abstract: With growing recognition that psychological science has primarily focused on White Euro-American samples, constructs, theories, and methods, there is an urgent need to broaden the scope and inclusiveness of the discipline. Although journals, funding agencies, and individual scientists each play important roles in advancing this shift, U.S.-based professional societies are particularly well positioned to promote globally engaged psychological science. Recognizing this potential, the U.S. National Committee for Psychological Science, with assistance from the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, undertook an effort to gather and compile information about what U.S.-based professional societies are doing to enhance global engagement. Representatives of 24 professional societies across clinical, cognitive, developmental, and social psychology; statistics; behavioral medicine; neuroscience; and general psychology completed an online survey. Our analysis indicated that international focus was very important or important to more than 70% of the society representatives surveyed, and various activities to promote global engagement were described, although membership of Majority World scientists remained low, with limited integration of these scientists in leadership structures. On the basis of these findings and prior scholarship, we outline key approaches for inclusive, strategic, and scaffolded efforts to promote global psychological science.

items.title: Parkin Modulates PFOS Induced Apoptosis via Bax Ubiquitination in Rat Dopaminergic Neuronal Cells.
items.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a group of synthetic compounds known for their high chemical stability and resistance to degradation. Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) is one such PFAS that has been found to produce mitochondrial stress and neurotoxicity, although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, is a critical regulator of mitochondrial quality control, and its dysfunction is associated with neuronal vulnerability. Here, we investigated the involvement of parkin and Bax ubiquitination in PFOS-induced apoptotic signaling. Using N27 dopaminergic cells, we assessed dose- and time-dependent effects of PFOS exposure. Early exposure induced an adaptive response characterized by increased parkin expression and enhanced ubiquitination of Bax, accompanied by reduced pro-apoptotic signaling. In contrast, prolonged or higher-dose exposure led to a decline in parkin levels, increased Bax expression, cytochrome c release, and activation of caspase-3/7, consistent with engagement of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction. Furthermore, PRKN knockdown exacerbated PFOS-induced cytotoxicity, supporting a protective role for parkin under PFOS-induced cellular stress. These findings suggest that alterations in parkin-associated Bax ubiquitination may contribute to the regulation of apoptotic signaling following PFOS exposure, shifting the balance toward cell death. Collectively, our results provide mechanistic insight into how environmental toxicants impair mitochondrial surveillance pathways and may contribute to dopaminergic neurodegeneration.

items.title: From localisation to network modulation: how instruments reshaped the structure-function question in clinical neuroscience.
items.abstract: How function is organised in the brain remains an open question for neuroscience as a whole; its history, clinical neuroscience included, is largely the history of its instruments and of the limits they impose on interpretation. That relation is visible from the outset: under the light microscope, Golgi's black reaction was compatible with both the reticular theory and the neuron doctrine, a dispute settled only in the 1950s, by electron microscopy. This contribution traces that pattern along the axis of neurostimulation, from Fritsch and Hitzig's experiments and Penfield's intraoperative mapping to contemporary therapeutic neuromodulation, and argues that the shift from the discrete locus to the distributed network, made conceivable by functional neuroimaging and connectomics, found its causal and clinical proving ground in stimulation rather than in observation. Mood disorders furnish the exemplary case. Explanation moved from a diffuse neurochemical model of monoamine depletion, through the humoral model of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal dysregulation, to a limbic-cortical circuit account that specified a place to intervene: the subgenual cingulate. What followed is instructive precisely because it disappointed. Encouraging open-label results gave way to a multicentre controlled trial halted for futility; connectivity-guided targeting, developed in parallel, is only now undergoing sham-controlled pivotal testing. Replication failures in connectivity-based subtyping, and the sample sizes now known to be required for stable brain-behaviour associations, suggest that the point is general rather than anecdotal. The sequence recurs: the instrument defines the target, the target generates conviction, and reproducibility is established last, when it is the criterion that should come first.

items.title: AI-assisted longitudinal MRI assessment in multiple sclerosis: diagnostic performance and reduction in reporting time.
items.abstract: Detection of new and enlarging lesions on longitudinal MRI is essential for monitoring disease activity in multiple sclerosis (MS) but is time-consuming and subject to inter-reader variability. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance and workflow impact of a CE-marked artificial intelligence (AI) platform compared with neuroradiologists of different experience. In this retrospective study, 59 patients with relapsing-remitting MS underwent baseline and follow-up brain MRI including 3D FLAIR sequences. Two neuroradiologists independently assessed examinations for new or enlarging lesions, blinded to AI output. The reference standard was an AI-blinded consensus of the two readers, with discordant cases adjudicated by an independent third neuroradiologist. Patient-level diagnostic performance was evaluated for each reader alone, the AI alone, and each reader assisted by AI. Agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa and reading times with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Among unassisted assessments, the experienced reader achieved the highest accuracy (88.1%), followed by the less experienced reader (83.1%) and the AI alone (79.7%). AI assistance was associated with higher accuracy for both readers (94.9%, κ = 0.90, and 89.8%, κ = 0.80, respectively). AI assistance significantly reduced reading time for both readers (median within-patient reduction 0.9 and 1.0 min; p < 0.001), independently of baseline T2 lesion volume. Against an AI-blinded consensus reference standard, AI assistance was associated with higher diagnostic performance of both readers, irrespective of experience, and significantly reduced reading time, supporting its role as a decision-support tool in the longitudinal MRI assessment of MS.

items.title: Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteomics Identifies Candidate Protein Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder with a Diagnostic Specificity Assessment against Schizophrenia.
items.abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined by |log2 fold change| > 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Using these criteria, we identified 358 DEPs (235 upregulated, 123 downregulated), which were enriched in complement activation, coagulation, and immune-inflammatory pathways. However, several of the most significant DEPs are abundant circulating plasma proteins that are common co-isolates of serum EVs, so part of this signal may reflect residual soluble serum protein, and-given that EVs were isolated from serum rather than platelet-poor plasma-the pathway enrichment should be interpreted with caution. In the validation cohort, EV-associated TNC and APLP1 were elevated and EV-associated TF was reduced in MDD relative to HCs (P < 0.05), whereas only serum APLP1 was elevated. Notably, EV-associated TNC was also elevated in SCZ, while APLP1 and TF were unchanged; moreover, direct MDD-versus-SCZ comparisons were not significant, indicating that the data do not support MDD-specific alterations. In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. Nevertheless, the panel remains exploratory and requires validation in larger, multi-center cohorts with diverse psychiatric controls.

items.title: Repeated enrichment of hexyl acetate in coreid bugs sympatric with weaver ants.
items.abstract: Predator-prey interactions are important potential drivers of chemical defense evolution, but how specific predators shape defensive composition remains unclear. Weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) exert strong predation pressure on arboreal insects, offering a model to test links between sympatry and chemical defense variation. Integrating distribution, chemical, and phylogenetic data for 45 coreid bug species, we show that coreids share a conserved chemical repertoire (aldehydes, alcohols, acids, esters), with no overall difference in major compound classes between sympatric and allopatric species. However, sympatric lineages exhibit a significantly higher occurrence frequency of hexyl acetate, with its occurrence distributed across multiple phylogenetic lineages. Bioassays revealed that the four tested esters showed measurable contact toxicity and repellency against O. smaragdina workers, whereas the tested aldehydes and alcohols showed weaker or contrasting effects, with hexyl acetate being particularly notable for its behavioral potency. In contrast, acetic acid and hexanol exhibited marked attractiveness to the ants. This functional reversal highlights the impact of functional group differences on biological activity. Our results are consistent with an association between sympatry and differences in the occurrence of specific compounds within a shared chemical repertoire, rather than gain or loss of compound classes. The association of hexyl acetate with sympatric lineages, together with its strong olfactory and behavioral effects on weaver ants, identifies it as a candidate compound for predator-associated chemical defense. However, whether predator-mediated selection contributed to its repeated occurrence remains unresolved.

items.title: Integrating asymmetry, geography and timescale analyses to uncover fish population synchrony patterns in a tropical reservoir.
items.abstract: Spatial population synchrony, broadly defined as the correlated temporal dynamics of a population metric (e.g. abundance, biomass or growth rates) across sampled areas, is a central theme in ecology. Here, we investigated spatial synchrony in the abundance of 38 fish species from the Jirau Reservoir, a large impoundment in the Amazonian basin, over a decade. We combined cross-correlation at zero lag, tail dependence, synchrony networks, species traits and wavelets to investigate asymmetry, geography and the temporal structure of spatial synchrony. We found that 12 species exhibited significant river-wide synchrony, with no asymmetrical or spatial patterns of within-river synchrony. Water level synchrony, dispersal difficulty and density dependence explained little of the variation in within-river synchrony. However, wavelet analyses showed that the strength of river-wide synchrony varied across temporal scales, and some species also shifted in the dominant timescale of synchrony over time. Furthermore, key species traits such as migratory strategy, body size and trophic level were not significantly correlated with river-wide synchrony levels. These findings underscore the necessity of using multifaceted analytical approaches to understand and manage fish populations in human-altered aquatic ecosystems, where local factors may override broad-scale drivers.

items.title: Epigenetic programming of immune cells: unleashing anti-tumor potential and clinical perspectives.
items.abstract: Immune cell plasticity is a defining feature of tumor immunity and is increasingly recognized as being governed by epigenetic regulation. Advances in single-cell and spatial multi-omics have uncovered an epigenetic checkpoint that integrates environmental cues within the tumor microenvironment (TME) to shape immune cell fate and function. In this review, we synthesize recent evidence supporting three interconnected paradigms of epigenetic control in tumor immunity from the perspective of immune cell heterogeneity, ecology, and state transitions. First, dynamic chromatin remodeling programs myeloid cell polarization and functional diversification. Second, epitranscriptomic regulation constrains T and B cell states, contributing to immune dysfunction and exhaustion. Third, spatially resolved epigenetic remodeling influences immune cell trafficking, positioning, and retention within tumors. Collectively, these mechanisms establish durable immune states that reinforce TME-driven immunosuppression. We further highlight emerging pharmacological strategies targeting epigenetic regulators to reprogram immune cell function and enhance anti-tumor immunity. This framework provides a foundation for leveraging epigenetic plasticity to improve the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: A hidden trigger of near-road microplastic release from asphalt surfaces: Low-frequency vibration from vehicle motion lowers the detachment threshold of tyre wear particles.
items.abstract: Tyre and road wear particles (TRWPs) are an important component of road dust and a major source of microplastic (MP) pollution. The mechanisms controlling their release from road surfaces are multifactorial with complicated interactions, and remain subject to field experimental and modelling investigation. Unlike most detachment studies, which treat surfaces as static, real pavements are repeatedly exposed to vibration from passing vehicles. Here, we developed a field-informed wind-tunnel approach using pristine car tyre wear particles (TWPs) as a well characterized and thus reproducible proxy for traffic-derived MPs. These particles were generated through vehicle motion on a laboratory test stand supplied by Continental Reifen Deutschland GmbH. The particles were deposited on asphalt that was thinly spray-coated white to allow optical detection. We investigated whether traffic-mimicking vibration lowers the threshold windspeed (u ∗ th ) of TWPs on asphalt. For the tested TWPs (80-300 μm), vibration increased the detached fraction and reduced the threshold windspeed across the field-relevant frequency range (5-30 Hz). Without vibration, asphalt retained most particles with only 19% detached at a u ∗ th of 0.39 ms -1 . Under the field-informed vibration scenario, the detached fraction increased to 41%. At the highest tested intensity, it reached 86%, while the u ∗ th decreased by 26% down to 0.29 ms -1 Particle size and shape also modulate detachment. Among the two size cohorts tested, vibration preferentially lowered the thresholds of smaller TWPs (80-135 μm), with more rounded particles being more readily mobilized than irregular ones. Our experiments demonstrate that pavement vibration can reduce the aerodynamic forcing needed to release TWPs retained on asphalt. This previously hidden mechanism increases their susceptibility to mobilization and has implications for the potential short-range transport and redistribution of near-road TRWPs into adjacent environmental compartments.

items.title: Alpine meadow degradation reshapes soil trace element-microbe relationships in community structure and functional potential.
items.abstract: Trace elements are closely linked to soil microbial communities and biogeochemical functions, yet how these relationships change during ecosystem degradation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how alpine meadow degradation reshapes relationships between soil trace elements and microbial community structure and functional potential in the Sanjiangyuan region of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Total and available concentrations of Fe, Al, Mn, Cu, Zn, Co and Ni were measured across degradation stages and related to bacterial and fungal community composition, microbial co-occurrence networks, and functional genes involved in C, N, P and S cycling. Degradation reorganised trace element-microbe relationships in a strongly stage-dependent manner. In lightly degraded meadows, trace elements were broadly associated with microbial abundance, community composition and network topology. As degradation intensified, these associations became more selective, with persistent relationships in highly degraded soils more frequently involving available than total trace elements. Bacterial and fungal communities showed stage-dependent compositional and network changes. Degradation also altered the coupling between trace elements and microbial nutrient-cycling genes. Associations with C- and N-cycle genes were strongest under light degradation and weakened thereafter, whereas P-cycle genes showed the greatest number of trace element associations under high degradation. Overall, alpine meadow degradation reorganised the ecological and functional linkages between trace elements and soil microorganisms in a stage- and element-form-dependent manner. These findings highlight the ecological relevance of trace element availability within the broader soil environmental context and provide new insight into belowground microbial functional potential during alpine meadow degradation.

items.title: Contrasting physiological and rhizosphere responses of wheat to benzotriazole UV stabilizers and phthalate esters.
items.abstract: The pervasive presence of plastic additives in agricultural soils poses emerging threats to crop productivity and rhizosphere ecology. However, comparative evidence linking plant physiological responses with rhizosphere biochemical and microbial changes across chemically distinct plastic additives remains limited. This study investigated the physiological, metabolic, and microbial responses of wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) to UV-328, UV-P, DBP, and DEHP at nominal concentrations of 0.1-1 mg/kg over a 30-day cultivation period. The four plastic additives induced distinct physiological and morphological responses in wheat roots. UV-328 generally caused pronounced root growth inhibition, ultrastructural alterations, and oxidative stress, whereas the relative effects of UV-P, DBP, and DEHP varied across the measured endpoints. These findings highlight the compound-specific and endpoint-dependent nature of phytotoxic responses to chemically distinct plastic additives. Root-exudate metabolomics revealed altered metabolic profiles, with glycerol and malic acid reaching 7.3- and 6.9-fold the control levels, respectively, under the highest UV-328 treatment. Metabolic pathway enrichment identified shared associations with tyrosine metabolism, glycerolipid metabolism, and isoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis. At 1 mg/kg, rhizosphere urease and sucrase activities were 1.25-1.42 and 2.72-8.64 times the control levels, respectively, indicating higher potential hydrolytic activity under the stressed conditions. In parallel, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed shifts in rhizosphere bacterial community composition and diversity. Correlation analyses further identified associations among root-exudate metabolites, soil enzyme activities, bacterial community characteristics, and plant antioxidant responses, suggesting interconnected physiological and rhizosphere responses to plastic additive exposure. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct physiological and rhizosphere responses of wheat to BUVSs and PAEs, highlighting potential associations among plant oxidative stress, metabolic alterations, and rhizosphere microbial community restructuring. These results provide insights into the ecotoxicological effects of chemically distinct plastic additives in agricultural soil-plant systems.

items.title: Species-specific responses and mixed-cultivation buffering of emergent macrophytes exposed to combined pollution of size-fractionated polyethylene terephthalate microplastics and sulfamethoxazole.
items.abstract: The co-occurrence of microplastics (MPs) and antibiotics is widespread in freshwater environments, yet their combined effects on emergent macrophytes remain unclear. A 42-day high-exposure pot experiment was conducted to evaluate the species-specific responses of Iris pseudacorus L. and Iris sibirica L. grown in monoculture or mixed cultivation and exposed to polyethylene terephthalate microplastics (PET MPs; 30 and 300 µm, at 1 g/kg soil) and sulfamethoxazole (SMX; 20 mg/kg soil), alone or in combination. SMX was the dominant toxic factor; PET MPs alone exerted weaker effects, with clear size-fraction differences; 300 µm particles generally produced stronger inhibition. I. pseudacorus maintained higher growth, biomass, and photosynthetic pigment contents, whereas I. sibirica exhibited greater oxidative stress and stronger antioxidant and osmotic responses. At these stress-test concentrations, combined PET MP-SMX exposure showed Abbott-model antagonism (RI = 0.67-0.75). Mixed cultivation generally increased biomass and photosynthetic performance, reduced oxidative damage, and partially alleviated soil nutrient imbalance, indicating preliminary species-level buffering. These findings identify species-specific response patterns and suggest that mixed cultivation may buffer combined MP-SMX stress, warranting further tests under environmentally relevant conditions in constructed wetlands.

items.title: A review of hydrological alteration assessment: refinements to indicators, reference conditions, and alteration-judgment methods since IHA-RVA.
items.abstract: The Indicators of Hydrologic Alteration (IHA) and the Range of Variability Approach (RVA) have served as the operational basis of hydrological alteration assessment for three decades. Later studies have refined three key assessment steps, namely indicators of river conditions, reference conditions for post-impact flows, and judgment rules that translate hydrological departures into alteration magnitudes. From 483 publications screened under the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, we trace the original setup, the limitations that motivated refinements, and the resulting insights, and make explicit the underlying assumptions. Indicator libraries have expanded from the 32 original IHA parameters to more than 170 metrics, and their ecological validity depends on coverage of the flow attributes and time scales governing habitat, life cycles, and channel geomorphology. Reference-condition techniques have advanced through record extension, control-impact designs, process-based and data-driven simulation, and time-varying modeling. Alteration-judgment workflows have evolved from in-range year counting toward distribution-aware metrics, significance testing, multi-metric aggregation, and ecology-grounded benchmarks. Target ranges, classification thresholds, and weighting schemes remain value-loaded choices seldom calibrated against ecological responses, so one flow record can yield divergent estimates under different conventions. Because the steps were refined largely independently, nine implicit assumptions (four for indicators, four for reference conditions, one for judgment) govern the cross-study comparability of reported magnitudes. Non-perennial, ice-affected, and tidal rivers violate several assumptions at once. We formulate reporting requirements and an assessment framework that tailors indicator selection, reference construction, and alteration judgment to hydrological processes, observational constraints, and ecological evidence.

items.title: Habitat selection differs between social and solitary foraging in a wide-ranging seabird.
items.abstract: Prey detection is driven by both environmental and social cues, but synergistic effects of these two processes are poorly studied. For example, foraging conditions may vary depending on the presence/absence of other animals with consequences for understanding habitat suitability and changing population size. Seabirds feed on prey patches structured by physical and biological oceanography, foraging alone or in groups. However, it is unclear whether habitat selection varies with the degree of sociality. Here, we use co-deployed bird-borne cameras and GPS loggers to quantify foraging habitat choice and determine how it varies under different social conditions for breeding Northern gannets Morus bassanus. Resource selection functions revealed dive bouts were associated with (a) distance to colony, (b) water depth, (c) fishing effort and (d) distance to fronts. However, the strength and direction of these relationships varied with gregariousness: (1) solitary dives occurred away from areas of high apparent fishing effort and ocean fronts, (2) social natural dives occurred in shallow water away from ocean fronts and (3) scavenging was highly localised in deep-water zones, and strongly correlated with remotely-sensed fishing effort. Our work shows how habitat selection varies with social context and how foraging at fisheries may uncouple scavengers from natural environmental cues. These findings also demonstrate that habitat selection plays a key role in shaping social organization in mobile marine predators and highlight the importance of considering environmental context when linking movement ecology and social behaviour.

items.title: Emotion regulation diversity and recovery from negative emotions: the moderating role of negative emotion differentiation.
items.abstract: Emotion regulation (ER) diversity, the variety and balance of strategies used, is often considered adaptive, yet findings have been inconsistent. This study examined whether ER diversity predicts recovery from negative emotions in daily life, and whether negative emotion differentiation (NED), the ability to distinguish between negative emotional states, moderates this relationship. Sixty-four participants completed ecological momentary assessments five times daily for one week (1,458 observations). Emotional recovery was operationalised as the percentage decrease in negative affect from the worst state since the previous prompt to the current one. Multilevel models examined within-person associations of momentary NED and ER diversity with emotional recovery. Participants recovered better during moments of higher NED and worse during moments of greater ER diversity. The negative association between ER diversity and recovery was weaker when NED was higher. When recovery was operationalised as current negative affect controlling for worst negative affect, the ER diversity association replicated, but the NED association and interaction did not. These findings suggest that ER diversity is not inherently beneficial in daily life and that NED may buffer its costs, though this depended on how recovery was operationalised. Understanding when diverse regulation helps or hinders recovery requires attention to momentary emotional processes.

items.title: Initial investigation of pain intensity and interference in children and adolescents seeking weight management treatment: a secondary analysis of data from the Stay in Treatment (SIT) study.
items.abstract: Chronic pain and obesity commonly co-occur in children and adolescents; however, few studies have investigated pain characteristics (e.g., intensity, interference) in youth seeking obesity treatment. We conducted a secondary analysis of baseline data from an observational study examining predictors of attrition from pediatric weight management treatment at four sites across the United States (i.e., the Stay in Treatment study). Youth with obesity (N = 437, 52.0% female, 45.5% White, 30.0% Black, and 22.2% identifying as Hispanic or Latino) completed PROMIS® measures assessing pain intensity and interference as well as aspects of social-emotional and physical functioning. Results indicated that pain intensity across the sample was in the mild range (M = 2.5, SD = 2.4), and 31.6% (n = 138) reported no pain. However, approximately one-third reported moderate (26.5%, n = 116) or severe (6.0%, n = 26) pain intensity, and 39.8% reported pain interference in a moderate or severe range based on published cut-offs in youth with chronic pain. Pain intensity and interference were significantly associated with anxiety and depressive symptoms, fatigue, mobility issues, and peer relationship challenges. These findings suggest that a considerable proportion of youth seeking obesity treatment experience clinically significant pain. Findings may inform screening, referral, and intervention efforts for pain concerns in pediatric weight management settings.

items.title: From Depression to Expression: A Community Expressive Arts Program for Alleviating Depressive Symptoms in Community-Dwelling Older Adults.
items.abstract: Background and objectives Growing evidence supports the use of arts to improve older adults' psychosocial and spiritual well-being. This study evaluated the effects of an expressive arts-based intervention (EABI) under the train-the-trainer program on depressive symptoms, spiritual well-being, and quality of life of older adults in Hong Kong. Research design and methods In a mixed-methods design, 84 healthcare workers in Hong Kong completed the train-the-trainer program as ambassadors and delivered the 8-week EABI to 915 older adults with mild to moderate depressive symptoms. Older adults completed validated measures of depression, spirituality, and quality of life (QoL) before and after EABI. Ten ambassadors and 34 older adults participated in focus groups. The EABI effects were analyzed by paired sample t-tests and multilevel modeling evaluated the associations between ambassadors' and older adults' changes. Results Ambassadors showed increased self-efficacy (d = 0.53) and older adults showed substantial declines in depressive symptoms (d = 0.91) and significant improvements in spiritual well-being, overall QoL, and QoL subscales (d = 0.18-0.45). Changes in ambassadors' self-efficacy showed significant indirect effects on older adults' depressive symptoms (αβ = -0.23, 95% CI: -0.46, -0.01) and overall QoL (αβ = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.52) via changes in spiritual well-being. Thematic analysis indicated improved psychosocial well-being among older adults and enhanced knowledge and service-delivery skills among ambassadors. Discussion and implications The EABI showed preliminary benefits on healthcare workers' self-efficacy and older adults' psychosocial well-being. The findings provide initial support on using EABI in geriatric care via a train-the-trainer framework.

items.title: Clinical and radiographic outcomes of SpineJack mechanical kyphoplasty versus conservative management in traumatic thoraco-lumbar compression fractures.
items.abstract: Study design Prospective, comparative, observational cohort study. Objective To compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of SpineJack mechanical kyphoplasty versus conservative management in neurologically intact patients with traumatic thoraco-lumbar compression fractures (AO type A). Background Thoraco-lumbar compression fractures can be managed conservatively, with prolonged bed rest and rigid orthoses; with minimally invasive techniques originally developed for osteoporotic fractures, such as vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty; or with open or percutaneous pedicle screw fixation. Methods A total of 246 consecutive patients with a Magerl type A thoraco-lumbar fracture were included in this non-randomized prospective study between January 2018 and December 2023. After counseling, 124 patients elected Group A (conservative management: bed rest and a three-point brace) and 122 elected Group B (percutaneous kyphoplasty with SpineJack). At the final 12-month follow-up, 104 patients in Group A and 100 patients in Group B were evaluated, with a total of 42 patients lost to follow-up. The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) were used to assess clinical outcome. Radiographic outcome was assessed by measuring the vertebral height loss rate (HLR) and regional kyphosis angle (RKA). Patients were followed up at 1, 6, and 12 months. Results Pain relief and recovery of functional ability were significantly better in Group B. Radiographic metrics showed a better outcome in the surgical group. Conclusions Mechanical kyphoplasty with the SpineJack system is a safe and effective treatment for post-traumatic compression fractures, providing a significant improvement in pain, disability, and radiographic morphometric parameters that is maintained at long-term follow-up.

items.title: Is Leadership Shared Across Cultures? Evidence from Social Network Analyses of 164 Football Teams in Eight Countries.
items.abstract: Shared leadership, where multiple team members take on leadership roles rather than relying on a single formal leader, has been shown to benefit sport teams. However, we know little about whether shared leadership is prevalent cross-culturally. In particular, it has been suggested that shared leadership may be less prevalent in cultures where hierarchical differences in power and authority are more widely accepted (i.e., cultures with higher power distance). To investigate this, we examined whether leadership structures varied as a function of country- and team-level power distance in 164 football (or soccer) teams across eight countries (N = 2,807 players and coaches). Contrary to theoretical expectations, we found that shared leadership was not only present across different levels of power distance but also tended to be more prevalent where power distance was higher. These findings challenge the view that shared leadership is incompatible with high power distance but merit further investigation.

items.title: Nonverbal reasoning in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy: associations with gross motor function, MRI, and EEG findings.
items.abstract: To examine the association between gross motor function level and Raven's Colored Progressive Matrices (CPM) performance in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy (CP), compare CPM performance with typically developing participants, and explore associations with MRI and EEG findings. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 40 participants with CP and 20 comparison participants aged 10-17 years. CPM totals were converted to center-derived age-referenced scores; the upper available normative age band was applied above age 11.5 years. Gross motor function was classified with the GMFCS. Clinically indicated MRI and EEG findings were categorized using prespecified systems. Median CPM score was 72 (IQR 64-81) in the CP group and 98 (IQR 92-104) in the comparison group (adjusted difference -26.4, 95% CI -31.2 to -21.6). GMFCS level was inversely associated with CPM score (Spearman rho = -.78, 95% CI -.85 to -.68). Predominant white matter injury was associated with lower CPM scores. The adjusted association with epileptiform EEG abnormalities was inconclusive. CPM performance was associated with GMFCS level and MRI pattern, but the cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Gross motor classification must not substitute for accessible neuropsychological assessment.

items.title: Comparing the Validity of Commonly Used Risk Assessment Tools in Men With Dual Histories of IPV and Sexual Offending.
items.abstract: Individuals with dual histories of sexual and intimate partner violence (IPV) offending represent a complex subgroup, yet little is known about how well offence-specific risk assessment tools work for them. This field validity study compared the discrimination of an IPV risk tool (Spousal Assault Risk Assessment-Version 2; SARA-V2) with two sexual offending risk tools (Static-99R and STABLE-2007, as well as their combined risk level) in 467 men in British Columbia with dual sexual-IPV offending histories. The sexual offending measures predicted sexual recidivism with small to moderate effects, IPV recidivism with small effects, and violent recidivism with small to moderate effects. SARA-V2 total scores predicted IPV and violent recidivism with small effects but failed to predict sexual recidivism. Confidence intervals for all effects overlapped, indicating the measures had comparable discrimination. The Static-99R and Static/STABLE were the most broadly relevant in incremental validity analyses, predicting all three outcomes over and above the SARA-V2, while results for the STABLE-2007 were mixed. The SARA-V2 added predictive value to the Static-99R and STABLE-2007 for IPV and violent recidivism and to the Static/STABLE for violent recidivism. Given the SARA-V2's risk management benefits, our findings support using the Static-99R or Static/STABLE alongside the SARA-V2 for dual sexual-IPV offending subgroups.
